title: PUL101 Introduction to Nigerian Legal Method

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: John Austin defined law as "a command set by a superior being to inferior beings and enforced by sanctions." Which school of thought does this definition represent?

options.a: The Historical School
options.b: The Natural Law School
options.c: The Positivist (Analytical) School
options.d: The Sociological School

questions.explanation: This is Austin's command theory, the classic positivist view: law is whatever the sovereign lays down and backs with a sanction, whether or not it is moral. Option B is wrong because natural lawyers test law against morality and right reason. Option A looks to the customs and spirit of the people, and Option D looks to how law actually works in society.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an element of Austin's definition of law?

options.a: The subjects are in the habit of obeying the sovereign because of his power to impose sanctions
options.b: A law is valid only if it agrees with morality
options.c: There must be a definite sovereign
options.d: The sovereign is not under any legal limitation

questions.explanation: Austin deliberately separated law from morality, so a moral test of validity is no part of his definition. His elements are a definite sovereign (Option C), a sovereign who is legally unlimited, the 'uncommanded commander' (Option D), and habitual obedience by subjects backed by sanctions (Option A).

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which jurist propounded the Pure Theory of Law, which sees law as a hierarchy of norms whose validity is traced back to a basic norm called the grundnorm?

options.a: Hans Kelsen
options.b: Friedrich Carl von Savigny
options.c: Jeremy Bentham
options.d: Eugen Ehrlich

questions.explanation: Kelsen described law as a system of norms, each valid because a higher norm created it, until you reach the grundnorm, which is not itself created by any norm. Option B founded the Historical School, Option D is known for the sociological idea of 'living law', and Option C founded the Utilitarian School.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: According to the Historical School associated with Savigny, for a law to be valid it must accord with

options.a: the command of a sovereign backed by sanctions
options.b: the volksgeist, that is, the spirit, history and customs of the people
options.c: principles of right reason that are the same everywhere
options.d: what the courts will actually decide in a given case

questions.explanation: Savigny taught that every people has a national spirit (volksgeist) and that law should grow out of their history and customs, so laws imposed against it will be ignored or evaded. Option A is the positivist command theory. Option C is the natural law view, which the Historical School was developed to counter, and Option D is the realist view.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which jurist said that "the centre of gravity of legal development lies not in legislation nor juristic science nor in judicial decisions but the society itself"?

options.a: Eugen Ehrlich
options.b: Hans Kelsen
options.c: John Austin
options.d: Thomas Aquinas

questions.explanation: Ehrlich, a leading European sociological jurist, argued that the 'living law' is found in how people actually behave, so you cannot know a society's law just by reading statutes and cases. Option C and Option B both focus on formally laid down rules, and Option D is a natural law thinker.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Roscoe Pound's sociological theory of law is built mainly on the idea that law should

options.a: be understood as a system of norms traceable to a grundnorm
options.b: restate the customs that have evolved in a society over time
options.c: balance competing claims and interests in society in a way that causes the least friction or harm
options.d: be obeyed only if it agrees with divine or moral principles

questions.explanation: Pound started from the premise that people make competing claims on limited resources, and saw the task of law, especially the courts, as balancing those interests with the least disruption. Option B describes the Historical School, Option D the Natural Law School and Option A Kelsen's Pure Theory.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: The Utilitarian School founded by Jeremy Bentham judges a law mainly by whether it

options.a: was made by a sovereign who is habitually obeyed
options.b: reflects the spirit and customs of the people
options.c: promotes the greatest happiness or good of the greatest number of people
options.d: agrees with the eternal law of God

questions.explanation: For Bentham, the task of law is to promote utility, meaning people's happiness, so a good law produces the greatest good for the greatest number. Option A is Austin's positivist test. Option B is the Historical School's test and Option D reflects the Natural Law School.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: The view that law is simply a prediction of what the courts will do in fact is most closely associated with which school of thought?

options.a: The Historical School
options.b: The Pure Theory of Law
options.c: The Natural Law School
options.d: The Realist School

questions.explanation: American realists such as Oliver Wendell Holmes looked at law from the standpoint of what judges actually decide, not what rules say in books. Option C measures law against morality, Option A looks to custom and the spirit of the people, and Option B looks to a formal hierarchy of norms.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Legal realists such as Jerome Frank argued that judicial decisions are often influenced by

options.a: the volksgeist of the people alone
options.b: eternal principles discoverable only through divine revelation
options.c: a grundnorm that cannot be questioned
options.d: extralegal factors such as the judge's background, personal likes and dislikes and prejudices

questions.explanation: The realists said too much attention was paid to bare legal rules and too little to the human factors in deciding cases, so they wanted judges to become aware of their hidden prejudices. Option A belongs to the Historical School, Option C to Kelsen's Pure Theory, and Option B to religious ideas of law, not realism.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which modern idea has been built most directly on the philosophy of the Natural Law School?

options.a: The grundnorm as the basis of a legal order
options.b: Law as the prediction of court decisions
options.c: The volksgeist as the basis of valid law
options.d: Fundamental human rights and equality of all persons

questions.explanation: Natural law holds that some principles of right and justice exist above man-made law, and this thinking supported human rights, democracy and struggles for independence. Option A comes from Kelsen's Pure Theory, Option C from the Historical School and Option B from the Realist School.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: A major criticism of the Natural Law School, known as the "multiple conscience problem", is that

options.a: different people may hold opposite ideas of what is fair, right or just on the same issue
options.b: it treats any law made by the sovereign as valid however unjust it is
options.c: it focuses only on trial courts and ignores the legislature
options.d: it ignores the customs and history of a people

questions.explanation: Because what is 'right' depends on each person's reason and conscience, two equally sincere people can both claim natural law while acting in opposite ways, which is why the theory has been used to defend very different ideologies. Option B is a criticism of positivism, not natural law. Option D and Option C are not what the multiple conscience problem refers to.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: In Nigeria, a rule of customary law will NOT be applied by the courts if it is

options.a: not separately approved by the National Assembly
options.b: observed by only one ethnic group
options.c: different from the rules of English common law
options.d: repugnant to natural justice, equity and good conscience

questions.explanation: Nigerian courts apply customary law only if it passes certain tests: it must not be repugnant to natural justice, equity and good conscience, not contrary to public policy, and not incompatible with any law in force. Customary law is by nature local, so Option B is no ground for rejection, and Option C and Option A are not tests the courts apply.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which jurist defined law as "a command set by a superior being to inferior beings and enforced by sanctions"?

options.a: Friedrich Carl von Savigny
options.b: Hans Kelsen
options.c: Eugen Ehrlich
options.d: John Austin

questions.explanation: This is the classic command theory of law, in which the superior is the sovereign and the inferiors are the subjects. Austin set it out in The Province of Jurisprudence Determined. Kelsen (B) saw law as a hierarchy of norms, Savigny (A) tied law to the spirit of the people, and Ehrlich (C) located law in the actual conduct of society.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the elements of the Austinian definition of law?

options.a: The subjects are in the habit of obeying the sovereign because of his power to impose sanctions
options.b: The sovereign's commands must agree with the principles of natural justice
options.c: The sovereign is without legal limitation in the exercise of power
options.d: There must be a definite sovereign

questions.explanation: Austin's theory has nothing to say about the moral quality of the sovereign's commands; a command is law simply because the sovereign issued it. The three real elements are a definite sovereign (D), a sovereign who is above the law (C), and habitual obedience by the subjects backed by sanctions (A).

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: In Austin's theory, the phrase "the uncommanded commander" describes

options.a: the basic norm that is presupposed rather than enacted
options.b: a sovereign who is the highest authority and is not subject to the command of anyone else
options.c: the people, from whom every government derives its powers
options.d: a judge who is bound to follow the decisions of higher courts

questions.explanation: For Austin, the sovereign issues commands but receives none; he is above the law and not subject to another's command. Option C reflects popular sovereignty, which is a modern constitutional idea, not Austin's, while A describes Kelsen's grundnorm.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: The fact that the law on wills does not compel anyone to make a will is used to criticise which theory of law?

options.a: The sociological school
options.b: Austin's command theory
options.c: The natural law school
options.d: The historical school

questions.explanation: Austin treated all law as commands couched in 'shall' or 'shall not'. Rules on wills, and the freedom to marry under the Marriage Act or customary law, show that many laws give choices rather than commands. The other schools do not claim that every law is a command, so the example does not attack them.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which Nigerian case is cited to show that even a military government is not above the law, contrary to Austin's idea of a sovereign without legal limitation?

options.a: Holman v Johnson
options.b: Lakanmi v A.G. (Western State)
options.c: Josiah v The State
options.d: Shaw v Director of Public Prosecutions

questions.explanation: In Lakanmi, the Supreme Court declared the Forfeiture of Assets (Validation) Decree No. 45 of 1968 null and void, showing that governmental power must be exercised according to law. Holman v Johnson (A) concerns the territorial limits of law, Shaw v DPP (D) concerns law and public morality, and Josiah v The State (C) concerns justice in criminal trials.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: During a radio phone-in, Kunle says: "The President has the power to introduce a fuel tax, and once he does, nobody can question it." Kunle's statement implicitly reflects which theory of law?

options.a: Austin's command theory
options.b: The natural law school
options.c: The historical school
options.d: The sociological school

questions.explanation: Treating whatever the authorised ruler lays down as binding, without asking whether it is fair, reflects the Austinian command theory. Such philosophies are often implicit: the speaker may never name Austin. A natural lawyer (B) would test the tax against what is just, and the historical school (C) would ask whether it fits the people's customs.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: "Many people do not smoke in public, not because a law forbids it, but because it is not their way of life." Which claim does this observation challenge?

options.a: That the conduct of society determines what the law is
options.b: That every legal norm draws its validity from a higher norm
options.c: That law must reflect the customs and history of the people
options.d: That people obey the law mainly because they fear the sovereign's sanction

questions.explanation: Austin assumed that people obey law because of fear of sanction, but many obey because the law agrees with their beliefs or normal way of life. The other options are the central ideas of the historical school (C), Kelsen's pure theory (B) and Ehrlich's sociological view (A), which the smoking example does not attack.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which jurist defined law as the union of primary rules of obligation and secondary rules of recognition?

options.a: John Austin
options.b: H.L.A. Hart
options.c: Roscoe Pound
options.d: Jeremy Bentham

questions.explanation: Hart moved beyond Austin's commands by showing that law is a system of two kinds of rules: primary rules that tell people what to do, and secondary rules that govern how laws are made, changed or recognised. Austin (A) relied on commands and sanctions alone, Pound (C) saw law as social engineering, and Bentham (D) judged law by utility.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: The constitutional rules that set out how a bill passes through the National Assembly and becomes an Act would, in Hart's terms, be classified as

options.a: the grundnorm
options.b: living law
options.c: secondary rules
options.d: primary rules of obligation

questions.explanation: Secondary rules tell us how laws are made, changed or recognised, such as a constitution or legislative process. Primary rules (D) directly tell people what they must or must not do, such as 'do not steal'. The grundnorm (A) belongs to Kelsen's theory and living law (B) to Ehrlich's.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: In Kelsen's pure theory of law, the ultimate norm from which all other norms derive their validity, but whose own validity cannot be traced to any other norm, is called the

options.a: rule of recognition
options.b: living law
options.c: volksgeist
options.d: grundnorm

questions.explanation: Kelsen saw law as a hierarchy of norms in which each norm is valid because a higher norm authorised it, until we reach the grundnorm, which is presupposed rather than enacted. The volksgeist (C) is Savigny's spirit of the people, the rule of recognition (A) is Hart's idea, and living law (B) is Ehrlich's.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: A student argues: "The rule against murder is valid because it is in the Criminal Code; the Code is valid because the legislature enacted it; the legislature is valid because the Constitution set it up." This chain of reasoning reflects

options.a: the utilitarian school
options.b: the realist school
options.c: the historical school
options.d: Kelsen's pure theory of law

questions.explanation: Tracing the validity of each rule to a higher norm, step by step up to the Constitution, is the hierarchy of norms at the heart of the pure theory. The historical school (C) tests law against custom, realists (B) look at what courts actually do, and utilitarians (A) judge law by its consequences for happiness.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which of the following is a criticism directed specifically at Kelsen's pure theory of law?

options.a: It stresses the formal validity of law rather than its content and effects in society
options.b: Different people have different consciences about what is just
options.c: It focuses on the courts and neglects the legislature
options.d: It assumes that customary rules are always rational and fair

questions.explanation: Because the pure theory asks only whether a rule was created by a higher norm, it ignores whether the rule is just, moral or useful, and may serve dictators. The multiple conscience problem (B) is a weakness of natural law, neglect of the legislature (C) is a weakness of the functional school, and assuming customs are fair (D) is a weakness of the historical school.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Soldiers overthrow an elected government, suspend parts of the Constitution and rule by decree, and the coup succeeds. Which criticism of the pure theory of law does this illustrate?

options.a: Law should be a restatement of the people's customs
options.b: Judges are influenced by their social background
options.c: Validity then depends on the effectiveness of the new legal order
options.d: Law is not always couched in commanding language

questions.explanation: Once the old grundnorm stops commanding effectiveness, it is no longer the basis of the legal order, so validity follows whoever is effectively in control. Had the coup failed, the plotters could have faced trial for treason. Option D attacks Austin, B is a realist insight, and A is the historical school's view.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a claim of Kelsen's pure theory of law?

options.a: The moral quality of a legal rule is irrelevant to its validity
options.b: A grossly unjust rule is not law at all and need not be obeyed
options.c: Law should be studied as a self-contained system separate from morality and politics
options.d: Each norm derives its validity from a superior norm

questions.explanation: The idea that an unjust rule is not true law belongs to the natural law school, which Kelsen rejected. Kelsen wanted a 'pure' study of law free from morality (C), held that a rule's moral quality does not affect its validity (A), and arranged norms in a hierarchy (D).

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which of the following thinkers is named as a chief protagonist of the natural law school?

options.a: Eugen Ehrlich
options.b: Savigny
options.c: Karl Llewellyn
options.d: Grotius

questions.explanation: Zeno, Thomas Aquinas and Grotius are the chief protagonists of natural law, which holds that there are objective principles of what is fair, just or right. Savigny (B) led the historical school, Ehrlich (A) was a sociological jurist, and Llewellyn (C) was an American realist.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: The school of thought which holds that there are objective principles in every person, whatever their race or colour, telling them what is fair, just or right, and against which man-made laws can be tested, is the

options.a: natural law school
options.b: realist school
options.c: historical school
options.d: positivist school

questions.explanation: Reduced to its simplest terms, natural law means what is fair, just or right, and it serves as a test for the validity of man-made law. Positivists (D) separate law from morality, the historical school (C) roots law in custom, and realists (B) look at what courts actually do.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Ten people from different countries are placed in separate rooms and each is asked, in a language he understands, whether stealing is good. Most say no. This illustration is used to support

options.a: the realist school
options.b: the consensus model of law
options.c: the natural law school
options.d: Kelsen's pure theory of law

questions.explanation: The point is that people everywhere share certain principles of right and wrong that exist apart from any human enactment, which is the natural law position. The pure theory (D) ignores morality, realists (A) focus on judicial behaviour, and the consensus model (B) is a theory of the functions of law, not of what law is.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Youth groups in an oil-producing community demand a fairer share of oil revenue, arguing that it is simply unjust for the area that produces the wealth to remain poor, whatever the current law says. Their argument draws mainly on

options.a: natural law
options.b: the functional school
options.c: the pure theory of law
options.d: the command theory

questions.explanation: Appealing to what is just or right as a standard above existing law is natural law reasoning; it has been invoked in independence struggles and in the Niger Delta's call for resource control. The command theory (D) and pure theory (C) would accept the current law as valid, and the functional school (B) would wait to see what the courts decide.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: The "multiple conscience problem" is a weakness of the natural law school. It refers to the fact that

options.a: a sovereign can never be found who is above the law
options.b: judges are unconsciously prejudiced by their backgrounds
options.c: customs differ from one ethnic group to another
options.d: people may hold different ideas of what is just on the same issue

questions.explanation: Two equally devout people can both claim to act according to natural law while acting in opposite ways, so natural law has been used to defend almost every ideology. Option A is a criticism of Austin, C relates to the historical school, and B is the realists' observation about judges.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which of the following statements about natural law is correct?

options.a: It focuses mainly on what is actually done rather than what ought to be done
options.b: It holds that law is valid only if it reflects the people's customs
options.c: Courts in practice enforce natural law in preference to statutes
options.d: Unless its principles are enacted into law, their violation cannot be legally penalised

questions.explanation: Natural law stresses what ought to be done; in practice, courts interpret and the executive enforces the law found in recognised sources, so a natural law principle carries legal sanction only once enacted. C is the reverse of the position, A inverts natural law's 'ought' focus, and B states the historical school's view.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which thinker defined law as the highest reason, rooted in nature, which commands what must be done and forbids the opposite?

options.a: Cicero
options.b: Aristotle
options.c: John Austin
options.d: Roscoe Pound

questions.explanation: Cicero saw law as universal and moral, rooted in nature and reason rather than created by man, and binding even on rulers. Aristotle (B) described law as 'reason without desire', Austin (C) saw law as the sovereign's command, and Pound (D) saw law as a social institution for satisfying human wants.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: "An ordinance of reason for the common good, made by him who has care of the community." This definition of law is associated with

options.a: Thomas Aquinas
options.b: Eugen Ehrlich
options.c: Oliver Wendell Holmes
options.d: John Austin

questions.explanation: Aquinas, a natural lawyer, held that for a law to be valid it must be just and in line with moral or divine principles. Holmes (C) defined law as a prediction of what courts will do, Austin (D) as a sovereign's command backed by sanctions, and Ehrlich (B) located law in social conduct.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: According to the historical school, the "spirit of the people" that binds a society together and from which its law should flow is called the

options.a: volksgeist
options.b: rule of recognition
options.c: living law
options.d: grundnorm

questions.explanation: Savigny taught that each people has a national spirit, the volksgeist, so a law is valid only if it accords with the people's history and customs. The grundnorm (D) is Kelsen's basic norm, living law (C) is Ehrlich's idea, and the rule of recognition (B) is Hart's.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: The historical school, led by Friedrich Carl von Savigny, was developed mainly to

options.a: support the codification of law by revolutionary governments
options.b: reform trial courts by exposing judges' prejudices
options.c: promote the greatest happiness of the greatest number
options.d: counter natural law ideas used to overthrow European monarchs

questions.explanation: Natural law ideas fuelled the overthrow of monarchs in 17th and 18th century Europe; Savigny, an aristocrat with an interest in the status quo, stressed slow evolution of law through custom instead. Reforming trial courts (B) was the realists' aim, and greatest happiness (C) is the utilitarian goal.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: A state government suddenly bans a burial custom that its people have practised for centuries. Most people ignore the ban or find clever ways around it. Which school would say this outcome was predictable because the law was not in tune with the people's customs?

options.a: The historical school
options.b: The utilitarian school
options.c: Kelsen's pure theory of law
options.d: The positivist school

questions.explanation: The historical school holds that law should be a formal restatement of prevailing customs, and that customs cannot be changed unless the people are in tune with the change; otherwise they circumvent or disregard the law. Positivists (D) and Kelsen (C) would treat the ban as valid simply because it was properly made.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which of the following is a criticism of the historical school?

options.a: It looks only at what courts do and ignores the legislature
options.b: It cannot identify the basic norm of a modern state
options.c: It treats the sovereign as above the law
options.d: It assumes customs are fair, though some prejudice women

questions.explanation: The historical school builds law on custom, but some customary rules have subjected people to servitude or prejudiced women, and following custom dogmatically can block desirable reforms. C criticises Austin, B criticises Kelsen, and A criticises the functional school.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the tests that a rule of customary law must pass to be applied in Nigeria?

options.a: It must not be incompatible with any law for the time being in force
options.b: It must not be repugnant to natural justice, equity and good conscience
options.c: It must have been written down and published by a court
options.d: It must not be contrary to public policy

questions.explanation: Customary law is largely unwritten, and there is no requirement that a court has written it down before it can apply. The three real tests are the repugnancy test (B), the public policy test (D) and the incompatibility test (A).

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: By the "facts of law", Eugen Ehrlich meant

options.a: the facts that a court finds proved at trial
options.b: how people actually behave in society
options.c: the rules set out in statutes and decided cases
options.d: the presupposed norm at the top of the legal order

questions.explanation: Ehrlich taught that law is based on how people act, and that society's conduct determines the rules laid down in formal sources. To know a society's law, you must go into the society and see how it is obeyed, ignored or modified. Statutes and cases (C) are the formal sources he said were not enough.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: A statute forbids extortion, yet some officers at highway checkpoints still openly collect N100 from motorists, and many motorists simply pay. A jurist who says "the real law here is what people actually do, not what the statute says" is applying the ideas of

options.a: Kelsen's pure theory of law
options.b: the natural law school
options.c: Eugen Ehrlich's sociological school
options.d: John Austin's command theory

questions.explanation: Ehrlich used the gap between formal law and conduct to show that society's conduct, the living law, determines what the law really is; if law is at variance with popular conduct, it is doomed as an instrument of social control. Austin (D) and Kelsen (A) would focus on the valid statute, and natural law (B) would ask whether the conduct is just.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Car owners in Abuja register their vehicles and stop at roadblocks only because the law requires them to. This is used to criticise which school?

options.a: The pure theory of law
options.b: The sociological school
options.c: The natural law school
options.d: The positivist school

questions.explanation: Ehrlich claimed that conduct determines law, but here the law is shaping conduct; sometimes the law moves ahead of society to educate it and change behaviour. This weakens the sociological claim. Positivists (D) and Kelsen (A) would happily accept that a valid law changes behaviour, so the example does not attack them.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which jurist, a former Dean of Harvard Law School, saw law as a way of satisfying human wants by balancing competing claims to limited resources with the least harm to established institutions?

options.a: Jerome Frank
options.b: Jeremy Bentham
options.c: Roscoe Pound
options.d: Eugen Ehrlich

questions.explanation: Pound was the greatest exponent of sociological jurisprudence on the western side of the Atlantic, and the courts were the main institutional focus of his balancing theory. Ehrlich (D) was the European sociological jurist of living law, Frank (A) was a realist judge, and Bentham (B) founded utilitarianism.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which of the following is a criticism of Roscoe Pound's balancing theory?

options.a: It treats every law as a command of the sovereign
options.b: It holds that unjust laws need not be obeyed
options.c: It ignores the role of the courts in resolving disputes
options.d: It gives no method for identifying and weighing interests

questions.explanation: Pound's core idea was balancing competing claims, but he did not identify the interests or say how to weigh them, so the same claims might balance differently at different times. A and B belong to Austin and natural law, and C is wrong because the court system was the main focus of Pound's theory.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: The view that government, by making the proper laws, should seek to promote the greatest good of the greatest number of people is the central idea of the

options.a: utilitarian school
options.b: historical school
options.c: realist school
options.d: pure theory of law

questions.explanation: Jeremy Bentham, the chief proponent of utilitarianism, taught that the task of law is to promote communal utility, meaning what affects people's happiness. The historical school (B) looks to custom, realists (C) to judicial behaviour, and the pure theory (D) to the formal validity of norms.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four main utilities identified by Jeremy Bentham?

options.a: Equality
options.b: Security
options.c: Abundance
options.d: Fraternity

questions.explanation: Bentham identified security, equality, liberty and abundance as the main utilities that law should promote. Fraternity is a slogan of the French Revolution, not one of Bentham's utilities. Security (B), equality (A) and abundance (C) are all on his list.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Among his four main utilities, which one did Bentham give the highest priority?

options.a: Abundance
options.b: Liberty
options.c: Equality
options.d: Security

questions.explanation: Bentham ranked security first and liberty second, with equality and abundance last. This explains why utilitarian reasoning accepts limits on individual freedom, such as routine searches, for the sake of the security of the many. Liberty (B) came second, not first.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: At Murtala Muhammed Airport, every passenger is searched before boarding, even without any suspicion. The authorities explain that a little inconvenience to each traveller is worth the greater safety of all. This justification reflects

options.a: the historical school
options.b: the utilitarian school
options.c: the natural law school
options.d: the realist school

questions.explanation: Utilitarians balance individual interest against communal interest; the individual's freedom is sacrificed to achieve the greater goal of security for the greater number. The historical school (A) asks about custom, realists (D) about how judges decide, and natural lawyers (C) about universal right and wrong.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: A major criticism of the utilitarian school is that it

options.a: insists that only customs can become law
options.b: ignores the consequences of laws for society
options.c: cannot locate the grundnorm of a legal system
options.d: does not explain how to balance individual and communal interests

questions.explanation: Utilitarianism requires the law to balance individual interest against the common good, but it does not solve how to strike that balance. B is wrong because utilitarians judge law precisely by its consequences, A describes the historical school, and C is a criticism of Kelsen.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which jurist viewed law from the standpoint of the "bad man", who cares nothing for legal theory and only wants to know what the courts will do?

options.a: Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr.
options.b: Eugen Ehrlich
options.c: Hans Kelsen
options.d: Friedrich Carl von Savigny

questions.explanation: Holmes, the distinguished United States jurist, expressed the pragmatic idea that law is best understood as what courts will actually do in a particular matter. Ehrlich (B) looked to social conduct, Kelsen (C) to a hierarchy of norms, and Savigny (D) to the spirit of the people.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which of the following is a shortcoming of the functional school?

options.a: It assumes all groups in society have equal bargaining power
options.b: It ignores the law-making power of the courts
options.c: It looks at the courts alone and neglects the legislature
options.d: It ties the validity of law to the customs of the people

questions.explanation: The functional school holds that one must wait for a court decision to know the law, which overlooks the legislature and agencies and forgets that courts are themselves created by law. B is the opposite of its view, since it recognises judicial law-making; D is the historical school, and A criticises the pluralist model.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Before his trial at the High Court, a lawyer advises his client, a well-known "area boy", to dress responsibly and not wear dark glasses when giving evidence. The lawyer's advice reflects which theory?

options.a: The historical school
options.b: Kelsen's pure theory of law
options.c: The realist school
options.d: The natural law school

questions.explanation: Realists argued that judges are unconsciously influenced by extralegal factors such as dress, appearance and the personality of the accused, so the judicial process is less objective than it looks in the books. The other schools say nothing about how a party's appearance might sway a judge.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: "Mr. A's case may be weak, but it will make a big difference if a celebrated human rights lawyer defends him and a judge who shares his faith hears it." This statement reflects

options.a: the utilitarian school
options.b: the consensus model
options.c: the positivist school
options.d: the realist school

questions.explanation: Realists focus on the human factors in deciding cases: the personality of the accused and his lawyer, and the judge's background and likes, can matter more than the bare rules. Utilitarians (A) judge law by its effect on happiness, positivists (C) by its source, and the consensus model (B) assumes the law is applied equally to all.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT named as an exponent of American realism?

options.a: Jerome Frank
options.b: Karl Llewellyn
options.c: Friedrich Carl von Savigny
options.d: John Chipman Gray

questions.explanation: Savigny was a German aristocrat who led the historical school. The exponents of American realism include Oliver Wendell Holmes, Justice Jerome Frank (A), John Chipman Gray (D) and Karl Llewellyn (B).

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: One of the main goals of the American realists was to

options.a: replace judges with juries in all criminal trials
options.b: make judges aware of their hidden prejudices
options.c: restore the authority of monarchs over the law
options.d: prove that law is a closed system of logical rules

questions.explanation: Realists studied trial courts and wanted judges to become aware of their latent prejudices, so the system would not favour the 'good boys' against the 'bad boys'. They rejected the idea that law is pure logic (D); for them, the life of the law was experience.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: "Law is the prediction of what the courts will do in fact." This definition reflects which approach to law?

options.a: The natural law approach
options.b: The realist approach
options.c: The historical approach
options.d: The pure theory of law

questions.explanation: Holmes's prediction theory treats law as practical outcomes in court rather than moral ideals or abstract rules. The historical approach (C) looks to custom, natural law (A) to what is just, and the pure theory (D) to the formal validity of norms.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: The story of the blind men who each touched a different part of an elephant is used to show that

options.a: the oldest definition of law is the most accurate
options.b: law can only be understood by those trained as lawyers
options.c: each definition of law is shaped by the perspective of the person defining it
options.d: only judges can give a complete definition of law

questions.explanation: Each blind man described the part he touched, so all were partly correct yet wrong. Jurists do the same: their backgrounds as judges, legislators, academics or clergymen shape their definitions, which is why all definitions are arbitrary and ad hoc. None of the other options draws that lesson.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the theories of law is NOT correct?

options.a: Each theory applies to one particular legal system to the exclusion of all others
options.b: The theories are often implicit rather than explicit
options.c: Virtually all legal systems have applied the theories in varying degrees
options.d: The ideas of one jurist may embrace more than one theory

questions.explanation: Students are warned against thinking each philosophy belongs to one legal system alone; in fact all have been applied in varying degrees by virtually every legal system. It is also true that one jurist's ideas may cut across theories (D) and that people often hold these philosophies without naming them (B).

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which of the following uses the word "law" in its general sense rather than its technical sense?

options.a: The law of demand and supply
options.b: The Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999
options.c: The Companies and Allied Matters Act
options.d: A rule laid down by the Supreme Court in a decided case

questions.explanation: Expressions such as the law of a club, the law of God or the law of demand and supply use 'law' in a general sense. The technical sense covers rules made by bodies with power to make binding rules, such as statutes (C), the Constitution (B) and case law (D).

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Which feature of law is the main factor that distinguishes legal rules from moral or ethical rules?

options.a: Its breach is sanctioned through organised institutions like courts
options.b: Legal rules are found in more than one source
options.c: Legal rules reflect the values of the society
options.d: Legal rules guide people on what they ought or ought not to do

questions.explanation: Moral rules are enforced, if at all, through social disapproval, while legal rules are backed by coercion through organised institutions like the police, courts and prisons. Being normative (D) and reflecting social values (C) are things law shares with moral and religious rules, so they cannot be the distinguishing factor.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: A church in Ibadan requires its members to fast every Wednesday and suspends those who refuse. In the technical sense, this rule is not law mainly because

options.a: it is not traceable to the Constitution, statutes or case law
options.b: it has a sanction attached to breaking it
options.c: it applies to only some people in the city
options.d: it is not written down in any document

questions.explanation: Law in the technical sense is man-made by bodies vested with power to make binding rules for the state; religious or moral rules are not law unless traceable to sources like the Constitution, statutes, case law or delegated legislation. Being unwritten (D) does not stop customary law being law, and having a sanction (B) is a feature law shares.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: In an old English case, a seller sold tea in Dunkirk knowing the buyer planned to smuggle it into England. The court allowed the seller to recover the price, because no country takes notice of the revenue laws of another. Which feature of law does this illustrate?

options.a: Element of coercion
options.b: Territorial limitation
options.c: Normative character
options.d: Dynamic nature

questions.explanation: In Holman v Johnson, the seller had not broken any English law, and enforcing the defence would have given English law extraterritorial effect; laws bind only within their own territory. Dynamic nature (D) is about law changing over time, and normative character (C) is about law guiding conduct.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Musa, a Muslim from Kano, travels to Lagos and drinks beer at a party. He cannot be prosecuted under the Penal Code for that act in Lagos. This illustrates that law

options.a: is a body of rules
options.b: is dynamic in nature
options.c: has territorial limitation
options.d: is man-made

questions.explanation: The Penal Code applies in the North and the Criminal Code in the South, and each covers offences committed within its own territory only. As a general rule, a Muslim from the North would be safe from prosecution for drinking alcohol in the South. The other options are real features of law but are not what the example shows.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Nigerian law under colonial rule differed from the law after independence in 1960, and military-era law differed again from law under elected governments. This illustrates that law is

options.a: territorially limited
options.b: normative
options.c: dynamic
options.d: coercive

questions.explanation: Law changes with prevailing social, political, economic and cultural conditions, so its content shifts from one era to another. Territorial limitation (A) concerns where law applies, not how it changes over time, and normative (B) and coercive (D) describe how law guides and is enforced.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Bisi and Tunde have lived together for ten years and have two children, but they never contracted a valid marriage. The law does not treat them as husband and wife. Which function of law does this illustrate?

options.a: Definition and regulation of social relationships
options.b: Dispute settlement and remedies
options.c: Identification and allocation of official authority
options.d: Change of law

questions.explanation: Law defines which relationships it recognises; a relationship must meet certain essential requirements to be a legal marriage, so prolonged cohabitation alone does not make a couple husband and wife. Allocating authority (C) concerns who exercises public power, and dispute settlement (B) concerns resolving conflicts.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Sections 4, 5 and 6 of the 1999 Constitution vest legislative, executive and judicial powers in three arms of government. Which function of law do these provisions perform?

options.a: Crime prevention and control
options.b: Dispute settlement and remedies
options.c: Definition and regulation of social relationships
options.d: Identification and allocation of official authority

questions.explanation: The law establishes institutions and vests them with authority to act for the state; each arm must keep within its powers or its action is ultra vires, null and void. Choosing class representatives in a university is a small-scale example of the same function. The other options are different functions of law.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Mr. A is paralysed after being knocked down by a tanker owned by an oil marketing company with which he has no prior relationship. In a modern complex society, his claim is most likely to be settled

options.a: by compromise, because the parties expect a continuing relationship
options.b: by the village elders through ostracism of the company
options.c: on a winner-takes-all basis, aiming to recover as much compensation as possible
options.d: by self-help, with Mr. A seizing the company's property

questions.explanation: In complex societies, many disputes involve parties who have no need to continue their relationship, so settlement tends to be winner-takes-all. Compromise (A) suits small, community-based societies where relations are permanent. Ostracism (B) and self-help (D) belong to early stages of the evolution of law.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: The model that sees law as protecting social values to which everyone in society subscribes, with Parliament representing all and the law equal and just to all, is the

options.a: conflict or pluralist model
options.b: Marxist model
options.c: consensus model
options.d: open model

questions.explanation: Talcott Parsons saw society as basically unitary with a shared value system. Critics reply that no society has a monolithic set of values, and that apparent consensus may be sectional interests presented as everyone's. The pluralist model (A) accepts competing groups, and Marxism (B) sees law as a tool of class domination.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: The conflict (pluralist) model of law has been criticised because it

options.a: denies that any conflict exists in society
options.b: regards the state as an instrument of the ruling class
options.c: assumes the competing groups have roughly equal bargaining power
options.d: insists that only revolution can resolve conflicts

questions.explanation: The pluralist model treats the state as a neutral arbiter between groups of more or less equal power, but dominant groups control economic and political institutions; the Pareto illustration says 10 per cent own 90 per cent of resources. Denying conflict (A) describes the consensus model, and the ruling-class view (B) is Marxist.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Workers and employers in Nigeria keep disagreeing over wages, but they settle their disputes through negotiation, strikes, arbitration, court cases and elections, never by revolution. This picture best matches the

options.a: historical school
options.b: open model
options.c: Marxist model
options.d: consensus model

questions.explanation: The open model sits between consensus and conflict: conflict continues, but it is resolved through legitimate processes such as negotiation, arbitration, judicial decision and electoral battle, backed by strikes but without revolution. The consensus model (D) denies real conflict, and Marxism (C) expects revolutionary confrontation.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: According to Karl Marx, why do many members of the working class accept the domination of a few capitalists?

options.a: The ruling class controls both coercion and the dominant ideas
options.b: The law reflects the spirit of the people
options.c: The state acts as a neutral arbiter between equal groups
options.d: The working class freely agrees with a shared value system

questions.explanation: Marx said the ruling class controls the army, police and law, and also the dominant ideas, so 'the ideas of the ruling class are in every epoch the ruling ideas'. A shared value system (D) is the consensus model, a neutral state (C) is the pluralist model, and the spirit of the people (B) is Savigny's historical school.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: "The suppression of vice is as much the law's business as the suppression of subversive activities." This statement was made by

options.a: Phil Harris
options.b: Viscount Simonds
options.c: Lord Devlin
options.d: Lord Eldon

questions.explanation: Lord Devlin argued that societies disintegrate when no common morality is observed, so society may protect its moral code as it protects its government. Viscount Simonds (B) gave the leading speech in Shaw v DPP, and Phil Harris (A) defined morality as a code of beliefs and standards of behaviour.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: Respect for elders is strictly observed in villages but has become relaxed in big cities like Lagos and Port Harcourt. This contrast illustrates

options.a: the element of coercion in law
options.b: the multiple conscience problem of positivism
options.c: the territorial limitation of law
options.d: the relativity of moral ideas

questions.explanation: Morality is relative: individuals and groups hold different ideas of right and wrong, and as society becomes more diffuse, some moral standards are lowered or abandoned. Respect for elders is a moral standard, not a legal rule, so territorial limitation of law (C) does not fit, and the multiple conscience problem (B) is a weakness of natural law, not positivism.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: In Shaw v Director of Public Prosecutions, Shaw published "The Ladies' Directory" advertising prostitutes. He was convicted of

options.a: treasonable felony
options.b: conspiracy to corrupt public morals
options.c: obtaining by false pretences
options.d: contempt of court

questions.explanation: The House of Lords upheld the conviction, with Viscount Simonds saying the court had a residual power to conserve the moral welfare of the state. What the court objected to was not prostitution itself but its public advertisement. The case shows law being used to protect public morality.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: In Knuller v Director of Public Prosecutions, the House of Lords held that the Sexual Offences Act 1967

options.a: made all private conduct between adults immune from the criminal law
options.b: gave no licence to publicly encourage what it decriminalised in private
options.c: abolished the offence of conspiracy to corrupt public morals
options.d: overruled the decision in Shaw v DPP

questions.explanation: Following Shaw v DPP, the Lords held that although the Act left consenting adults in private alone, it gave no licence to others to encourage the practice through advertisements, so the publishers were convicted. The case applied Shaw (D) rather than overruling it, and the offence (C) survived.

questions.topic: Law in Social Context: Meaning, Definitions and Schools of Thought
questions.question: A properly enacted law requires every resident of a state to pay a levy of N5,000 to fund a project only the rich will use. A strict positivist would most likely say that the levy

options.a: is valid law because it was made by the proper authority, even if it is unjust
options.b: is law only if it reflects long-standing custom
options.c: is not law at all because it offends natural justice
options.d: is law only if the courts decide to enforce it

questions.explanation: For positivists, law's validity depends on its source, not its moral quality, so even unjust laws remain valid if made and enforced by the proper authority. Saying it is not law at all (C) is the natural law view, waiting for the courts (D) is the realist or functional view, and testing it against custom (B) is the historical view.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Louis XIV's famous claim "I am the state" best reflects which idea of the relationship between the ruler and the state?

options.a: The rule of law, where the ruler is subject to the law
options.b: Popular sovereignty, where power belongs to the people
options.c: Separation of powers among three arms of government
options.d: Absolute rule, where the ruler claims all power, often based on divine right

questions.explanation: By saying he was the state, Louis XIV merged the state with his own person, the mark of an absolute ruler whose authority rested on divine right, much like traditional kings seen as second to none. Option B, Option C and Option A are all ideas that developed later precisely to limit that kind of power.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four basic elements of a state?

options.a: A population
options.b: A definite territory
options.c: Sovereignty
options.d: A written constitution

questions.explanation: A state is an organised political community made up of a definite territory, a population, a government and sovereignty. A written constitution is common, but it is not one of these elements of statehood. Option B, Option A and Option C are all listed elements.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Under section 14(2)(a) of the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, sovereignty belongs to

options.a: the National Assembly
options.b: the people of Nigeria, from whom government derives all its powers and authority
options.c: the President as Head of State
options.d: the Supreme Court of Nigeria

questions.explanation: Section 14(2)(a) states that sovereignty belongs to the people of Nigeria, from whom government through the Constitution derives all its powers and authority. The President (Option C), the legislature (Option A) and the courts (Option D) only exercise powers given to them by the people through the Constitution.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Which French writer introduced the doctrine of sovereignty into Western political theory?

options.a: Jean Bodin
options.b: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
options.c: Voltaire
options.d: Montesquieu

questions.explanation: Jean Bodin is credited with introducing the idea of sovereignty, the supreme power within a state, into Western political thought. Option D is famous for separation of powers and Option B for the social contract and the general will. Option C was a writer of the Enlightenment, not the originator of sovereignty theory.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Which of the following theories was NOT developed to curtail the power of rulers?

options.a: The rule of law
options.b: The social contract theories
options.c: Separation of powers
options.d: The divine right of kings

questions.explanation: The divine right of kings justified absolute power by claiming the ruler's authority came from God, so it supported rulers rather than limiting them. Social contract theories (Option B), the rule of law (Option A) and separation of powers (Option C) all grew up to restrain those in authority.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Which thinkers are best known as social contract theorists?

options.a: Thomas Hobbes, John Locke and Jean-Jacques Rousseau
options.b: Savigny, Ehrlich and Roscoe Pound
options.c: John Austin, Hans Kelsen and H.L.A. Hart
options.d: Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jerome Frank and Karl Llewellyn

questions.explanation: Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau each explained the state as arising from an agreement among people, which shapes how we see the ruler's duties to citizens. Option C are positivist thinkers, Option D are American realists, and Option B are associated with the historical and sociological schools.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: A state is an artificial entity and must act through human agents. The structure through which those agents act for the state is called

options.a: the territory
options.b: the government
options.c: the citizenry
options.d: sovereignty

questions.explanation: The government is the machinery for running the state, made up of the legislature, executive and judiciary and their agencies. A state does not stop existing just because its government changes. Option D is the supreme power the state holds, while Option C and Option A are the people and land of the state, not its acting machinery.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Section 1(2) of the 1999 Constitution forbids any person or group from taking control of the government of Nigeria except in accordance with the Constitution. This provision mainly deals with

options.a: the legitimacy of how power over the state is acquired
options.b: the fundamental rights of citizens
options.c: the rules for interpreting statutes
options.d: the sharing of revenue among the states

questions.explanation: Section 1(2) prescribes the only lawful way of gaining control of government, which is why an unsuccessful coup is treated as treason. It is about legitimate access to power, not Option B, which is in Chapter IV, nor Option D or Option C.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: The doctrine of separation of powers, which divides government into legislative, executive and judicial arms, is most famously associated with

options.a: Jean Bodin
options.b: Friedrich Carl von Savigny
options.c: Montesquieu
options.d: Thomas Hobbes

questions.explanation: Montesquieu developed separation of powers, building on John Locke, as a way to stop any one ruler from holding all power. Option A is linked with the idea of sovereignty, Option D argued for a strong sovereign, and Option B founded the Historical School of law.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: The statement that justice is "in the eye of the beholder" is best explained by which observation?

options.a: Justice is only relevant in criminal cases and not in civil cases
options.b: Justice has one fixed meaning that every person agrees on
options.c: Justice is the same thing as whatever the legislature enacts
options.d: What counts as justice depends on the person's position, interests and background, so the winner and loser of the same case may see it differently

questions.explanation: Factors such as home background, education, religion and self-interest shape each person's idea of justice, which is why the party who wins a case says justice was done while the loser speaks of a miscarriage of justice. Option B is the opposite of the statement. Option C confuses law with justice, and Option A is simply untrue.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Who defined justice as "the constant and perpetual will to render to everyone his due"?

options.a: Ulpian, the Roman jurist
options.b: Plato
options.c: Jeremy Bentham
options.d: John Rawls

questions.explanation: This classic Roman definition comes from Ulpian and was adopted in Justinian's Institutes; Aquinas later used very similar words. Option B saw justice as each person doing what he is fitted for. Option D spoke of justice as fairness, and Option C focused on utility rather than defining justice this way.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Which thinker described justice as "the first virtue of social institutions, as truth is of systems of thought" and developed the idea of justice as fairness?

options.a: Aristotle
options.b: John Rawls
options.c: Ulpian
options.d: John Austin

questions.explanation: Rawls treated justice as fairness in how basic rights, opportunities and advantages are distributed in society. Option A is known for dividing justice into corrective and distributive. Option C gave the 'render to everyone his due' definition, and Option D was a positivist who separated law from justice.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: The view that justice is when each person does that for which he or she is fitted or suited is associated with

options.a: Thomas Aquinas
options.b: Plato
options.c: Jeremy Bentham
options.d: John Rawls

questions.explanation: Plato saw a just society as one where each person performs the role he is suited for. Critics point out that this idea can be used to justify rigid systems such as caste or the Osu system. Option D spoke of fairness, Option A of rendering each his due, and Option C of the greatest happiness of the greatest number.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Aristotle classified justice into two types. They are

options.a: formal justice and substantive justice
options.b: corrective justice and distributive justice
options.c: commutative justice and retributive justice
options.d: procedural justice and technical justice

questions.explanation: Aristotle distinguished corrective justice, which rectifies wrongs between two parties, from distributive justice, which shares honours and rewards in society according to desert. Option A is a different modern pairing about how strictly judges apply law. Option D names what is essentially one type twice, and the commutative label in Option C is linked with Aquinas.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: The Federal Character principle in the Nigerian Constitution, which seeks a fair spread of public appointments across the country, is an example of

options.a: commutative justice
options.b: procedural justice
options.c: corrective justice
options.d: distributive justice

questions.explanation: Distributive justice is about how the state shares out benefits, offices and burdens among members of society, which is exactly what Federal Character does. Option C and Option A deal with putting things right or keeping fairness between two individuals, and Option B is about fair process in deciding cases.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: The right to fair hearing guaranteed by section 36 of the 1999 Constitution mainly embodies which type of justice?

options.a: Distributive justice
options.b: Corrective justice
options.c: Procedural justice
options.d: Poetic justice

questions.explanation: Procedural or technical justice is concerned with how a decision is reached: an impartial hearing, a chance to be heard and a fair trial. That is the heart of section 36. Option A concerns sharing resources in society, Option B concerns repairing a wrong between parties, and Option D is a literary idea, not a legal one.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: The theory of justice that requires a judge to apply the law strictly as it is, without regard to extra-legal considerations or the harshness of the result, is called

options.a: distributive justice
options.b: substantive justice
options.c: judicial activism
options.d: formal justice

questions.explanation: Under formal justice, justice is done when a case is decided strictly according to law, which is said to promote certainty and impartiality. Option B lets the judge consider wider factors to avoid absurdity or injustice, and Option C is the name for that liberal approach. Option A is about sharing benefits in society.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: When Nigerian courts insist that "justice should not be sacrificed on the altar of technicalities", as in Chinwendu v. Mbamali, they are promoting

options.a: substantial (substantive) justice
options.b: commutative justice
options.c: technical justice
options.d: formal justice

questions.explanation: Substantial justice looks at whether the outcome is truly fair, so courts prefer to decide cases on their merits rather than dismiss them on a technical slip. Option D and Option C are the strict, rule-bound approaches the courts are warning against, and Option B concerns fairness in dealings between two persons.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: In Josiah v. The State, justice in criminal matters was described as a three-way traffic. The three parties to whom justice is owed are

options.a: the legislature, the executive and the judiciary
options.b: the judge, the prosecutor and defence counsel
options.c: the accused person, the victim and the state (society)
options.d: the plaintiff, the defendant and the witnesses

questions.explanation: Oputa JSC explained that criminal justice must serve the accused, the victim and the society represented by the state, not just one of them. Option B are the people who administer the trial, Option A are the arms of government, and Option D describes parties in a civil case.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: The classical function of any government, often described as the foremost justification for modern government, is to

options.a: guarantee every citizen paid employment
options.b: maintain law and order and protect lives and property
options.c: redistribute wealth equally among all citizens
options.d: promote one official religion

questions.explanation: Maintaining law and order is the first objective of law; its opposite is anarchy and chaos. The other options describe policies some governments may pursue, but they are not the classical function on which modern government is justified.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: During an armed conflict, the warring parties are bound by rules protecting religious houses, children, pregnant women and Red Cross workers. This shows that

options.a: law still sets minimum standards of conduct even in war
options.b: law ceases to operate once war begins
options.c: only domestic law applies during war
options.d: justice is in the eye of the beholder

questions.explanation: Even in war, law plays a basic role in keeping certain minimum standards of behaviour, for example through the Geneva Conventions, which protect civilians, vulnerable groups and relief workers. B is the opposite of the point, and C is wrong because these protections come from international law.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: As distinct from the everyday view that law and justice mean the same thing, justice has been described as

options.a: the punishment of every wrongdoer without trial
options.b: the correct application of a law, as opposed to arbitrariness
options.c: the law of a club or association
options.d: whatever the most powerful person in society decides

questions.explanation: In ordinary speech, law and justice are treated as synonyms, but justice is better seen as applying the law correctly rather than arbitrarily. Law seeks justice and is a means to it, not an end in itself. D describes arbitrariness, and A ignores fair process.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Which statement best describes the relationship between law and justice?

options.a: Law and justice are always identical in content
options.b: Law and justice have no connection with each other
options.c: Justice is the means, and law is the end it seeks
options.d: Law is the means, and justice is the end it seeks

questions.explanation: Law is the instrument or machinery through which justice is realised, and justice gives law its moral force. C reverses the relationship. A is wrong because a law may be legal yet unjust, as with apartheid laws, and B ignores that the primary objective of law is justice.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as a factor that shapes a person's conception of justice?

options.a: Socio-political affiliation
options.b: Home background
options.c: Height and physical build
options.d: Religious belief

questions.explanation: Justice means different things to different people because of factors such as home background, education, religious belief, enlightened self-interest, personal idiosyncrasies and socio-political affiliation. Physical build is not one of them, while B, D and A are all on the list.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: After a court rules on a wage dispute, the union says "justice has been done", while the employers call the ruling "a miscarriage of justice". This best illustrates the view that

options.a: justice is following laid down rules
options.b: justice is the first virtue of social institutions
options.c: justice, like beauty, is in the eye of the beholder
options.d: justice is a three-way traffic

questions.explanation: There is no universally accepted definition of justice; it depends on the definer's perspective. Before a court, the winner feels justice has been done while the loser sees a miscarriage of justice. The other options are definitions of justice, but they do not explain why the two sides see the same ruling differently.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Who described justice as "the first condition of humanity"?

options.a: Emily Thorne
options.b: Wole Soyinka
options.c: Harold Lasswell
options.d: John Rawls

questions.explanation: Prof. Wole Soyinka described justice as the first condition of humanity. Rawls (D) called justice the first virtue of social institutions, Emily Thorne (A) said justice is in the eye of the beholder, and Lasswell (C) defined politics as who gets what, when and how.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: The theory of justice which holds that a judge must apply the law strictly, with no discretion to soften its harshness and no regard to extra-legal considerations, is

options.a: formal justice
options.b: natural justice
options.c: distributive justice
options.d: substantive justice

questions.explanation: Under formal justice, justice is done when a case is decided strictly according to law. Substantive justice (D) allows the judge to consider extra-legal factors to avoid absurd or unjust results, and distributive justice (C) concerns the fair sharing of resources and burdens in society.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: At the end of a politically charged treason trial, the judge tells the court: "Whatever my sympathies for the accused, my hands are tied," and convicts him. The judge's approach is an example of

options.a: formal justice
options.b: judicial activism
options.c: substantive justice
options.d: corrective justice

questions.explanation: 'My hands are tied' captures formal justice: the judge applies the law as it is, whatever his sympathies. Judicial activism (B) is the liberal interpretation of law to achieve substantive justice (C), which is the opposite approach. Corrective justice (D) concerns rectifying wrongs between individuals.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a justification offered for formal justice?

options.a: It lets the judge soften the law's harshness
options.b: It promotes impartiality and independence in adjudication
options.c: It ensures the certainty of the law
options.d: It ensures the clarity of the law

questions.explanation: Formal justice denies the judge any discretion to mitigate the law's harshness; that flexibility belongs to substantive justice. Its supporters say it ensures clarity (D) and certainty (C) and makes for impartial adjudication (B) because the judge cannot favour either party.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: The practice of judges liberally interpreting the provisions of the law in order to advance substantive justice is commonly known as

options.a: the literal rule
options.b: formal justice
options.c: judicial activism
options.d: judicial precedent

questions.explanation: Substantive justice allows a judge to consider extra-judicial factors where strict application would produce manifest absurdity or injustice, and this attitude also led to the development of equity. Formal justice (B) is the opposite approach. Judicial precedent (D) is about following earlier decisions, not liberal interpretation.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Chika's evidence clearly proves that a supplier owes her N450,000, but the court strikes out her case because her lawyer used the wrong form. Which type of justice has most clearly been denied?

options.a: Substantive justice
options.b: Distributive justice
options.c: Commutative justice
options.d: Formal justice

questions.explanation: Substantive justice looks at whether the outcome is fair; dismissing a case on a mere technicality when the evidence supports the claimant denies it. Formal or procedural justice (D) has arguably been followed, since the rules of procedure were strictly applied. Distributive justice (B) concerns the state's allocation of resources.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: In his book A Theory of Justice (1971), which writer defined justice as fairness and called it "the first virtue of social institutions"?

options.a: Wole Soyinka
options.b: Aristotle
options.c: John Rawls
options.d: Ulpian

questions.explanation: Rawls saw a just society as one where basic rights, equality of opportunity and advantages are fairly distributed. Ulpian (D) spoke of the constant and perpetual will to render each his due, and Soyinka (A) called justice the first condition of humanity, not the first virtue of institutions.
