questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: According to Aristotle, justice is two-fold. It consists of

options.a: obedience to the king, and loyalty to the state
options.b: charity, and forgiveness
options.c: the will of the majority, and the will of the ruler
options.d: conduct in agreement with law, and equality

questions.explanation: Aristotle saw justice both as conduct in agreement with an authoritative rule and as equality. That is why justice is also described as treating like cases alike. The other pairs are virtues or political ideas that do not reflect Aristotle's two-fold account.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: A society insists that people born into a particular group may only do menial work and must never hold leadership positions, because that is what they are "fitted for". This reasoning reflects which writer's view of justice?

options.a: Plato
options.b: Wole Soyinka
options.c: Ulpian
options.d: John Rawls

questions.explanation: Plato said justice is when one does that for which one is fitted or suited, an idea linked to the caste system in India and the Osu system in Eastern Nigeria. Rawls (D) would reject it because justice as fairness requires equality of opportunity. Ulpian (C) spoke of rendering each his due.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: When justice is seen as "equality according to law", it is mainly expressed through

options.a: letting each community make its own criminal law
options.b: treating like cases alike, as in universal adult suffrage
options.c: giving more votes to those who pay more tax
options.d: allowing judges to decide cases on personal sympathy

questions.explanation: Justice as equality means treating like alike, for example equal treatment in legal proceedings and one vote for every adult. Its benefit is that it can reduce discrimination. C would be unequal treatment, and D replaces law with personal sympathy.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: A mother shares food and clothing exactly equally among her three children, although one of them is physically challenged and needs more care. This example is used to show that

options.a: justice is following laid down rules
options.b: justice is a three-way traffic
options.c: strict equality can sometimes work injustice
options.d: equality always produces justice

questions.explanation: Treating unequal situations the same can be unfair, so equality may work injustice. That is why the law sometimes treats people unequally on grounds such as infancy, insanity or poverty. D is exactly what the example disproves.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: A state provides free legal aid only to poor litigants and awards scholarships only to the poorest students. Treating these groups differently from others is best explained by the idea that

options.a: only commutative justice matters to the state
options.b: justice is whatever the ruler says
options.c: justice is always strict equality
options.d: unequal treatment can itself be a form of justice

questions.explanation: On the basis of justice, persons may be treated unequally on grounds of insanity, infancy or poverty, for example through legal aid for indigent persons and scholarships for the poorest of the poor. C is the view this practice departs from, and B reflects absolutism.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: The type of justice concerned with fairness in dealings and exchanges between two individuals, such as enforcing a contract, and described as "justice of coordination", is

options.a: distributive justice
options.b: social justice
options.c: commutative justice
options.d: procedural justice

questions.explanation: Commutative justice concerns voluntary transactions between persons in private law; it is individual-centred, not societal. Distributive justice (A) concerns how the community shares goods among its members and is called justice of subordination. Procedural justice (D) concerns the fairness of the process.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: The Constitution requires that appointments to federal offices reflect the federal character of Nigeria, so that no state or ethnic group dominates. This is an example of

options.a: distributive justice
options.b: procedural justice
options.c: commutative justice
options.d: corrective justice

questions.explanation: Distributive justice concerns how the state allocates resources, honours, rights and burdens among members of the community according to need, merit or equality; the Federal Character principle is a standard example. Commutative (C) and corrective (D) justice deal with transactions and wrongs between individuals.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: After removing fuel subsidy, the federal government pays N25,000 in palliatives to the poorest households to ease the burden. This policy is best described as an attempt at

options.a: distributive justice
options.b: procedural justice
options.c: commutative justice
options.d: corrective justice

questions.explanation: Spreading the benefits and burdens of public policy fairly across society, according to need, is distributive justice; fuel subsidy removal and palliatives are given as examples. There is no private transaction (C) and no individual wrong being rectified (D) here.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Tunde steals Ada's generator worth N180,000. The court orders him to return it and pay a penalty to correct the imbalance. Which type of justice, developed by Aristotle to rectify wrongs between individuals, does this reflect?

options.a: Social justice
options.b: Corrective justice
options.c: Procedural justice
options.d: Distributive justice

questions.explanation: Corrective justice restores the balance when one party suffers harm or unfair loss at the hands of another, mainly in criminal law and tort; the wrongdoer must make amends or face punishment. Distributive justice (D) is about allocating society's resources, and procedural justice (C) concerns the fairness of the process.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: How does corrective justice differ from distributive justice in terms of time?

options.a: Both are concerned only with future arrangements
options.b: Both are concerned only with past wrongs
options.c: Corrective justice is prospective, while distributive justice is retrospective
options.d: Corrective justice is retrospective, while distributive justice is prospective

questions.explanation: Corrective justice looks back to fix past wrongs, such as compensating a victim of fraud, while distributive justice looks forward to fair future arrangements, such as economic policies that reduce poverty. C reverses the two, and A and B wrongly treat them as the same.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Thomas Aquinas classified justice into

options.a: natural justice and divine justice
options.b: formal justice and substantive justice
options.c: corrective justice and retributive justice
options.d: commutative justice and distributive justice

questions.explanation: Aquinas divided justice into commutative justice, dealing with transactions between persons, and distributive justice, dealing with the community's relation to each person. Aristotle paired corrective justice with distributive justice, and formal and substantive justice (B) are the two theories of judicial approach.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: The type of justice that focuses on fairness in how a decision is reached, through impartial trials and hearings, rather than on the outcome, is

options.a: procedural justice
options.b: commutative justice
options.c: distributive justice
options.d: substantive justice

questions.explanation: Procedural or technical justice requires legal procedures to be conducted impartially and transparently; 'justice must not only be done, but must be seen to be done'. Section 36 of the 1999 Constitution, guaranteeing fair hearing, embodies it. Substantive justice (D) looks at the fairness of the result itself.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: A customary court convicts Emeka of land trespass without telling him the charge or letting him call witnesses. Which constitutional guarantee, embodying procedural justice, has most clearly been breached?

options.a: The right to fair hearing under section 36 of the 1999 Constitution
options.b: Freedom of association under section 40
options.c: The vesting of legislative powers under section 4
options.d: The procedure for amending the Constitution under section 9

questions.explanation: Procedural justice requires that an accused be heard, have access to counsel and be presumed innocent, and section 36 guarantees fair hearing. Section 40 (B) protects freedom of association, section 4 (C) vests legislative power, and section 9 (D) deals with constitutional amendment.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Dennis Lloyd suggested ways of making law conform to criteria of rightness so as to achieve substantial justice. Which of the following is NOT one of them?

options.a: Judicial discretion
options.b: Political or affirmative action such as gender mainstreaming
options.c: Legislative reforms
options.d: Strict literal application regardless of outcome

questions.explanation: Because procedural or formal justice can itself be unjust, Lloyd proposed judicial discretion (A), legislative reforms (C) and political or affirmative action (B) to secure substantial justice. Strict literal application regardless of outcome is formal justice, the very approach that can produce injustice.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: In judging whether substantial justice has been done, the standard applied by Nigerian courts is that of

options.a: a reasonable man
options.b: the majority of the community's elders
options.c: the most senior lawyer in court
options.d: the presiding judge's personal conscience

questions.explanation: The test is objective: whether a reasonable person observing the proceedings would conclude that justice was done. A judge's personal conscience (D) would make justice subjective, which the reasonable man standard is meant to avoid.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Apartheid laws in South Africa and racial segregation laws in the United States before 1964 are cited to show that

options.a: unjust laws are never enforced by states
options.b: a law may be legal yet unjust
options.c: justice and law always coincide
options.d: only customary law can be unjust

questions.explanation: Law and justice are closely linked but can come apart: such laws were validly made yet deeply unjust. This is why scholars debate whether justice should be the ultimate measure of a law's validity. Brown v Board of Education (1954), which declared school segregation unconstitutional, later realigned law with justice.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: A journalist publishes a false and malicious story about a businessman and argues that freedom of speech protects him. The best response is that

options.a: freedom of speech applies only to politicians
options.b: fundamental rights are moral ideas the courts cannot enforce
options.c: freedom of speech is absolute and cannot be limited
options.d: rights are not absolute and must be balanced against others' rights

questions.explanation: Law recognises freedom but regulates its exercise; leaving freedom totally unrestricted would encroach on others' freedom and lead to anarchy. Freedom of speech does not include freedom to publish malicious falsehoods. B is wrong because Chapter IV rights are justiciable in Nigerian courts.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a limitation that the law places on freedom of contract?

options.a: The law may control the prices of certain essential goods
options.b: Every person must accept any offer a trader makes to him
options.c: A contract is void if it contemplates the commission of a crime
options.d: A trader may be barred from using a trade name closely resembling an existing one

questions.explanation: Freedom of contract includes the right to refuse to contract, so no rule forces anyone to accept every offer, and Option B is not a real limitation. The real limitations are voiding illegal or anti-public-policy contracts (C), price control for essential goods (A) and preventing confusing trade names or trademarks (D).

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Seventeen-year-old Ifeoma tries to register as a voter for a National Assembly election but is turned away. This is an example of

options.a: a breach of freedom of contract
options.b: a violation of procedural justice
options.c: the territorial limitation of law
options.d: a lawful limitation on political freedom

questions.explanation: Political freedom includes the right to vote, but the law may disqualify some people, such as those below eighteen, from voting. The Constitution entitles every citizen who has attained eighteen years to register, which by implication excludes those below that age. The other options do not describe this situation.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: A state is an organised political community with four basic elements. Which of the following is NOT one of them?

options.a: Sovereignty
options.b: An official state religion
options.c: A population
options.d: A definite territory

questions.explanation: The four basic elements of a state are a definite territory, a population, a government and sovereignty. A state religion is not required, and Nigeria, for example, has none. Territory (D), population (C) and sovereignty (A) are all elements.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: A breakaway region controls its territory and population and has an effective government, but no other state recognises it. Which statement best describes its position?

options.a: It is a state only if its old parent state's courts approve
options.b: It can never be a state because it was once part of another state
options.c: Recognition matters politically but is not strictly conclusive
options.d: It automatically becomes a full state once it declares independence

questions.explanation: Under the Montevideo criteria, a state needs a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and capacity to enter relations with other states. Recognition affects international standing but is not strictly conclusive, so such a region may operate in practice while lacking full international personality. D ignores the capacity and recognition problem.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Section 2(1) of the 1999 Constitution describes Nigeria as

options.a: a unitary state with no component states
options.b: a union that any state may leave at will
options.c: one indivisible and indissoluble sovereign state
options.d: a confederation of independent regions

questions.explanation: Section 2(1) provides that Nigeria is one indivisible and indissoluble sovereign state known as the Federal Republic of Nigeria, and section 2(2) makes it a federation of states and a Federal Capital Territory. It is a federation, not a unitary state (A), and the word indissoluble rules out D and B.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: A country's government becomes oppressive and racist, but it does not threaten neighbouring states. As a rule, international law treats that country as

options.a: a state only if its citizens approve the government
options.b: still a state, as an oppressive government does not end its personality
options.c: a state only until the United Nations dissolves it
options.d: no longer a state, because its government has become unjust

questions.explanation: International law as a rule pays little attention to a state's internal affairs as long as other states' interests are not affected, so an oppressive government does not end the state's personality. D confuses the state with its government, which is only the machinery through which the state acts.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Louis XIV's statement "I am the state" best reflects a period when

options.a: judges could declare the ruler's acts null and void
options.b: sovereignty belonged to the people under a written constitution
options.c: the powers of government were separated among three arms
options.d: rulers wielded absolute power and based their authority on divine right

questions.explanation: Louis XIV interrupted a judge who spoke of 'the king and the state' to declare 'I am the state', reflecting an era when ruler and state were fused, as with African kings regarded as demi-gods. Popular sovereignty (B), separation of powers (C) and judicial review (A) are later ideas that curtailed such power.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Under section 14(2)(a) of the 1999 Constitution, sovereignty in Nigeria belongs to

options.a: the President as head of state
options.b: the Supreme Court as the final court
options.c: the people of Nigeria
options.d: the National Assembly as the law-making body

questions.explanation: Over time, sovereign power was taken from a few individuals and vested in the people collectively, who exercise it through their representatives. Section 14(2)(a) states this plainly. The President (A), the National Assembly (D) and the courts (B) exercise powers derived from the people through the Constitution.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: The doctrine of separation of powers is most closely associated with which writer?

options.a: A.V. Dicey
options.b: Jean Bodin
options.c: Montesquieu
options.d: Talcott Parsons

questions.explanation: Separation of powers, traced back to John Locke, was developed by Montesquieu in The Spirit of the Laws; it divides government into legislature, executive and judiciary to prevent concentration of power. Bodin (B) introduced sovereignty, Dicey (A) is linked with the rule of law, and Parsons (D) with the consensus model.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Bayo is arrested and charged for an act that was not an offence under any law when he did it. Which principle that limits state power protects him?

options.a: The principle of legality
options.b: The doctrine of sovereignty
options.c: The doctrine of judicial precedent
options.d: The consensus model of law

questions.explanation: The principle of legality, nullum crimen sine lege (no crime without law), means no one can be punished for conduct that no law made an offence. It is one of the theories that curtail the power of those in authority. Sovereignty (B) concerns supreme authority, not protection from punishment.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Police detain a trader for three weeks without charging him or bringing him before a court. Which principle has the state most clearly violated in enforcing the law?

options.a: Sovereignty
options.b: Separation of powers
options.c: Distributive justice
options.d: The rule of law

questions.explanation: The state holds a monopoly of legitimate force, but the rule of law requires that force be used lawfully and proportionately; an arrest needs a legal basis and the detainee must be brought before a court within a specified period. Sovereignty (A) is the state's supreme authority, not a limit on how force is used.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: The National Assembly passes a law, and the Supreme Court later declares it void for being inconsistent with the Constitution. This is an example of

options.a: the extinction of the state by dissolution
options.b: the people changing their elected leaders
options.c: the executive exercising legislative power
options.d: checks and balances among the arms of government

questions.explanation: Separation of powers divides government into legislature, executive and judiciary, and each arm checks the others; here the judiciary reviews the legislature's action for constitutionality. The other options describe different situations entirely.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: In the modern period, legitimacy is said to rest not on mere legality but on what Farrar and Dugdale called "impersonal rational authority". This means

options.a: the decrees of whoever holds military power
options.b: a rule of law accepted by both officials and the people
options.c: the personal charisma of a strong leader
options.d: the divine right of traditional rulers

questions.explanation: In early legal systems, legitimacy rested on the charismatic qualities of leaders and traditional rulers, then on legality. Today it rests on a rule of law accepted by both officials and the people. Charisma (C) and divine right (D) belong to earlier stages, and A confuses force with legitimacy.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: A group of officers attempts to seize power by force, but the coup fails and they are arrested. Under Nigerian law, they are most likely to be charged with

options.a: a minor public order offence attracting a fine
options.b: treason, as no one may take over government except under the Constitution
options.c: no offence, because the coup did not succeed
options.d: contempt of court, because they ignored judicial orders

questions.explanation: Section 1(2) of the 1999 Constitution forbids anyone from taking control of the government except in accordance with the Constitution, so an unsuccessful coup attempt is treated as treason, punishable with death. Experience shows the provision cannot stop a coup from happening or make a successful one illegal in practice.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Under Kelsen's pure theory of law, a law passed by the legislature and assented to by the President, following constitutional procedure, is legitimate

options.a: only if it reflects the customs of the people
options.b: only after the courts have applied it in a case
options.c: because it follows from higher norms, even if many citizens consider it unjust
options.d: only if most citizens consider it morally right

questions.explanation: For Kelsen, legitimacy is grounded in legal validity: a norm is legitimate if it follows from higher norms up to the grundnorm, regardless of moral justification. Critics say this ignores the role of morality in public acceptance. D is a moral test, A is the historical school's test, and B is a realist idea.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Residents of a state say they trust their governor's government because it has delivered security, good roads and working hospitals. This is an example of which source of legitimacy?

options.a: Constitutionalism
options.b: Performance legitimacy
options.c: Democratic consent
options.d: Charismatic legitimacy

questions.explanation: Performance legitimacy arises when a government provides security, welfare and prosperity, so citizens regard it as legitimate. Democratic consent (C) comes from elections and participation, and constitutionalism (A) from following constitutional procedures. Here the trust is based on results delivered.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: The Westphalian model of the state, from the treaties of 1648, emphasises

options.a: a single world government with authority over all states
options.b: sovereign equality of states and non-interference
options.c: the right of powerful states to annex weaker ones
options.d: the duty of states to adopt one common religion

questions.explanation: The Westphalian model rests on territorial sovereignty, centralised authority, legal equality of states and non-intervention. Globalisation, human rights obligations and the responsibility to protect have since softened strict non-interference. The other options contradict the model.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: Country X is absorbed by its larger neighbour and ceases to exist as a separate state. Which mode of extinction of a state is this?

options.a: Merger
options.b: Recognition
options.c: Dissolution
options.d: Annexation

questions.explanation: Annexation occurs when a state ceases to exist because another state absorbs it, a mode that is controversial and often unlawful. Merger (A) is when two or more states unite, and dissolution (C) is when a state breaks into successor states. Recognition (B) is not a mode of extinction at all.

questions.topic: Objectives of Law, Law and Justice, and the State
questions.question: The State is said to hold a "monopoly of legitimate use of force". This means that

options.a: any citizen may use force to enforce his own rights
options.b: the State alone may ordinarily use or authorise coercion, channelled through law
options.c: the State may use force without any legal limits
options.d: only international bodies may authorise the use of force

questions.explanation: The State, through the police and military, ordinarily has the exclusive right to use or authorise coercion, and law channels that force through arrest powers, courts and due process. A describes self-help, and C is wrong because the rule of law limits how force may be used.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: The aspect of law that governs the relationship between the state and its citizens, in which the state is 'higher' in legal status than the other party, is called

options.a: municipal law
options.b: public law
options.c: procedural law
options.d: private law

questions.explanation: Public law covers relationships where the state, as the superior party, deals with citizens, as in constitutional, administrative and criminal law. Option D concerns relations between private individuals. Option C is about how cases are conducted in court, and option A simply means the internal law of a country, which includes both public and private law.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Which of the following best describes private law?

options.a: Law concerned with the protection of the state and its organs
options.b: Law laying down the steps for commencing and conducting cases in court
options.c: Law concerned with relationships between individuals and the protection of individual rights
options.d: Law governing relationships between independent states and international organisations

questions.explanation: Private law deals with dealings between private persons, such as contract, torts, trusts and succession. Option A describes public law, option D describes international law, and option B describes procedural (adjectival) law.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an example of public law?

options.a: Administrative law
options.b: Criminal law
options.c: Constitutional law
options.d: Law of contract

questions.explanation: The law of contract governs agreements between private persons, so it is private law. Constitutional law (option C), administrative law (option A) and criminal law (option B) all involve the state acting in its public capacity, which makes them classic examples of public law.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Bola lent Emeka N250,000 under a written agreement. Emeka refuses to repay, and Bola sues him in the High Court to recover the money. Which pair of classifications best fits Bola's claim?

options.a: Public law and civil law
options.b: Private law and civil law
options.c: Public law and criminal law
options.d: Private law and criminal law

questions.explanation: A claim by one private person against another to recover money under a contract is both private law (relations between individuals) and civil law (redress for a breached right). Options C and D wrongly call it criminal, since nobody is being prosecuted or punished. Option A wrongly calls it public law, since the state is not a party.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: How does the Nigerian legal system treat the public law/private law divide compared with a country like France?

options.a: Nigeria has no separate body of rules and courts for state matters, but special procedures apply in some public-duty cases
options.b: Nigeria, like France, has a separate system of courts for all cases involving the government
options.c: Nigeria applies different substantive rules to the government in every case it is a party to
options.d: Nigeria has abolished any distinction between public and private law in all respects

questions.explanation: Unlike France, Nigeria has not developed separate rules and courts for matters affecting the state; litigation between the state and citizens follows the same rules as private litigation. The distinction that has emerged is procedural, for example in fundamental rights enforcement and judicial review. Options B and C describe the French-style system, and option D ignores the special procedures that now exist.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Kemi wants to challenge a decision of a state agency by an application for judicial review, but her lawyer files it as an ordinary civil claim without following the special procedure for that kind of application. What is the likely consequence?

options.a: The case may be struck out for failure to follow the special procedure
options.b: The court must hear it because public and private law cases follow identical procedures
options.c: The case will be transferred automatically to a separate administrative court
options.d: The case becomes a criminal prosecution because a state agency is involved

questions.explanation: Where the aim is to enforce a public duty, such as in judicial review or fundamental rights enforcement, Nigerian law requires special procedures, and a case that ignores them may be struck out. Option C is wrong because Nigeria has no separate administrative courts. Option B ignores the procedural distinction that has emerged. Option D confuses public law with criminal law.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: The branch of law that defines the rights and duties of persons to one another and gives an injured person a way to be compensated for the wrongful act of another is

options.a: adjectival law
options.b: criminal law
options.c: public international law
options.d: civil law

questions.explanation: In this context civil law is the body of rules on rights and duties between persons, with compensation for the injured party as its aim. Option B aims at punishment for conduct harmful to society. Option C governs relations between states, and option A is the procedural law used to enforce rights rather than the rights themselves.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Which statement best describes criminal law?

options.a: It enables an injured person to recover compensation from the wrongdoer
options.b: It sets out the steps for initiating actions and giving evidence in court
options.c: It regulates relations between Nigeria and other sovereign states
options.d: It protects the public at large by punishing conduct considered harmful to society

questions.explanation: Criminal law protects society as a whole by punishing harmful conduct, usually by imprisonment, fine or both. Option A describes civil law, whose aim is compensation. Option B describes procedural law, and option C describes international law.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: In a criminal trial in Nigeria, the prosecution must prove its case

options.a: beyond reasonable doubt, as provided in section 135 of the Evidence Act 2011
options.b: beyond reasonable doubt, as provided in section 134 of the Evidence Act 2011
options.c: on the balance of probabilities, as provided in section 134 of the Evidence Act 2011
options.d: on the balance of probabilities, as provided in section 135 of the Evidence Act 2011

questions.explanation: Section 135 of the Evidence Act 2011 requires proof beyond reasonable doubt in criminal cases. Option C states the civil standard found in section 134. Options B and D mix up the two sections.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: The standard of proof under which judgment goes to the party who proves its case more convincingly than the other is

options.a: proof on the balance of probabilities
options.b: proof beyond all doubt
options.c: proof beyond reasonable doubt
options.d: prima facie proof

questions.explanation: Civil cases are decided on the balance of probabilities, so judgment goes to whichever side has proved its case more successfully. Option C is the higher criminal standard. Option B is not a legal standard at all, and option D only means enough evidence to call for an answer.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Why does the law demand a higher standard of proof in criminal cases than in civil cases?

options.a: To reduce the number of criminal cases that reach the courts
options.b: Because criminal cases are always tried in the High Court
options.c: To protect the accused from the power of the state and the danger of wrongful conviction
options.d: Because the victim of a crime is always entitled to compensation

questions.explanation: The higher standard protects an accused person from the state's great power and from wrongful conviction, with its loss of liberty and livelihood; this is the presumption of innocence. Option B is false because minor offences are tried summarily in Magistrate Courts. Options D and A give reasons that have nothing to do with the standard of proof.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts the burden of proof in criminal and civil cases?

options.a: In criminal cases it shifts to the accused once charged; in civil cases it stays on the plaintiff
options.b: In both kinds of case it stays permanently on the defendant
options.c: In both kinds of case it shifts freely between the parties
options.d: In criminal cases it stays on the prosecution; in civil cases it may shift between the parties

questions.explanation: In a criminal trial the burden of proof does not shift from the prosecution, while in civil cases it moves between the parties as each tries to establish its case. Option A reverses the position and would undermine the presumption of innocence. Options B and C ignore the difference between the two kinds of case.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Tunde takes Ngozi's bicycle without her permission and sells it. Which statement best describes Tunde's legal position?

options.a: He may be prosecuted for stealing and also sued by Ngozi in the tort of conversion
options.b: He may only be sued for conversion, since the bicycle was private property
options.c: He may only be prosecuted, since stealing is a crime and cannot also be a civil wrong
options.d: He can be neither prosecuted nor sued until Ngozi gets a customary court order

questions.explanation: The same conduct can be both a crime and a civil wrong: taking B's bicycle is the offence of stealing and also the tort of conversion. Options C and B wrongly assume the two kinds of liability cannot exist together. Option D invents a requirement that does not exist.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT given as an example of a wrong that is both a crime and a tort?

options.a: Defamation
options.b: Assault
options.c: Breach of contract
options.d: False imprisonment

questions.explanation: Breach of contract is a purely civil wrong remedied by damages or similar relief; it is not a crime. Assault (option B), false imprisonment (option D) and defamation (option A) are the standard examples of conduct that is both a crime and a tort, which shows how the line between civil and criminal law overlaps.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Chidi's shop in Yaba is burgled, and the suspect is charged to court for burglary. In such a criminal case, who prosecutes?

options.a: Chidi's insurer
options.b: The State, on behalf of society
options.c: The Yaba community leaders
options.d: Chidi, as the person who suffered the loss

questions.explanation: In criminal law the State prosecutes on behalf of society, because the conduct is treated as harmful to the public at large. Option D describes the claimant in a civil action, not a criminal prosecution. Options A and C have no role as prosecutors.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: In Nigeria, criminal law has been codified mainly in

options.a: a single Criminal Code applicable uniformly in every state
options.b: the Criminal Code for the Southern States and the Penal Code for the Northern States
options.c: the Penal Code for the Southern States and the Criminal Code for the Northern States
options.d: the Evidence Act and the Sheriffs and Civil Process Act

questions.explanation: The Criminal Code applies in the Southern States and the Penal Code in the Northern States. Option C reverses the two. Option A ignores the North/South split, and option D names procedural statutes that do not define offences.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Ada is charged with a minor traffic offence, while Femi is charged with armed robbery. Which statement best reflects how such offences are normally tried?

options.a: Both offences must be tried in the High Court because both are crimes
options.b: Both offences are civil wrongs and go to a customary court
options.c: Ada's offence is tried summarily in a Magistrate Court; Femi's serious offence is normally tried in the High Court
options.d: Ada's offence is tried in the High Court; Femi's offence goes to a Magistrate Court

questions.explanation: Serious crimes such as robbery, murder and rape are normally tried in the High Court, while lesser offences such as minor traffic offences are tried summarily in the Magistrate Court. Option A ignores this split, option D reverses it, and option B wrongly treats crimes as civil wrongs.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: To members of the armed forces, the word 'civil' generally means

options.a: law that is enacted by the legislature as opposed to case law
options.b: the law of a state as opposed to international law
options.c: everything that is not peculiar to the military, as in a civil court contrasted with a court martial
options.d: only the law of contract and torts

questions.explanation: The word 'civil' has several meanings; in the military context it means whatever is not peculiar to the armed forces, so a civil court is contrasted with a court martial. Option B states a different meaning (domestic as against international law). Options D and A are not meanings of the word given in this sense.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: The body of legal rules that states rights, duties and liabilities, defines a code of conduct and prescribes a penalty for its breach is

options.a: substantive law
options.b: unwritten law
options.c: adjectival law
options.d: procedural law

questions.explanation: Substantive law is the law itself: the rules stating what people may or may not do and what follows from a breach, as in contract, torts and criminal law. Options D and C are two names for the same thing: the rules on how substantive law is enforced in court. Option B is a different classification, about whether a rule was enacted.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Procedural or adjectival law is best described as the law that

options.a: determines whether a contract exists and what its terms are
options.b: deals with the methods of proceedings by which substantive rights and duties are enforced in court
options.c: governs the relationship between the state and its citizens
options.d: defines offences and prescribes their punishment

questions.explanation: Procedural law covers how a case is started, how evidence is given, how witnesses are examined, how judgment is delivered and how it is enforced. Options D and A describe the content of substantive criminal and contract law. Option C describes public law.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Which of the following Nigerian enactments is procedural law in relation to the Criminal Code and the Penal Code?

options.a: Criminal Code Act
options.b: Land Use Act
options.c: Administration of Criminal Justice Act 2015
options.d: Companies and Allied Matters Act

questions.explanation: The Administration of Criminal Justice Act 2015 lays down how criminal cases are conducted, so it is procedural law in relation to the Criminal and Penal Codes. Option D and option B are substantive statutes on companies and land. Option A is itself the substantive criminal law that the procedure serves.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Section 419 of the Criminal Code, which defines the offence of obtaining goods by false pretences and prescribes imprisonment for it, is an example of

options.a: procedural law
options.b: unwritten law
options.c: conflict of laws
options.d: substantive law

questions.explanation: A provision that defines an offence and fixes its punishment is substantive law. Option A would cover rules on how the trial is conducted, not what the offence is. Option C deals with cases that have foreign elements, and option B is wrong because the Criminal Code is an enactment.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Before filing a claim for breach of contract, Barrister Okafor studies the High Court of Lagos State (Civil Procedure) Rules to find out how to begin the action and serve the defendant. Which kind of law is he consulting?

options.a: International law
options.b: Substantive law
options.c: Procedural law
options.d: Divine law

questions.explanation: Rules of court that state how an action is begun and how processes are served are procedural (adjectival) law. Option B would be the law of contract itself, which decides whether there was a breach and what remedies are available. Options A and D have nothing to do with how a Lagos court action is conducted.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a matter dealt with by procedural law?

options.a: The enforcement of the judgment of the court
options.b: The way in which an action is to be initiated in court
options.c: The examination of witnesses at trial
options.d: Whether particular conduct amounts to an offence

questions.explanation: Whether conduct is an offence is decided by substantive law, such as the Criminal Code or Penal Code. Starting an action (option B), examining witnesses (option C) and enforcing judgment (option A) are all listed as matters governed by procedural law.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: The law that denotes the internal law of a particular country, regulating relations between individuals and between individuals and the State, is called

options.a: eternal law
options.b: international law
options.c: conflict of laws
options.d: municipal law

questions.explanation: Municipal law, also called national, domestic or local law, is a country's internal law. Option B governs relations between states. Option C deals with domestic cases that have foreign elements, and option A is a philosophical idea of unchanging universal law.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: International law is best defined as the law that governs

options.a: the procedure of courts in hearing cases involving foreigners
options.b: relations between States inter se or between States and international organisations
options.c: relations between a state government and its local governments
options.d: relations between individuals within a particular country

questions.explanation: International law regulates relations between States themselves and between States and international organisations. Option D describes municipal private law. Option C is a domestic constitutional matter, and option A confuses international law with procedural law.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the recognised sources of international law?

options.a: Treaties
options.b: International custom
options.c: Bye-laws made by a Nigerian local government council
options.d: General principles of law recognised by civilised nations

questions.explanation: Bye-laws of a local government are domestic law with no international effect. Treaties (option A), international custom (option B) and general principles of law recognised by civilised nations (option D) are listed, together with judicial decisions and the teachings of highly qualified publicists, as the bases of international law.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Nigeria has signed and ratified an international treaty on workers' rights, but the National Assembly has not enacted it into law. A worker relies on the treaty alone in a Nigerian court. What is the treaty's status?

options.a: It applies only if a state House of Assembly adopts it
options.b: It automatically binds Nigerian courts once it is ratified
options.c: It overrides the Constitution because it is international law
options.d: It does not have the force of law in Nigeria until enacted by the National Assembly

questions.explanation: Under section 12(1) of the 1999 Constitution, a treaty has the force of law in Nigeria only to the extent that the National Assembly has enacted it into law. Option B ignores this domestication requirement. Option C is wrong because the Constitution is supreme, and option A names the wrong legislature.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Two Nigerians make a contract in England to sell goods situated in London. A dispute about the contract's validity comes before a Nigerian court, which applies English law. Which branch of law deals with this kind of question?

options.a: Criminal law
options.b: Private international law (conflict of laws)
options.c: Constitutional law
options.d: Public international law

questions.explanation: Private international law, or conflict of laws, deals with cases inside a legal system in which foreign elements arise, raising questions about which country's law or courts apply. Option D is a separate system governing relations between States. Options A and C do not deal with choosing which country's law governs a contract.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes private international law from public international law?

options.a: Private international law handles foreign elements in domestic cases; public international law is a separate system altogether
options.b: Private international law is unwritten while public international law is always written
options.c: Both are parts of the same domestic legal order and differ only in name
options.d: Private international law governs relations between States; public international law governs relations between individuals

questions.explanation: Private international law works inside a particular legal system, dealing with cases that involve foreign elements. Public international law is not an attachment to any domestic legal order but a separate system altogether. Option D reverses the roles. Option C ignores the separateness of public international law, and option B states a false contrast.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of international law?

options.a: The Criminal Code Act
options.b: The Companies and Allied Matters Act
options.c: The Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999
options.d: The African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights

questions.explanation: The African Charter is an agreement between states, so it is international law. The 1999 Constitution (option C) applies only in Nigeria, which makes it municipal law, and so do CAMA (option B) and the Criminal Code (option A).

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: In the classification of law, the word 'written' has a technical meaning. A written law is

options.a: a rule formally enacted into a statute by the legislature
options.b: any rule recorded in the law reports by a judge
options.c: any customary rule recorded by a chief's secretary
options.d: any rule that appears in a document or book

questions.explanation: 'Written' here means formally enacted by the legislature, usually after debate and passage through several stages. Option D is the trap: being in a document is not enough. Options B and C describe rules that are written down but not enacted, and these count as unwritten law.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Written laws go by different names in different jurisdictions and at different times. Which of the following is NOT one of those names?

options.a: Judicial precedents
options.b: Decrees
options.c: Edicts
options.d: Ordinances

questions.explanation: Judicial precedents are decisions of the courts, which count as unwritten law because they are not enacted. Edicts (option C), Decrees (option B) and Ordinances (option D) are among the names for enacted written law, together with Codes, Statutes, Acts, Laws and Rules.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: The term 'unwritten law' covers

options.a: rules not written down at all, such as customary law and conventions, and unenacted rules even if written, such as case law
options.b: statutes that have been repealed by the legislature
options.c: only case law reported in the law reports
options.d: only rules that have never been written down anywhere

questions.explanation: 'Unwritten law' has two meanings: rules not written down at all, such as customary law and conventions, and rules that are written down but never enacted, such as case law. Options D and C each give only half of the meaning, and option B has nothing to do with the classification.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: A Nigerian court applies the neighbour principle from Donoghue v Stevenson, which is printed in the law reports but is not found in any statute. How is this principle classified?

options.a: Unwritten law, because it was not enacted by a legislature
options.b: International law, because it came from a foreign court
options.c: Written law, because it appears in printed law reports
options.d: Written law, because Nigerian courts apply it

questions.explanation: Case law is unwritten law in the technical sense even though it is recorded in documents, because the legislature did not enact it. Option C relies on the everyday meaning of 'written'. Option D confuses being applied with being enacted, and option B confuses a foreign judicial decision with law between States.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Which of the following is a well-known example of an unwritten constitution?

options.a: The Charter of the United Nations
options.b: The 1963 Republican Constitution of Nigeria
options.c: The 1999 Constitution of Nigeria
options.d: The British Constitution

questions.explanation: The British Constitution is the classic example of unwritten law at constitutional level, because it is not contained in a single enacted document. The Nigerian constitutions (options C and B) were formally enacted, and option A is a treaty, not an unwritten constitution.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: A woman in a village is convicted of adultery under an unwritten local custom, although no written law defines adultery as an offence or prescribes a penalty for it. Which principle makes the conviction unlawful?

options.a: Unwritten law can never be applied by any Nigerian court
options.b: Customary courts have no power to try anyone
options.c: A person cannot be convicted of an offence unless it is defined and its penalty prescribed in a written law
options.d: Adultery can only be tried by a court martial

questions.explanation: Section 36(12) of the 1999 Constitution bars conviction for an offence not defined, with its penalty, in a written law; in Aoko v Fagbemi a conviction for adultery was set aside on this basis. Option B overstates things, since customary courts exist and apply customary law. Option D is irrelevant, and option A is wrong because unwritten customary and case law are applied in civil matters.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: As a division of law, 'common law' means

options.a: the customary law common to all ethnic groups in Nigeria
options.b: the law developed by the Lord Chancellor in the Court of Chancery
options.c: statutes enacted by the English Parliament
options.d: the law developed by the old common law courts of England: the King's Bench, the Court of Common Pleas and the Court of Exchequer

questions.explanation: As a division of law, common law means the judge-made law of England's old common law courts: the King's Bench, the Common Pleas and the Exchequer. Option B describes equity. Option A misreads the word 'common', and option C describes legislation rather than judge-made law.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT one of the old common law courts of England?

options.a: Court of Exchequer
options.b: Court of King's Bench
options.c: Court of Chancery
options.d: Court of Common Pleas

questions.explanation: The Court of Chancery was the Lord Chancellor's court, which administered equity and stood apart from the common law courts. The King's Bench (option B), Common Pleas (option D) and Exchequer (option A) were the three old common law courts.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: How did the English common law first emerge after the Norman Conquest of 1066?

options.a: The Church courts adopted the Ten Commandments as the law of England
options.b: Royal judges on circuit compared local customs and kept the more sensible ones, producing uniform rules for the whole realm
options.c: Parliament enacted a single code to replace all local customs
options.d: The Lord Chancellor issued decrees based on conscience and natural law

questions.explanation: The King's judges first applied local customs, then compared them at Westminster and preferred the more logical ones, until uniform rules emerged as 'the common law of the realm'. This makes common law judge-made law. Option C describes legislation, option D describes the later rise of equity, and option A confuses divine law with common law.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Which of the following was a major defect of the early common law that led to the rise of equity?

options.a: It was enacted by Parliament and could not be changed by judges
options.b: A plaintiff had no remedy unless his claim fell within an existing writ, and the main remedy was damages
options.c: It granted injunctions too readily
options.d: It allowed judges to decide every case purely on conscience

questions.explanation: The common law was strict, formal and legalistic: with no fitting writ there was no remedy, and even a successful plaintiff usually got only damages. Option D describes the approach of equity, not its cause. Option A wrongly treats common law as statute, and option C is wrong because injunctions were an equitable remedy.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Plaintiffs who failed to get redress at common law began petitioning the King. The official who dealt with these petitions, and whose court became the Court of Chancery, was

options.a: the Archbishop of Canterbury
options.b: the Attorney General
options.c: the Lord Chancellor
options.d: the Chief Justice of the King's Bench

questions.explanation: The Chancellor, as the King's chief minister, handled the petitions and in time decided them in his own court, which became the Court of Chancery. Option D was the head of a common law court. Option B was the office Bacon held when the dispute was referred to him, and option A had no such role.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: In the Earl of Oxford's case (1615), what did the Chancellor, Lord Ellesmere, do after the common law court gave judgment for the landowner?

options.a: He granted an injunction restraining the landowner from ejecting the plaintiff from the house he had built
options.b: He confirmed the common law judgment and dismissed the petition
options.c: He referred the case to Parliament for legislation
options.d: He awarded the plaintiff damages for wrongful ejection

questions.explanation: Relying on equity and good conscience, Lord Ellesmere granted an injunction stopping the owner from ejecting the plaintiff, who had built the house. This led Coke CJ to protest that the Chancellor was frustrating the common law. Option D is wrong because the Chancery could not award damages. Options B and C did not happen.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: How was the conflict between the common law courts and the Court of Chancery resolved after the Earl of Oxford's case?

options.a: Coke CJ ruled that common law always prevails over equity
options.b: It was referred to Lord Bacon and resolved in favour of Chancery: where common law and equity clash directly, equity prevails
options.c: The two courts agreed that each would ignore the other's decisions
options.d: The Court of Chancery was abolished immediately

questions.explanation: The dispute was referred to Lord Bacon, who resolved it in favour of Chancery: where common law and equity directly conflict, the rules of equity prevail. Option A reverses the outcome. Option D is wrong because the two courts continued separately until the Judicature Acts, and option C did not happen.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: What was the effect of the Judicature Acts, which came into operation in 1875, on common law and equity?

options.a: They made equity subordinate to the common law in every case
options.b: They fused the administration of the two systems in the same courts but did not abolish the distinction between legal and equitable rights
options.c: They abolished equity entirely and kept only the common law
options.d: They merged common law and equity into one identical set of rules

questions.explanation: The Acts fused the administration of common law and equity so that one court applies both, but legal and equitable rights remain distinct; hence 'the two streams now flow into one, their waters do not mix'. Options C and D wrongly say one system disappeared or that the rules became identical. Option A reverses the rule that equity prevails in a conflict.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Before fusion, the common law courts could not grant certain remedies that were available only in the Court of Chancery. Which of the following was NOT such an equitable remedy?

options.a: Injunction
options.b: Damages
options.c: Specific performance
options.d: Rescission

questions.explanation: Damages were the common law remedy, and the Court of Chancery could not award them. Injunction (option A), specific performance (option C) and rescission (option D) were equitable remedies that the common law courts had no power to grant, which forced litigants to sue in both courts.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Uche signs a written agreement transferring his car to Lola for N500,000. Uche later shows that he agreed only because Lola made a misrepresentation about the deal. On what basis may the contract be rescinded?

options.a: Criminal law, because every misrepresentation is a crime
options.b: The doctrine of equity, which can set aside a contract induced by fraud, mistake or misrepresentation
options.c: International law, because the contract involves a sale of goods
options.d: The strict common law, which enforces every signed agreement as written

questions.explanation: A signed agreement creates a legal right enforceable at law, but where fraud, mistake or misrepresentation induced it, equity may rescind it. This is equity softening the strictness of common law. Option D states the common law position that equity corrects. Options A and C apply the wrong branches of law.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Before 1875, an English litigant wanted to establish a common law right and also needed an injunction to protect it. What did he usually have to do?

options.a: Sue only in Chancery, which could award both damages and injunctions
options.b: Petition Parliament directly for an injunction
options.c: Sue only in the King's Bench, which could grant injunctions
options.d: Sue first in a common law court to establish the right, then in Chancery for the injunction

questions.explanation: Because the systems were run in separate courts, a litigant often had to establish a legal right in a common law court and then go to Chancery for an equitable remedy, at great cost and inconvenience. Option A is wrong because Chancery could not award damages. Option C is wrong because common law courts could not grant injunctions, and option B was not the route.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Which statement best illustrates that there is no watertight classification of law?

options.a: Much Nigerian land law has become public law since the Land Use Act, and tax law is as much private as public law
options.b: Public law and private law are tried in completely separate court systems in Nigeria
options.c: Criminal law and civil law never overlap
options.d: Every rule of law belongs to exactly one classification

questions.explanation: The classifications overlap: land law has become largely public law under the Land Use Act, taxation straddles public and private law, and assault is both a crime and a tort. Option B is false for Nigeria. Options D and C contradict the overlap that the classifications actually show.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Aisha loses her job after an accident at work leaves her unable to perform her duties, and she asks a solicitor to sue her employer. Which approach best reflects how classifications of law work in practice?

options.a: The case belongs only to criminal law, because an accident occurred
options.b: The solicitor may rely only on the law of contract, because subjects cannot be combined
options.c: The solicitor must combine contract law, labour law and the law of tort to build her claim
options.d: The solicitor must first decide whether the case is divine or natural law

questions.explanation: Classifications overlap in real life, and a practitioner must combine subjects: here contract, industrial or labour law, and tort. Option B wrongly treats the subjects as sealed off from each other. Options D and A apply categories that do not fit an employment claim.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Classified by origin, law has been described as eternal, divine, natural or human (positive) law. Which of the following is NOT one of these types?

options.a: Divine law
options.b: Eternal law
options.c: Natural law
options.d: Procedural law

questions.explanation: Procedural law belongs to the classification of law by function (substantive versus procedural), not to the types of law by origin. Eternal law (option B), divine law (option A) and natural law (option C), together with human or positive law, are the four types listed.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Which of the following is given as a perfect example of divine law?

options.a: The Ten Commandments in the Holy Bible
options.b: The Criminal Code Act
options.c: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
options.d: The Judicature Act 1875

questions.explanation: Divine law means the law of God or law from God, and the Ten Commandments are the standard example. Options B and D are laws made by human legislatures, and option C is an international instrument, so all three are positive law.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: A student argues that the Companies and Allied Matters Act is valid law simply because it was enacted by the National Assembly, whatever anyone thinks of its morality. Which type of law, and which view of law, does this reflect?

options.a: Eternal law, which governs all creation
options.b: Natural law, which requires law to conform to moral principles
options.c: Positive (human) law, as understood by legal positivism
options.d: Divine law, which comes from God

questions.explanation: Positive law is law laid down by a human authority in society, and legal positivism holds that such law is valid without regard to morality. Option B would test the Act against higher moral principles. Options D and A describe law that does not come from human enactment.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: What is one practical importance of the classification of law into civil and criminal law for a lawyer?

options.a: It decides whether the case will be governed by divine law or natural law
options.b: It helps decide whether to bring a civil action, set the criminal process in motion, or wait for a criminal case to end before suing
options.c: It determines whether a treaty has been domesticated
options.d: It shows whether a law was enacted by the legislature

questions.explanation: The civil/criminal classification separates private injuries from matters of public order and helps a lawyer choose the right way to obtain redress. Option A mixes in types of law by origin. Option D is the job of the written/unwritten classification, and option C belongs to municipal versus international law.

questions.topic: Aspects and Classifications of Law
questions.question: Which pairing correctly matches a classification of law with its main focus?

options.a: Municipal v international: punishment versus compensation
options.b: Written v unwritten: law within a country versus law between countries
options.c: Substantive v procedural: the rules themselves versus how they are enforced in court
options.d: Public v private: enacted law versus case law

questions.explanation: Substantive law is the body of rules on rights and duties, while procedural law governs how those rules are enforced. Option D actually describes written versus unwritten law. Option B describes municipal versus international law, and option A describes criminal versus civil law.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven techniques of social control through law?

options.a: The grievance-remedial technique
options.b: The penal technique
options.c: The fiscal technique
options.d: The judicial precedent technique

questions.explanation: The seven techniques are the penal, grievance-remedial, private arranging, constitutive, administrative-regulatory, fiscal and conferral of social benefit techniques. Judicial precedent is a doctrine for following earlier court decisions, not a technique of social control. Option B, Option A and Option C are all on the list.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Robert Summers identified five basic techniques of social control through law. Which two techniques were later added to his list to make seven?

options.a: The conferral of social benefit technique and the penal technique
options.b: The constitutive technique and the fiscal technique
options.c: The penal technique and the grievance-remedial technique
options.d: The private arranging technique and the administrative-regulatory technique

questions.explanation: Summers listed the penal, grievance-remedial, private arranging, administrative-regulatory and public-benefit conferral techniques; the constitutive and fiscal techniques were added later. Option C and Option D are all on Summers' original list. In Option A, the social benefit technique is Summers' public-benefit conferral technique renamed, not a new addition.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: The distinctive feature of the constitutive technique of social control is

options.a: the payment of damages to a person who has been wronged
options.b: the punishment of persons who commit crimes
options.c: the use of taxes to discourage harmful conduct
options.d: the creation of a new legal person separate from its members, such as an incorporated company

questions.explanation: Through the constitutive technique, the law helps people pool efforts and resources by giving the group its own legal personality, which brings perpetual succession and limited liability. Option B is the penal technique, Option A the grievance-remedial technique and Option C the fiscal technique.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: What principle was established by the House of Lords in Salomon v. Salomon & Co. Ltd?

options.a: A company is merely an agent of its majority shareholder
options.b: A manufacturer owes a duty of care to the final consumer of its products
options.c: A duly incorporated company is a legal person separate and distinct from its members
options.d: A statute must be interpreted by looking at the mischief it was meant to cure

questions.explanation: The House of Lords held that Salomon & Co. Ltd was a different person from Mr Salomon, so as a secured creditor he could be paid first. This separate legal personality is the bedrock of the constitutive technique. Option B is the rule in Donoghue v. Stevenson, Option D is the mischief rule, and Option A is the argument the House of Lords rejected.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: A food manufacturer must obtain NAFDAC approval after meeting set standards before starting production. This is an example of which technique of social control?

options.a: The penal technique
options.b: The conferral of social benefit technique
options.c: The administrative-regulatory technique
options.d: The private arranging technique

questions.explanation: Under the administrative-regulatory technique, government agencies set minimum standards and enforce them through licensing, inspection, warnings and revocation, as NAFDAC and the NCC do. Option A prohibits and punishes anti-social conduct, Option D leaves people to arrange their own affairs within a legal framework, and Option B provides amenities like roads and health care.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: How does the administrative-regulatory technique mainly differ from the grievance-remedial technique?

options.a: It creates new legal persons, while the grievance-remedial technique punishes offenders
options.b: It applies only to criminal offences, while the grievance-remedial technique applies only to taxation
options.c: It is used only by private individuals, while the grievance-remedial technique is used only by government
options.d: It works preventively, before a grievance arises, while the grievance-remedial technique gives a remedy after a wrong has occurred

questions.explanation: Regulation tries to stop harm before it happens, for example by making sure food is produced in safe conditions, while the grievance-remedial technique compensates a consumer who has already been harmed. Option B, Option A and Option C misdescribe both techniques.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Government increases the penalty charged for gas flaring and uses income tax to narrow the gap between the rich and the poor. These measures illustrate

options.a: the fiscal technique
options.b: the constitutive technique
options.c: the private arranging technique
options.d: the grievance-remedial technique

questions.explanation: The fiscal technique uses taxes, levies and charges not only to raise money but also to redistribute income and discourage anti-social conduct such as gas flaring. Option B creates legal persons, Option C gives people a framework for arranging their own affairs, and Option D provides remedies for civil wrongs.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: A person is free to choose whether to make a will, but if he does, it must be in writing, signed and witnessed as the law requires. This illustrates

options.a: the fiscal technique
options.b: the administrative-regulatory technique
options.c: the private arranging technique
options.d: the penal technique

questions.explanation: In the private arranging technique, the law provides a framework of rules for valid private transactions, such as wills, marriages and trusts, and leaves the individual to decide whether to use it. Option D punishes crimes, Option A works through taxation, and Option B involves government agencies licensing and inspecting activities.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: The grievance-remedial technique, which defines remediable grievances, specifies remedies and provides for their enforcement, operates mainly in the area of

options.a: the incorporation of companies
options.b: civil law, such as contract, tort and property
options.c: criminal law and the prisons
options.d: taxation and customs duties

questions.explanation: This technique gives an aggrieved person remedies such as damages, injunction or specific performance through the courts, which is the domain of civil law. Criminal law and prisons (Option C) belong to the penal technique, taxation (Option D) to the fiscal technique, and incorporation (Option A) to the constitutive technique.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Government programmes that provide roads, education, health care and poverty relief, aiming to improve welfare so as to prevent social strife, illustrate

options.a: the constitutive technique
options.b: the conferral of social benefit technique
options.c: the grievance-remedial technique
options.d: the penal technique

questions.explanation: The conferral of social benefit technique does not directly regulate conduct; it improves people's welfare in the expectation that this will bring order and peace. Option D works by punishing deviant conduct, Option A by creating legal persons, and Option C by giving remedies for civil wrongs.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: A victim agrees not to press criminal charges against an offender in return for payment of compensation. This alternative to the penal system is called

options.a: compounding
options.b: caution
options.c: self-help
options.d: insurance

questions.explanation: Compounding is receiving property or some other consideration in return for an agreement not to prosecute someone who has committed a crime. Option B is a warning given instead of full punishment, Option C is the victim taking the law into his own hands, and Option D is an alternative to the grievance-remedial technique for civil losses.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: In Aoko v. Fagbemi, adultery was held not to be a criminal offence because

options.a: the accused had already been punished under customary law
options.b: it was not defined as an offence, with its penalty prescribed, in any written law
options.c: the parties had settled the matter privately
options.d: the High Court has no jurisdiction over matrimonial matters

questions.explanation: Under the Nigerian Constitution, now section 36(12) of the 1999 Constitution, a person cannot be convicted of an offence unless it is defined and its penalty prescribed in a written law. Since adultery was not so defined, it could not be punished. Option A, Option C and Option D were not the basis of the decision.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: The control of social behaviour, that is, behaviour that affects others, is loosely described as

options.a: social order
options.b: social control
options.c: social engineering
options.d: non-intervention

questions.explanation: Social control is loosely the control of behaviour that affects other people. Option C is Pound's idea of law as a tool for balancing competing interests. Option D is an alternative to the penal technique, and option A is a wider idea than social control.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: The term 'social control' was coined by sociologists. Who first used it, to refer to institutions that keep individual behaviour in line with group demands?

options.a: William G. Sumner
options.b: Edward A. Ross
options.c: Richard Quinney
options.d: Robert S. Summers

questions.explanation: Edward A. Ross, one of the fathers of American sociology, first used 'social control' for regulative institutions such as public opinion, morals, education and law. Option A, a contemporary of Ross, used the term to show how folkways control conduct. Option D classified legal techniques, and option C wrote later about law as the most explicit form of control.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Roscoe Pound described law as

options.a: social control through the systematic application of the force of politically organised society
options.b: the body of rules regulating human conduct regarded as binding by members of a community
options.c: the most specialised and highly finished engine of control employed by society
options.d: the command of a sovereign backed by sanction
