questions.explanation: Pound, a leading figure of the sociological school, described law as social control through the systematic application of the force of politically organised society. Option D is the positivist command theory. Option B is Elias's definition, and option C is Ross's description of law.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: In his work on social control through law, Roscoe Pound wrote that in the modern world law has become

options.a: the paramount agent of social control
options.b: a minor agent compared with religion
options.c: less important as societies grow more complex
options.d: an agency of control only in criminal matters

questions.explanation: Pound accepted that the household, church, school and voluntary bodies share the task, but held that 'the brunt of the task falls on the legal order' and that law has become the paramount agent of social control. Options B and D understate his view. Option C contradicts the view that complex societies rely more on law.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Roscoe Pound's idea of law as 'social engineering' sees law mainly as a tool for

options.a: keeping law completely separate from society
options.b: punishing every immoral act in society
options.c: enforcing the command of the sovereign without regard to society
options.d: balancing and harmonising competing social interests

questions.explanation: Pound saw law as social engineering: a means of balancing competing claims and interests in society so that the most wants are met with the least friction or disruption. Option B is not his aim and is impossible anyway. Option C reflects the command theory, and option A reflects the pure theory, which Pound's sociological approach rejected.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an informal means of social control?

options.a: Imprisonment after a criminal trial
options.b: Ridicule
options.c: Ostracism
options.d: Gossip

questions.explanation: Imprisonment after trial is a formal legal sanction applied through the criminal justice system. Ridicule (option B), gossip (option D) and ostracism (option C), together with censure, are informal means that societies usually use spontaneously.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: After a scandal, the people of a village refuse to buy from or sell to a family and stop their children from mixing with the family's children, in line with local custom. What kind of social control is this?

options.a: Informal social control through ostracism
options.b: The administrative-regulatory technique
options.c: The fiscal technique
options.d: Formal social control through the penal technique

questions.explanation: Shunning a family by refusing to trade or mix with them is ostracism, an informal and spontaneous means of social control. Option D would need the State to define an offence and prosecute it in court. Options C and B are legal techniques that use taxes and licensing, which play no part here.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Law has advantages that no other instrument of social control can match. Which of the following is NOT one of them?

options.a: A wealth of detailed rules
options.b: Explicit sanctions
options.c: Organised institutions and machinery for enforcement
options.d: Rules that are never broken

questions.explanation: Law is often broken, and some laws are seen in breach more than in enforcement, so 'rules that are never broken' is not an advantage it can claim. A wealth of detailed rules (option A), explicit sanctions (option B) and organised enforcement machinery (option C), together with regularised procedure, are its distinctive strengths.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Some sociologists deny that law is the paramount instrument of social control. Which of the following is NOT one of the factors behind their view?

options.a: Some laws are seen in breach more than in enforcement
options.b: Law has explicit sanctions backed by organised enforcement machinery
options.c: Enforcement agencies exercise discretion in enforcing laws
options.d: There are dead-letter laws in the statute books

questions.explanation: Explicit sanctions and organised enforcement are strengths of law, not reasons to doubt it. Frequent breach (option A), dead-letter laws (option D) and the discretion of enforcement agencies (option C) are the factors that weaken law's hold, along with the fact that enforcement does not always prevent the evil aimed at.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Explaining why the legal system is the most explicit form of social control, Quinney said law consists of three elements. Which of the following is NOT one of them?

options.a: Planned use of sanctions to support the rules
options.b: Specific rules of conduct
options.c: Designated officials to interpret and enforce the rules
options.d: Spontaneous public ridicule of offenders

questions.explanation: Spontaneous ridicule is an informal means of control, not an element of law. Quinney's three elements are specific rules of conduct (option B), planned use of sanctions (option A) and designated officials to interpret and enforce the rules (option C).

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the functions of law as an instrument of social control?

options.a: Facilitating co-operative action
options.b: Constituting and regulating the principal organs of power
options.c: Maintaining public order and suppressing deviant behaviour
options.d: Guaranteeing that no crime will ever be committed

questions.explanation: No legal system can guarantee that crime will never happen; deviants exist in every society. Law does maintain public order and suppress deviance (option C), facilitate co-operative action (option A), constitute and regulate the organs of power (option B), and communicate and reinforce social values.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Robert S. Summers identified five basic techniques used in modern law. Which of the following was NOT on his original list?

options.a: The penal technique
options.b: The grievance-remedial technique
options.c: The administrative-regulatory technique
options.d: The constitutive technique

questions.explanation: Summers' five were penal, grievance-remedial, private arranging, administrative-regulatory and public-benefit conferral. The constitutive technique was one of the two that Farrar and Dugdale later added, together with the fiscal technique. Options A, B and C were all on Summers' original list.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Farrar and Dugdale added two techniques to Summers' list. These were

options.a: the private arranging and administrative-regulatory techniques
options.b: the constitutive and fiscal techniques
options.c: the warning and compounding techniques
options.d: the penal and grievance-remedial techniques

questions.explanation: Farrar and Dugdale added the constitutive and fiscal techniques, bringing the total to seven. Options D and A were already among Summers' five. Option C names alternatives to the penal technique, not techniques of social control in their own right.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Farrar and Dugdale renamed the last technique on Summers' list, the 'public-benefit conferral' technique, as

options.a: the conferral of social benefits technique
options.b: the fiscal technique
options.c: the private arranging technique
options.d: the constitutive technique

questions.explanation: Summers' 'public-benefit conferral' was renamed 'conferral of social benefits' by Farrar and Dugdale. Options B and D are the two new techniques they added, not a renaming. Option C was already a separate technique on Summers' list.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: The legal techniques of social control are found

options.a: only in international treaties
options.b: only in statutes enacted by the legislature
options.c: both in legislation and in rules developed by the courts (judge-made law)
options.d: only in customary law

questions.explanation: Law here is not limited to rules made by the legislature: some techniques are firmly rooted in judge-made law, and the techniques show both main elements of modern law, legislation and judge-made law. Options B, D and A each wrongly limit the techniques to a single kind of law.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: The penal technique of social control works mainly by

options.a: spelling out prohibited conduct, the penalty for breach, the procedure for determining guilt and the appropriate punishment
options.b: setting minimum standards and licensing lawful activities in advance
options.c: granting compensation to persons whose private rights have been breached
options.d: providing social amenities such as roads, schools and health care

questions.explanation: The penal technique discourages deviance by stating what is forbidden, what the penalty is, how guilt is decided and what punishment follows. Option C describes the grievance-remedial technique. Option B describes the administrative-regulatory technique, and option D describes conferral of social benefits.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: The criminal justice system is created to apply the penal technique. Which of the following is NOT part of it?

options.a: Rules setting out acts and omissions that violate the criminal law
options.b: Insurance companies settling motor accident claims
options.c: The Police Force and other enforcement agencies
options.d: Prisons and other approved detention centres

questions.explanation: Insurance settlement is an alternative to the grievance-remedial technique, not part of the criminal justice system. That system is made up of the rules defining crimes (option A), the police and other enforcement agencies (option C), and prisons and detention centres (option D).

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Ifeoma's phone is snatched in Ikeja. Instead of hunting the thief down herself, she reports to the police, who investigate. The decision whether to prosecute is then taken by the police or the Attorney-General, based on the evidence. This process illustrates

options.a: the private arranging technique
options.b: how the penal technique brings about social control
options.c: reciprocity and self-help
options.d: the conferral of social benefits technique

questions.explanation: Under the penal technique the victim reports to the police instead of resorting to vengeance, the State investigates and decides whether to prosecute, and guilt must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. Option A concerns individuals arranging their own affairs, and option D concerns welfare provision. Option C is exactly what Ifeoma avoided.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Evidence emerges that Mr. Okon committed a fraud twelve years ago. Under the general rule, can he still be prosecuted?

options.a: Yes, but only if the victim first sues him in a civil court
options.b: No, because crimes become statute-barred after ten years
options.c: Yes, because as a general rule limitation periods do not run against crimes
options.d: No, because all criminal prosecutions must begin within six years

questions.explanation: As a general rule the statute of limitation does not run against a crime, so an offender can be prosecuted however long ago the offence was committed. Options D and B borrow the five, six or ten year limitation periods that apply to civil actions. Option A invents a requirement.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: The alternative to the penal system under which society deliberately chooses not to criminalise certain socially disapproved or immoral conduct is called

options.a: non-intervention
options.b: reciprocity
options.c: warning or caution
options.d: compounding

questions.explanation: Non-intervention reflects that society cannot, and sometimes should not, penalise every immoral act, as when adultery was held not to be a crime in Aoko v Fagbemi. Option D is an agreement not to prosecute in return for some benefit. Option C still involves the system acting on an offender, and option B is private vengeance.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Two brothers living in the same house have a minor scuffle over a borrowed shirt. The police at the station they visit encourage them to settle the matter within the family instead of charging either of them. Which alternative to the penal system does this reflect?

options.a: Reciprocity and self-help
options.b: Compounding for money
options.c: Non-intervention
options.d: Administrative regulation

questions.explanation: Where members of the same household are involved in less serious matters, there may be good reason not to intervene, and the police encourage private settlement; this is non-intervention. Option A means private vengeance. Option B involves receiving property in return for not prosecuting, and option D concerns licensing and standards.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: During a High Court sitting, a spectator's phone rings loudly and disturbs proceedings. Instead of committing him for contempt of court, the judge warns him and lets him go. This is an example of

options.a: the grievance-remedial technique
options.b: warning or caution
options.c: compounding
options.d: non-intervention

questions.explanation: A judge warning someone who disturbs court proceedings, instead of committing him for contempt, is the standard example of warning or caution as an alternative to full punishment. Option C needs an agreement with a victim. Option D is wrong because the judge did act, and option A is a civil-law technique.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: A man suspected of stealing a phone at a market is stripped, beaten and set on fire by a mob without any trial. Which alternative to the penal system does this represent, and how is it regarded?

options.a: Reciprocity and self-help; it is dangerous and a symptom of an underdeveloped system
options.b: Compounding; it is a lawful private settlement
options.c: Warning or caution; it is suitable for petty offenders
options.d: Non-intervention; the State has chosen not to act

questions.explanation: Mob 'jungle justice' is reciprocity and self-help, the 'eye for an eye' approach, which is described as a symptom of an underdeveloped system and is unfit for modern times. Option B needs an agreement in return for not prosecuting. Option C is a mild official response, and option D misdescribes a violent private act.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Which of the following is a key danger of self-help ('jungle justice')?

options.a: The offender always receives a lighter sentence than in court
options.b: It is too slow compared with court proceedings
options.c: It protects the perpetrators from civil and criminal liability
options.d: An innocent person may be punished without a fair hearing

questions.explanation: Self-help risks punishing an innocent person without a fair hearing, and those who take part are themselves liable to civil and criminal sanctions. Options A and B are not the dangers identified. Option C is false, since the perpetrators expose themselves to liability.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: The receipt of property or other consideration in return for an agreement not to prosecute someone who has committed a crime is called

options.a: compounding
options.b: non-intervention
options.c: restitutio in integrum
options.d: arbitration

questions.explanation: Compounding is an arrangement under which the victim agrees not to press criminal charges once certain conditions, usually compensation, are met. Option B is a policy choice not to criminalise conduct at all. Option D is a way of settling civil disputes, and option C is a civil remedy restoring the original position.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: A driver negligently knocks down a pedestrian in Ibadan, causing minor injuries. The pedestrian's relatives agree not to insist on prosecution after the driver promises to pay N150,000 as compensation. This arrangement is an example of

options.a: the fiscal technique
options.b: the constitutive technique
options.c: warning or caution
options.d: compounding

questions.explanation: An agreement by the victim's side not to press charges in return for compensation is compounding, and a minor accident is the classic example. Option A uses taxes and levies. Option C is a warning by an official such as a judge, and option B concerns creating legal persons.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: In Federal Civil Service Commission v Laoye, Oputa JSC criticised dismissing a civil servant accused of conspiracy and stealing a large sum of hard currency without first prosecuting him. What point did he make?

options.a: Summary dismissal is always a better remedy than prosecution
options.b: Compounding is the preferred way of dealing with serious fraud
options.c: Justice is reached through finding the truth, and the means of finding the truth of a criminal charge is trial in open court
options.d: Civil servants can never be dismissed for misconduct

questions.explanation: Oputa JSC held that justice is reached through finding the truth, and that the truth of a criminal charge is tested by trial in open court; the employer could dismiss after conviction. This casts doubt on private alternatives such as dismissal in place of prosecution. Options A and B contradict his reasoning, and option D overstates it.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Professor Summers explained the grievance-remedial technique as one that

options.a: creates new legal persons separate from their members
options.b: uses taxation to discourage anti-social behaviour
options.c: spells out prohibited conduct and prescribes punishment
options.d: defines remediable grievances, specifies remedies and provides for enforcement of remedial awards

questions.explanation: The grievance-remedial technique, used mainly in civil law, defines which grievances can be remedied, states the remedies and provides for their enforcement. Option C is the penal technique. Option A is the constitutive technique, and option B is the fiscal technique.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: The grievance-remedial technique is used mainly in civil law. Which of the following areas does NOT mainly employ it?

options.a: Law of contract
options.b: Criminal law
options.c: Family law
options.d: Law of torts

questions.explanation: Criminal law employs the penal technique, which punishes rather than remedies. Contract (option A), torts (option D) and family law (option C), along with commercial law, property, equity and trusts, and labour law, are the areas that use the grievance-remedial technique.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a remedy available under the grievance-remedial technique?

options.a: Special damages
options.b: Injunction
options.c: Specific performance
options.d: Imprisonment

questions.explanation: Imprisonment is a penal sanction, not a civil remedy. Special damages (option A), specific performance (option C) and injunction (option B), together with general damages and restitutio in integrum, are remedies for an aggrieved person under this technique.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: What is the logical basis of the grievance-remedial technique as a means of social control?

options.a: Punishing offenders deters others from committing crimes
options.b: Licensing prevents harm before it occurs
options.c: An adequately remedied person is pacified, which discourages injustice and stops people taking the law into their own hands
options.d: High taxes discourage harmful activities

questions.explanation: If an aggrieved person gets an adequate remedy, he is likely to be truly pacified, so the law discourages injustice and self-help. Option A is the logic of the penal technique, option D of the fiscal technique, and option B of the administrative-regulatory technique.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Under the rule in Smith v Selwyn, where a wrongful act is a felony,

options.a: the victim may sue in tort but the State can never prosecute
options.b: the victim loses any right to sue once a complaint is made to the police
options.c: the civil action and the prosecution must always be heard together
options.d: no action in tort can be brought until the defendant has been prosecuted or a reasonable excuse is shown for not prosecuting

questions.explanation: The rule in Smith v Selwyn holds back a tort action for a felony until the defendant has been prosecuted or a reasonable excuse for not prosecuting is shown. Its application in Nigeria is disputed, and it has been called archaic. Options A, C and B misstate the rule.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: A supply contract between Adeola Foods Ltd and a transporter states that the transporter will pay N50,000 for each day of late delivery. When a delivery is three days late, the transporter pays N150,000 without going to court. Which alternative to the grievance-remedial technique does this illustrate?

options.a: Compounding
options.b: The penal technique
options.c: Private settlement through a liquidated damages clause
options.d: The fiscal technique

questions.explanation: Parties may agree in advance exactly how much a defaulting party will pay, and if they carry it out there is no need for litigation; this is private settlement. Option A concerns crimes, not contract breaches. Option B involves prosecution, and option D involves the government's financial policy.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Two cars collide on the Third Mainland Bridge. Both drivers have comprehensive cover, so they exchange details and refer the matter to their insurance companies instead of suing each other. Which alternative to the grievance-remedial technique is this?

options.a: Non-intervention
options.b: Insurance
options.c: Compounding
options.d: Arbitration

questions.explanation: Handling a motor crash through the parties' insurers instead of the courts is the insurance alternative, and it depends on the type of cover taken. Option D involves an arbitrator making an award. Option C concerns criminal charges, and option A is an alternative to the penal system.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a recognised advantage of arbitration over litigation?

options.a: The dispute is usually disposed of much more quickly
options.b: An arbitrator familiar with the technical background of the dispute can be chosen
options.c: It is always cheaper than going to court
options.d: Proceedings can be kept secret and informal

questions.explanation: Experience shows that arbitration is not necessarily cheaper, and it can cost more if a party goes to court to set aside the award. Speed (option A), expert arbitrators (option B) and secrecy and informality (option D) are recognised advantages.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: A construction contract contains a clause requiring disputes to be referred to arbitration. Before any arbitration, one party rushes to the High Court with a claim. What is the position?

options.a: The arbitration clause makes the matter a criminal offence
options.b: The court must hear the case because arbitration clauses are void
options.c: The court can freely rehear any later arbitral award on its merits
options.d: Going to court is premature; the dispute should first be submitted to arbitration

questions.explanation: Where a contract has an arbitration clause, it is premature to go to court without first submitting the dispute to arbitration, and courts can set aside an award only within narrow limits. Option B wrongly treats the clause as void. Option A confuses civil and criminal matters, and option C ignores the narrow scope of court intervention.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: The private arranging technique is best described as a system whereby

options.a: the law provides a framework of rules for the validity of private transactions, leaving individuals to arrange their affairs within it
options.b: the state prosecutes persons who break the criminal law
options.c: the state directly provides social amenities to citizens
options.d: government agencies license and inspect private operators

questions.explanation: Under the private arranging technique, the law sets the rules that determine whether private transactions such as marriages, trusts and wills are valid, and individuals choose whether and how to act within them. Option C is conferral of social benefits. Option D is the administrative-regulatory technique, and option B is the penal technique.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Alhaji Musa writes and signs his will, but only one witness is present when he signs. Assuming the general rule applies, what is the consequence under the private arranging technique?

options.a: The will is invalid and his property will be distributed under the rules of intestacy
options.b: The will is valid because no special form is required for a will
options.c: The will is valid because he signed it himself
options.d: The will is invalid and the state confiscates his property

questions.explanation: A person is free to make a will or not, but if he does, it must meet the legal requirements: generally it must be in writing and signed by the testator in the presence of at least two witnesses present at the same time, who attest it. Otherwise it is invalid and intestacy rules apply. Options B and C ignore the witness requirement, and option D invents confiscation.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Segun married Funmi under the Marriage Act. While that marriage subsists, he goes through a customary marriage with Halima. How does the private arranging technique treat the second marriage?

options.a: It is valid if Segun pays tax on it
options.b: It is valid, because each person may choose the form of marriage freely at any time
options.c: It is invalid, because a person in a subsisting statutory marriage cannot validly contract another marriage under any system
options.d: It is valid, because customary law permits more than one wife

questions.explanation: A person may choose to marry under the Marriage Act, customary law or Islamic law, but once he chooses one system he must comply with its rules. A person in a subsisting statutory marriage cannot validly marry anyone else under any of the systems. Options D and B ignore the binding effect of the first choice, and option A is absurd.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Mrs. Eze holds a statutory right of occupancy in Lagos and agrees to sell her interest to a buyer. Although this is a private transaction, she must first obtain the Governor's consent. This shows that

options.a: areas once left to private arranging are moving towards direct government intervention
options.b: private arrangements no longer need to comply with any legal framework
options.c: land transactions are governed only by the penal technique
options.d: the constitutive technique has replaced private arranging

questions.explanation: Under the Land Use Act a holder must obtain the Governor's consent before assigning, mortgaging or otherwise alienating an interest in land, which is an example of law stepping into an area once left to private arranging. Option C is wrong because no crime is involved. Option D concerns creating legal persons, and option B contradicts the point.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Kola buys a car on hire purchase for a total hire-purchase price of N4,000,000 and has paid N2,600,000 when he falls behind with his instalments. Under section 9 of the Hire Purchase Act, which bars an owner of a motor vehicle from recovering it except by court action once three-fifths of the price has been paid, what may the owner do?

options.a: Seize the car without a court action, because Kola has not paid the full price
options.b: Recover the car only by court action, because Kola has paid more than three-quarters of the price
options.c: Recover the car only by an action in court, because Kola has paid more than three-fifths of the price
options.d: Seize the car at once without going to court, because instalments are in arrears

questions.explanation: Kola has paid 2,600,000/4,000,000 = 0.65, or 65 percent, which is more than three-fifths (60 percent), so the owner can recover the car only by court action. Options D and A state the old position before the Act, as in Atere v Amao, where owners could seize goods even when nearly all the instalments had been paid. Option B uses the wrong threshold, and 65 percent is below three-quarters anyway.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: How is the constitutive technique related to the private arranging technique?

options.a: It is identical to private arranging and was not separately recognised
options.b: It is an offshoot of private arranging: nobody must form a company, but those who do must meet the legal requirements, so it takes off where private arranging stops
options.c: It replaces private arranging by banning private contracts
options.d: It is the opposite of private arranging because it compels everyone to form a company

questions.explanation: Individuals are free to choose whether to form a company, as with other private arrangements, but those who do must comply with the law so that the company comes into existence. In that sense the constitutive technique takes off where private arranging stops. Option D is false because nobody is compelled. Option A ignores its separate recognition by Farrar and Dugdale, and option C is false.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Ada and two friends incorporate AdaTech Ltd. The company borrows N20,000,000 and later fails, and the bank seeks to make the three shareholders personally liable for the company's debt. Which principle supports the shareholders' defence?

options.a: The rule in Smith v Selwyn bars all claims against shareholders
options.b: A duly incorporated company is a legal person separate from its members, as held in Salomon v Salomon
options.c: Debts of a company are cancelled once it is incorporated
options.d: Shareholders are always personally liable for company debts

questions.explanation: Salomon v Salomon established that an incorporated company is a separate legal person, which brings limited liability for its members. This principle is the bedrock of company law, though it may not be used as a tool for fraud. Option A concerns tort claims arising from felonies. Option D denies separate personality, and option C is absurd.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: In Salomon v Salomon, why was Mr. Salomon entitled to be paid before the company's unsecured creditors?

options.a: Salomon was the managing director and so had priority
options.b: The court found that the company was a sham
options.c: The company was a separate legal person, and Salomon was a secured debenture holder
options.d: Salomon held all the shares and therefore owned the company's assets

questions.explanation: The House of Lords held that Salomon and Co. Ltd. was a separate person, so it could owe Salomon money, and as a secured creditor holding debentures he was paid first. Option A confuses office with priority. Option B states the liquidator's argument, which was rejected, and option D contradicts the company's separate ownership of its assets.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: The constitutive technique is used to create many kinds of bodies. Which of the following is given as an example of a group the law recognises WITHOUT giving it legal personality?

options.a: A political party
options.b: A religious body registered as incorporated trustees
options.c: A university established by statute
options.d: A statutory corporation

questions.explanation: The law gives a framework to some collective groups, such as partnerships, labour unions, political parties and professional bodies, without vesting legal personality in them. Statutory universities (option C), statutory corporations (option D) and incorporated trustees (option B) are created as legal persons through the constitutive technique.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Under the administrative-regulatory technique, government agencies

options.a: adopt regulatory standards, communicate them to private operators and take steps to ensure compliance
options.b: compensate victims of breach of contract
options.c: punish offenders after a crime has been committed
options.d: distribute social amenities such as low-cost housing

questions.explanation: The administrative-regulatory technique sets minimum standards in the public interest, makes them known to operators and enforces compliance through licensing, inspection and similar steps. Option C is the reactive penal technique. Option B is grievance-remedial, and option D is conferral of social benefits.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: In enforcing the administrative-regulatory technique, which step is normally the last resort?

options.a: Writing warning letters
options.b: Civil litigation or criminal prosecution
options.c: Licensing
options.d: Inspection

questions.explanation: Agencies usually rely first on licensing, inspection, warning letters or revoking a licence, and turn to administrative proceedings, civil litigation or criminal prosecution only as a last resort. Options C, D and A are the earlier, preventive steps.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Mrs. Adeyemi plans to open a private nursery and primary school in Surulere. Before admitting pupils, she must apply to the Ministry of Education for a permit, which is granted only if the school meets set standards. Which technique of social control is at work?

options.a: The penal technique
options.b: The fiscal technique
options.c: The private arranging technique
options.d: The administrative-regulatory technique

questions.explanation: Requiring a permit from the Ministry of Education before a private school opens, with standards checked in advance, is the administrative-regulatory technique. Option A would apply only after an offence. Option C concerns the validity of private transactions, and option B uses taxes.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: A new company wants to provide mobile telephone services in Nigeria and must first obtain a licence from the Nigerian Communications Commission and comply with its standards. This is an example of

options.a: the conferral of social benefits technique
options.b: the grievance-remedial technique
options.c: the administrative-regulatory technique
options.d: compounding

questions.explanation: The Federal Government regulates mobile and wireless service providers through the NCC, which is an administrative-regulatory technique. Option B would come into play only after a customer suffered a wrong. Option A is government provision of welfare, and option D is an alternative to prosecution.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: How does the administrative-regulatory technique differ from the penal technique?

options.a: It applies only after harm has occurred, while the penal technique is preventive
options.b: It punishes offenders more severely than the penal technique
options.c: It regulates wholesome activities, while the penal technique prohibits and sanctions anti-social behaviour
options.d: It is enforced only by private individuals

questions.explanation: The administrative-regulatory technique regulates lawful, wholesome activities such as food production and schooling, while the penal technique prohibits and punishes anti-social conduct. Option B is false because punishment is a last resort under regulation. Option A reverses the preventive nature of regulation, and option D ignores the role of government agencies.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: A food regulator inspects factories to ensure that drinks are produced hygienically, while a consumer made ill by a contaminated drink sues the manufacturer for compensation. Which pairing is correct?

options.a: Inspection is fiscal; the lawsuit is constitutive
options.b: Both are examples of the penal technique
options.c: Inspection is grievance-remedial; the lawsuit is administrative-regulatory
options.d: Inspection is administrative-regulatory (preventive); the lawsuit is grievance-remedial

questions.explanation: Regulation works before any harm, aiming to stop a manufacturer from breaching its duty to consumers, while the grievance-remedial technique compensates a consumer after harm has happened. Option C reverses the two. Options B and A apply techniques that do not fit either activity.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Although the classical aim of taxation is to raise money, the fiscal technique is also used in modern times to

options.a: redistribute income, stimulate economic growth and discourage anti-social behaviour
options.b: punish crimes through imprisonment
options.c: license schools and telecom operators
options.d: create new legal persons

questions.explanation: Beyond raising revenue, taxation and related financial measures are used to redistribute income, stimulate growth and discourage harmful conduct. Option D is the constitutive technique, option B the penal technique, and option C the administrative-regulatory technique.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: To discourage oil companies from flaring gas, the Federal Government sharply increases the financial penalty payable for each unit of gas flared, so that flaring becomes more expensive than using the gas. Which technique of social control is this?

options.a: The private arranging technique
options.b: The constitutive technique
options.c: Warning or caution
options.d: The fiscal technique

questions.explanation: Using government financial measures, here a heavier charge on gas flaring, to discourage environmentally harmful conduct is the fiscal technique; the 1998 budget increased the gas-flaring penalty for this purpose. Option B concerns creating legal persons. Option A concerns private transactions, and option C is an alternative to penal punishment.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: The conferral of social benefits technique is best described as one that

options.a: directly regulates conduct by prescribing punishments
options.b: creates companies with separate legal personality
options.c: provides social amenities and welfare to improve citizens' well-being, without directly regulating their conduct
options.d: sets licensing standards for private businesses

questions.explanation: This technique has government provide roads, education, electricity, housing, health care and social security. It does not directly regulate behaviour; it expects better welfare to bring order and peace. Option A is the penal technique, option D the administrative-regulatory technique, and option B the constitutive technique.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: To reduce unrest in an oil-producing area, the government sets up a development commission to build roads, schools and health centres, and funds a poverty eradication programme for young people there. Which technique of social control does this mainly use?

options.a: The penal technique
options.b: Conferral of social benefits
options.c: The grievance-remedial technique
options.d: Compounding

questions.explanation: Providing amenities and welfare programmes, as with the NDDC or NAPEP, to improve living standards and so promote order is the conferral of social benefits technique. Option A would punish offenders. Option C compensates individual civil wrongs, and option D is a private alternative to prosecution.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: What has been identified as a major weakness of the conferral of social benefits technique in Nigeria?

options.a: It cannot be supported by any law
options.b: Programmes have often been poorly implemented and hijacked by elites, so only crumbs reach the target group
options.c: The technique has been used so effectively that poverty has disappeared
options.d: It relies entirely on imprisonment, which is costly

questions.explanation: Despite many welfare programmes, poverty and welfare remain dismal because most programmes were poorly implemented and hijacked by elites. Option C contradicts the poor outcomes. Option D confuses this technique with the penal one, and option A is wrong because laws on social security, education, health and industry fall within it.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Which statement best reflects the relationship between the different techniques of social control?

options.a: Each technique operates in complete isolation and can never be combined
options.b: The penal technique has replaced all the other techniques
options.c: Only one technique may be used in any area of law
options.d: They often overlap and complement each other, and government may combine more than one technique to achieve an objective

questions.explanation: There are many similarities and overlaps between the techniques; they can complement each other, and when legislating, government must choose which technique or combination will best achieve its goals. Options A and C deny that they can be combined, and option B is false.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Two promoters form a company that sells a baby drug without NAFDAC approval, and several children who used it die. Sued, the promoters argue that they cannot be personally responsible because the company is a separate person. Which two techniques are mainly involved in analysing this problem?

options.a: The fiscal technique and the conferral of social benefits technique
options.b: The administrative-regulatory technique and the constitutive technique
options.c: Compounding and warning or caution
options.d: The private arranging technique and non-intervention

questions.explanation: Failing to obtain NAFDAC approval raises the administrative-regulatory technique, and the promoters' reliance on separate legal personality raises the constitutive technique and Salomon v Salomon. That principle was not meant to shield fraud or harm to the public. Options A, D and C do not address regulation of drugs or corporate personality.

questions.topic: Methods of Social Control through Law
questions.question: Bisi, a cashier of a co-operative society, steals society funds, then refunds everything at the police station and begs for forgiveness. The prosecutor suggests dropping the charges, but the society's executive committee resolves to press the case to the end. Why is compounding unavailable here?

options.a: Compounding is available only when the accused has not refunded the money
options.b: Compounding applies only to offences committed by children
options.c: Compounding needs a compromise between the accused and the complainant, and the society refuses to compromise
options.d: Compounding can be ordered by the prosecutor against the victim's wishes

questions.explanation: Compounding rests on an agreement by the victim not to prosecute in return for some satisfaction, so it fails where the complainant, here the society, insists on prosecution. Option B confuses compounding with warning or caution for child offenders. Option A reverses the facts, and option D ignores that the victim must agree.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: A process in which only the disputing parties themselves confer with each other and agree on how to restore cordiality and harmony in their relationship, without any third party, is called

options.a: conciliation
options.b: arbitration
options.c: mediation
options.d: reconciliation

questions.explanation: Reconciliation is the act of harmonising differences where the only parties involved are the disputants themselves. Options A and C both bring in a neutral third party to help the parties settle, and option B involves a third party who actually decides the dispute.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Which of the following best describes arbitration?

options.a: A process whereby the disputants alone confer with each other to restore harmony in their relationship
options.b: A process whereby a neutral third party offers suggestions for settlement which the parties are free to accept or reject
options.c: A process whereby the parties agree to have their dispute settled by an independent third party and to be bound by his decision
options.d: A process whereby a judge appointed by the state hears the parties in a court of law and gives a self-executing judgment

questions.explanation: Arbitration rests on the parties' agreement to submit the dispute to an independent third party whose decision, called an award, binds them. Option B describes mediation, option D describes litigation in court, and option A describes reconciliation.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Among reconciliation, conciliation, mediation and arbitration, in which method does the third party actually decide the dispute on its merits?

options.a: Arbitration
options.b: Mediation
options.c: Conciliation
options.d: Reconciliation

questions.explanation: The arbitrator probes into the facts in fair detail and renders a decision on the merits, so he determines who is right and who is wrong. A conciliator or mediator (options C and B) only helps the parties reach their own settlement, and reconciliation (option D) has no third party at all.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: What is the main distinguishing factor between conciliation and reconciliation?

options.a: The number of parties involved, since conciliation brings in a third party as intermediary
options.b: Conciliation always produces an award that is enforceable like a court judgment
options.c: Reconciliation can only take place inside a court of law
options.d: Conciliation is used only for criminal matters while reconciliation is used for civil matters

questions.explanation: Reconciliation involves only the disputants, while conciliation adds a third person who acts as intermediary, so the difference lies in the number of parties. Option B is wrong because a conciliator's proposal is generally only a guide, option C is wrong because reconciliation is an informal, out-of-court process, and option D invents a division that does not exist.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: A neutral third party who rarely inquires into the facts of a dispute, does not attempt to apportion blame, and merely offers suggestions on terms of settlement which the disputants may accept or reject is

options.a: an arbitrator
options.b: a prosecutor
options.c: a judge
options.d: a mediator

questions.explanation: A mediator facilitates an amicable settlement and has no authority to make decisions that bind the parties. An arbitrator (option A) and a judge (option C) both find facts and decide who is right, while a prosecutor (option B) is a party who brings a criminal charge, not a neutral helper.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Which of the following statements about negotiation as a method of dispute resolution is correct?

options.a: Negotiation requires a conciliator appointed by the Minister of Labour
options.b: Once a third party such as a mediator is brought in, it is no longer negotiation
options.c: Negotiation ends with a binding award that the parties cannot later challenge
options.d: Negotiation can only begin after a suit has been filed and served in court

questions.explanation: Negotiation is the informal process in which the parties meet and settle their dispute themselves, so bringing in any third party changes its character. Option D is wrong because negotiation is usually the first attempt at resolving a conflict, option C describes arbitration, and option A describes statutory conciliation.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Which feature distinguishes the decision of a court in the adjudicatory method from the outcome of most non-adjudicatory methods?

options.a: It is binding and self-executing without another tribunal
options.b: It depends entirely on the parties' later acceptance of it
options.c: It is reached without the court ascertaining any facts
options.d: It is kept confidential and can never be taken on appeal

questions.explanation: A court judgment binds the parties and is self-executing, unlike most ADR outcomes. Option B describes mediation or reconciliation, whose terms the parties may accept or reject, option C is wrong because a court must first ascertain the facts before applying the law, and option D is wrong because court judgments may be reversed on appeal.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: The two main methods a judge or adjudicator may adopt in finding the facts of a dispute are the

options.a: deductive and inductive methods
options.b: conciliation and arbitration methods
options.c: adjudicatory and non-adjudicatory methods
options.d: adversarial and inquisitorial methods

questions.explanation: Once a dispute is before a court or tribunal, the adjudicator ascertains the facts either by the adversarial method or by the inquisitorial method. Option C names the two broad methods of dispute resolution, not of fact-finding, option A names forms of legal logic, and option B names forms of ADR.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: In a trial, the process by which a party calls his own witness and tries to establish, through that witness, the evidence needed for the success of his case is known as

options.a: examination-in-chief
options.b: cross-examination
options.c: address of counsel
options.d: re-examination

questions.explanation: Examination-in-chief is the questioning of a witness by the party who called him. Cross-examination (option B) is done by the opposing counsel, re-examination (option D) only clears up matters arising from cross-examination, and the address (option C) is counsel's final argument, not the questioning of a witness.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: What is the main object of cross-examination in the adversarial method?

options.a: To allow the witness to explain any seeming inconsistency in his earlier answers
options.b: To weaken, neutralise or demolish the case of the party who called the witness
options.c: To enable the judge to investigate facts on his own initiative
options.d: To introduce the witness to the court before his evidence is taken

questions.explanation: Cross-examination is conducted by counsel for the opposite party to test and break down the other side's case. Option A is the purpose of re-examination, option C describes the inquisitorial judge, and option D is not a purpose recognised for cross-examination.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: In the adversarial method, the role of the judge is best likened to that of

options.a: an umpire who ensures evidence is presented according to the ground rules
options.b: a prosecutor who presents and argues the case on behalf of the state
options.c: an investigator who gathers and tests evidence on behalf of both parties
options.d: a mediator who suggests terms of compromise acceptable to both parties

questions.explanation: The adversarial judge is a neutral umpire who enforces the ground rules and decides on the evidence the parties choose to present. Option C describes the inquisitorial judge, option D describes ADR, and option B confuses the judge with a party.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: In a civil suit at the Lagos High Court for N2,500,000 owed on a supply contract, the judge privately knows of a witness whose evidence would decide the case, but neither counsel calls that witness. Under the adversarial method, what should the judge do?

options.a: Decide on the evidence presented, without descending into the arena
options.b: Summon the witness himself and question him fully in open court
options.c: Adjourn the case until the plaintiff agrees to call that witness
options.d: Rely on his private knowledge of what the witness would have said

questions.explanation: An adversarial judge must make up his mind on the evidence presented and must not search for evidence for the parties, even if the facts are known to him. Options B and C would make the judge take over the parties' role, and option D would mean deciding on evidence that was never tested in court.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the ground rules a judge enforces in an adversarial trial?

options.a: A party must not take the other side by surprise at trial
options.b: A lawyer must not ask his own witness a leading question
options.c: Hearsay evidence is generally inadmissible at the trial
options.d: The judge may call his own witnesses to fill gaps in a case

questions.explanation: In the adversarial method the judge may not call his own witnesses; he may question a witness only to clear an ambiguity. Options C, B and A are the ground rules of evidence and procedure that the umpire-judge enforces.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: In a civil trial, if the imaginary scale of justice tilts even 51% in favour of one party, judgment will be given in his favour. This describes proof

options.a: beyond reasonable doubt
options.b: by res ipsa loquitur alone
options.c: on the balance of probabilities
options.d: beyond all possible doubt

questions.explanation: Civil cases are decided on the balance of probabilities, so the party whose version is more probable wins, however narrowly. Option A is the higher criminal standard, option D is a standard the law does not require, and option B is a rule of evidence for accident cases, not a standard of proof.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Kunle is charged with stealing N450,000 from his employer's shop in Yaba. The prosecution proves only that he was the last person seen near the till and that he had argued with the employer. On this evidence, what should the court do?

options.a: Require Kunle to prove that he did not take the money
options.b: Convict him, because he failed to explain where the money went
options.c: Convict him, because the evidence makes his guilt more probable than not
options.d: Acquit him, because suspicion, no matter how grave, can never ground a conviction

questions.explanation: In criminal cases the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and mere suspicion cannot ground a conviction. Option C applies the civil standard, while options A and B wrongly place on the accused a burden to prove his innocence, which the law does not impose.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Which provision of the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria states that every person charged with a criminal offence shall be presumed innocent until he is proved guilty?

options.a: Section 4(1)
options.b: Section 35(2)
options.c: Section 6(5)
options.d: Section 36(5)

questions.explanation: Section 36(5) of the 1999 Constitution contains the presumption of innocence, which keeps the burden of proof on the prosecution. Section 35(2) (option B) gives an arrested person the right to remain silent, section 6(5) (option C) lists the superior courts, and section 4(1) (option A) vests legislative powers in the National Assembly.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Ngozi is arrested in Onitsha on suspicion of fraud. At the police station she refuses to answer any question until she has spoken with a lawyer of her choice. Which constitutional right is she exercising?

options.a: The right to be tried before an inquisitorial tribunal instead of a court
options.b: The right to have the complaint heard first by an independent arbitrator
options.c: The right to remain silent until she has consulted a lawyer of her choice
options.d: The presumption that an accused person is innocent until proved guilty

questions.explanation: An arrested or detained person may remain silent or avoid answering any question until after consulting a legal practitioner of his choice. Option D is a related but different protection about who bears the burden at trial, while options A and B are not rights given to an arrested person.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: The Latin expression res ipsa loquitur means

options.a: the reason for the decision
options.b: the facts speak for themselves
options.c: it is for the court to know the law
options.d: let the decision stand

questions.explanation: Res ipsa loquitur is a rule of evidence for accident victims: where the accident would not normally happen without someone's carelessness, the facts themselves suggest negligence. Option D translates stare decisis, option A translates ratio decidendi, and option C translates jura novit curia.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: After an abdominal operation at a private hospital in Ibadan, Mrs. Olu discovers that a surgical swab was left inside her. She sues the hospital. If she successfully relies on res ipsa loquitur, what is the effect?

options.a: Mrs. Olu must first name the exact staff member who left the swab
options.b: The hospital must show a specific cause or that it used reasonable care
options.c: The case must be transferred to an arbitral tribunal for expert findings
options.d: The hospital becomes liable automatically and may offer no explanation

questions.explanation: When res ipsa loquitur applies, the plaintiff need only show the accident and that she was its victim; the defendant must then explain it or show it used reasonable care. Option A is exactly what the rule relieves her of, option C has no basis, and option D is wrong because the defendant can still rebut the presumption.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of the adversarial method of fact-finding?

options.a: It can enhance the development of the law through ingenious arguments by lawyers
options.b: It reduces the element of bias in the adjudicator
options.c: It gives each party the chance to present his case and discredit the other side's case
options.d: It ensures speedy disposal of cases because a time limit is usually prescribed for concluding them

questions.explanation: Speed and prescribed time limits are advantages of the inquisitorial method; the adversarial method is in fact criticised for delay. Options B, C and A are recognised advantages of the adversarial method.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: The criticism that, under the adversarial method, those with the best lawyers (often the rich) are the most likely to win is described as the

options.a: doctrine of res ipsa loquitur
options.b: presumption of innocence
options.c: sporting theory of justice
options.d: win-lose theory of ADR

questions.explanation: The 'sporting theory' of justice is the complaint that the adversarial trial becomes a contest won by the side with the better lawyer. Option D refers to a different point about litigation's winner-takes-all character, and options B and A are rules of evidence and proof, not criticisms.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: A land dispute in Abeokuta has been in court for many years. Two key witnesses have died, another has relocated abroad, and the remaining witnesses can no longer recall events clearly. Which disadvantage of the adversarial method does this illustrate?

options.a: Long delay may impair the fact-finding efficiency of the system
options.b: Multi-party disputes cannot be consolidated and heard together
options.c: Trials held in camera escape the scrutiny of the public and press
options.d: Hasty trials may lead to a miscarriage of justice for the parties

questions.explanation: Because the parties control the pace of an adversarial case, long delays can occur, and over time witnesses die, relocate or forget, and evidence is lost. Options C and D are disadvantages of the inquisitorial method, and option B is a disadvantage of non-adjudicatory methods.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: What is the main distinguishing feature of the inquisitorial method of fact-finding?

options.a: The adjudicator has considerable control over how evidence is collected and presented
options.b: The judge acts only as an umpire and may never question any of the witnesses
options.c: No facts are found and no blame is apportioned between the disputing parties
options.d: The parties and their lawyers alone decide which witnesses are called and when

questions.explanation: In the inquisitorial method the adjudicator can enter the arena, investigate facts, question parties and witnesses and even appoint expert assessors. Options D and B describe the adversarial method, and option C describes non-adjudicatory methods.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: A statutory benefits tribunal relied partly on the written opinions of two doctors who never appeared before it, so the claimant could not cross-examine them. The court held this was not a breach of natural justice. What principle does this illustrate?

options.a: A tribunal must act purely as a neutral umpire between the two parties
options.b: Any evidence not tested by cross-examination is always inadmissible anywhere
options.c: An inquisitorial body may rely on expert opinions of persons not before it
options.d: Expert medical opinions can only ever be received by arbitral tribunals

questions.explanation: This reflects the inquisitorial character of such tribunals, which may form their own view and rely on experts not personally before them, as in the Ex parte Moore case. Option B states an adversarial rule too absolutely, option A describes the adversarial judge, and option D has no basis.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Titi was caught cheating in an examination. The invigilator recorded the facts on the official irregularity form, which Titi countersigned as true, and then travelled abroad. An Examination Malpractices Panel found her guilty on the form alone. Titi argues the panel erred because the invigilator was not present to be cross-examined. Her argument is likely to

options.a: fail, because the inquisitorial panel may rely on the signed report
options.b: fail, because students have no right to be heard by any panel at all
options.c: succeed, because only an arbitrator may ever rely on written reports
options.d: succeed, because every tribunal must follow the full adversarial procedure

questions.explanation: An examination panel is not a regular court and adopts an inquisitorial approach, so the absence of cross-examination does not by itself vitiate a report she countersigned. Option D wrongly assumes all tribunals are adversarial, option C has no basis, and option B overstates the position because she is still entitled to a fair opportunity to defend herself.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: The saying 'justice rushed is justice crushed' is used to describe which disadvantage of the inquisitorial method?

options.a: Parties may use delay tactics to frustrate the other side
options.b: Lawyers may procure witnesses to lie on oath
options.c: Miscarriage of justice may result from a hasty trial
options.d: The decision is not binding on the parties

questions.explanation: An investigative body working to a deadline may ignore important details, so a hasty trial can produce injustice. Options A and B are disadvantages of the adversarial method, and option D is wrong because inquisitorial decisions bind the parties.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: A special tribunal tried and convicted several officers for an alleged coup plot in closed sessions, with no members of the public or press allowed. Critics later argued the coup never existed. Which disadvantage of the inquisitorial method does this illustrate?

options.a: Delay that impairs fact-finding as witnesses die or forget
options.b: The sporting theory of justice, which favours the richer party
options.c: Inquisitions held in camera are not open to public scrutiny
options.d: Inability to consolidate multi-party disputes in one hearing

questions.explanation: Many inquisitions are conducted in camera, so mistakes or abuses escape public scrutiny; the convictions of officers for phantom coups are given as an example. Options B and A are criticisms of the adversarial method, and option D is a disadvantage of ADR.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the adjudicatory method from the non-adjudicatory method of dispute resolution?

options.a: Adjudication involves fact-finding and apportioning blame; ADR generally does not
options.b: ADR is unknown to law and has no rules, while adjudication is regulated by statute
options.c: ADR always takes place in a formal court, while adjudication takes place outside it
options.d: Adjudication relies only on reconciliation, while ADR relies on state-appointed judges

questions.explanation: Adjudication finds facts by adversarial or inquisitorial procedure and apportions blame; ADR generally does neither. Option C reverses the formal and informal settings, option D reverses the methods, and option B is wrong because the law recognises ADR and lays down rules for it.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: How does the task of a judge in the adjudicatory method generally differ from that of a non-adjudicator such as a mediator?

options.a: The judge suggests compromise terms, while the non-adjudicator applies the law strictly to past events
options.b: The judge applies the law to past events, while the non-adjudicator suggests solutions for future harmony
options.c: The judge's task is mainly to reconcile the parties, while the non-adjudicator punishes the wrongdoer
options.d: Both of them are bound to apply the rules of evidence strictly before reaching any decision

questions.explanation: A judge's task is generally not to reconcile the parties but to examine past events and apply the law, whereas a non-adjudicator tries to reconcile them by suggesting solutions. Options A and C reverse the two roles, and option D is wrong because ADR is free from the strict rules of evidence.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of the non-adjudicatory method of dispute resolution?

options.a: It enables the parties to control their own fate instead of a judge
options.b: It saves time and avoids the delays and uncertainties of court trials
options.c: It allows multi-party disputes to be consolidated and heard together
options.d: Proceedings are free from the formalities of the rules of evidence

questions.explanation: ADR does not allow consolidation of actions, because it depends on voluntary agreement and parties cannot be compelled to join; this is a disadvantage. Options B, A and D are recognised advantages of ADR.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: A Kano textile company and a foreign supplier settle a N40,000,000 dispute by arbitration. They must hire a hall for the hearings and jointly pay the arbitrators' fees and administrative expenses. Which feature of the non-adjudicatory method does this reflect?

options.a: It requires the parties to prove their facts beyond reasonable doubt
options.b: It is self-executing like a court judgment without any agreement
options.c: It is not financed by the state, so the parties bear its costs
options.d: It is conducted by a state-appointed judge in a public courtroom

questions.explanation: ADR is not funded by the state: the parties hire venues and pay the arbitrators' fees and expenses, which can be substantial in international commercial cases. Option B misstates the basis of arbitration, which rests on agreement, option D describes litigation, and option A is the criminal standard of proof.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an essential element of arbitration?

options.a: The arbitrator must be a serving judge of a High Court
options.b: The arbitrator's decision (award) must be binding on the parties
options.c: There must be an existing dispute, or one the parties envisage arising in future
options.d: The parties must have voluntarily agreed to refer the dispute to arbitration

questions.explanation: An arbitrator is an independent third party chosen by the parties, often a professional with technical knowledge, not a serving judge. Options C, D and B are the three essential elements before a process can be called arbitration.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: A charter contract between a Lagos shipping firm and a foreign ship owner contains a clause referring all disputes to arbitration. When a dispute arises, the Lagos firm goes straight to the Federal High Court. How is the court likely to respond?

options.a: It will refer the dispute to reconciliation between the two firms instead of arbitration
options.b: It will hold the firm to the clause, as it cannot approbate and reprobate the contract
options.c: It will ignore the clause, because only the regular courts can resolve shipping disputes
options.d: It will hear the case and treat the arbitration clause as no more than a suggestion

questions.explanation: Where parties have agreed to arbitrate, courts have a prima facie duty to act on that agreement, and going to court in breach of it is reprobating the contract (M.V. Lupex case). Options C and D contradict the courts' attitude to valid arbitration clauses, and option A has no basis in the clause.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: A dispute between an Abuja estate developer and a contractor turns on whether concrete used in a building met engineering specifications. The parties appoint a structural engineer as arbitrator. Which advantage of arbitration does this choice illustrate?

options.a: The arbitrator's decision is never binding on the parties who appointed him
options.b: The arbitrator is often a specialist with technical knowledge, unlike a judge
options.c: The process allows many unrelated parties to be joined and heard together
options.d: The state pays the arbitrator's fees and the cost of the hearing venue

questions.explanation: An arbitrator is often an independent professional with technical knowledge and experience of the subject, which improves fact-finding. Option A is wrong because an award binds the parties, option C is wrong because ADR does not allow consolidation, and option D is wrong because the parties pay the fees.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: The decision of a conciliator is generally only a guide. In which situation can the terms reached through conciliation become binding by law in Nigeria?

options.a: In a trade dispute, once the signed memorandum of settlement is reported to the Minister
options.b: In any family dispute, once the elders of the family publicly announce the agreed terms
options.c: Never, because the outcome of a conciliation can never be binding on anyone by law
options.d: In any commercial dispute, once the conciliator writes and signs his own final report

questions.explanation: Under the Trade Disputes Act, a conciliator appointed for a trade dispute who achieves a settlement reports it to the Minister, and the signed memorandum of terms binds the employers and workers; breach is an offence. Options B and D have no such legal backing, and option C ignores this statutory exception.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Which statement about the decision reached through mediation is correct?

options.a: It binds the parties only if it apportions the blame
options.b: It can be enforced as a court judgment without agreement
options.c: It does not bind the parties, even in a trade dispute
options.d: It binds the parties once the mediator signs it

questions.explanation: A mediator has no authority to make binding decisions; he only helps the parties negotiate, and his decision does not bind them even in a trade dispute. Options D and B wrongly give the mediator a decision-making power, and option A is wrong because a mediator does not apportion blame at all.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: In the Middle Ages, disputes were often 'resolved' by subjecting disputants to terrible ordeals, and survival was taken as proof of innocence. What is the position of trial by ordeal in Nigeria today?

options.a: It is a recognised form of alternative dispute resolution
options.b: It is permitted in customary courts only
options.c: It is prohibited by the Criminal Code
options.d: It is allowed if both parties consent in writing

questions.explanation: Trial by ordeal, a method of 'proof' rather than trial, is now prohibited by the Criminal Code; modern dispute resolution relies on objective standards and procedures. Options A, D and B wrongly suggest that such crude methods still have legal recognition.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Four co-tenants in a 'face-me-I-face-you' house in Ajegunle suspect one another after Mrs. A's jewellery box goes missing. Mrs. A wants to find the thief by 'tying the Holy Book with a key' and calling each name. Mrs. C refuses to take part, and the others conclude she is the thief. Which advice is correct?

options.a: The method is a valid form of mediation because the other co-tenants agreed
options.b: The method is outlawed, and Mrs. C's refusal is not proof of her guilt
options.c: Mrs. A must first prove her own innocence before she can report to the police
options.d: Mrs. C's refusal is sufficient evidence for a court to convict her of theft

questions.explanation: Methods like the Holy Book and key are similar to the old ordeals; they are no longer acceptable and have been criminalised, so refusing to take part is not evidence of guilt. If the matter goes to court, guilt must be proved beyond reasonable doubt, which rules out option D; option A misdescribes mediation, and option C has no basis in law.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Under the Evidence Act 2011, which of the following falls within the definition of a 'fact'?

options.a: A rule of law contained in a statute
options.b: An opinion expressed by a judge in passing
options.c: A decision of the Supreme Court on a point of law
options.d: Any mental condition of which a person is conscious

questions.explanation: A fact includes anything, state of things or relation of things capable of being perceived by the senses, and any mental condition of which a person is conscious. Options A, C and B are matters of law or legal opinion, not facts.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: In a civil case, 'facts in issue' are best described as

options.a: all the facts mentioned by any of the witnesses at any stage of the trial
options.b: the facts the judge discovers through his own investigation of the dispute
options.c: the rules of law which the court must apply in deciding the case before it
options.d: the facts a plaintiff must prove to establish his claim, unless admitted

questions.explanation: Facts in issue are those facts the plaintiff must prove to establish his claim unless the defendant admits them expressly or by implication, and only these need to be proved. Option A is too wide, option C confuses facts with law, and option B describes inquisitorial investigation.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: The term 'burden of proof' is used in two senses. In which sense is 'shifting of fact' a shifting of the burden of proof?

options.a: The legal burden to persuade the court that the whole case is established
options.b: The evidential burden: the duty to adduce evidence on a particular fact
options.c: The duty of the judge to know and apply the law relevant to the case
options.d: The obligation of the prosecution to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt

questions.explanation: Burden of proof means either the obligation to establish one's whole case (the legal burden) or the obligation to adduce evidence on a particular fact (the evidential burden); shifting of fact refers to the evidential burden. Option A is the burden that does not shift in this way, option C relates to shift of law, and option D is the prosecution's overall burden in criminal cases.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: The Latin maxim affirmanti non neganti incumbit probatio means that

options.a: it is for the court, not the parties, to know the law
options.b: the burden of proof lies on the one who affirms, not the one who denies
options.c: ignorance of the law is no excuse for anyone who breaks it
options.d: the decision of a higher court must be followed by lower courts

questions.explanation: The maxim places the burden of proving a fact on the party who asserts it, so when a defendant denies the plaintiff's claim, the plaintiff must prove it.
