Option C translates ignorantia juris non excusat, option A translates jura novit curia, and option D describes stare decisis.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Emeka sues Bayo for N60,000, the balance of the N150,000 price of a laptop. Bayo denies that he ever promised to pay any balance. Emeka then produces a memorandum of the payment terms signed by Bayo. On whom does the evidential burden now lie?

options.a: On neither party, because the case must go to mediation
options.b: On Bayo, to prove that the signed memorandum is not genuine
options.c: On the judge, who must investigate the memorandum himself
options.d: On Emeka, who must now prove the case beyond reasonable doubt

questions.explanation: Emeka first bore the burden because he affirmed the promise, but once he produced the signed memorandum, the evidential burden shifted to Bayo to disprove it. Option D applies the criminal standard to a civil case, option C describes inquisitorial investigation, and option A has no basis.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: A landlord sues his tenant for N300,000 unpaid rent. In his defence, the tenant admits that the rent was due but states that he had already paid it to the landlord's agent. What is this type of defence called, and who must prove the payment?

options.a: Per incuriam; the court must summon the agent to testify
options.b: Res ipsa loquitur; the landlord must now prove non-payment
options.c: Stare decisis; the agent must prove that he received payment
options.d: Confessing and avoiding; the tenant must prove the payment

questions.explanation: When a defendant admits the allegation but supplies new facts that put a different complexion on the case, he is confessing and avoiding, and the burden of proving those new facts lies on him. Option B is a rule for accident cases, while options A and C are doctrines of judicial precedent.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Aisha sues Tunde for N80,000 owed on a sale of goods. In his statement of defence, Tunde expressly admits that he promised to pay the N80,000 within two weeks and failed to do so. What is the effect on Aisha's burden regarding these facts?

options.a: The admission must be ignored unless Tunde gives oral evidence
options.b: She must still prove the admitted facts beyond reasonable doubt
options.c: The burden shifts to the judge to prove the facts
options.d: She is discharged of the burden of proving the admitted facts

questions.explanation: Only facts in issue, those not admitted, need to be proved; once Tunde admits the promise and the failure to pay, Aisha no longer has to prove them. Option B applies the criminal standard and ignores the admission, option C confuses shift of fact with shift of law, and option A has no basis.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: In criminal cases the burden of proving facts generally rests on the prosecution. Which of the following is NOT an exception where the burden of proving certain facts shifts to the accused?

options.a: Where special facts are within the knowledge of the accused
options.b: Where the accused raises the defence of insanity or intoxication
options.c: Where the accused simply pleads not guilty and denies the charge
options.d: Where a statute specifically places the onus of proving certain facts on the accused

questions.explanation: A plain denial does not shift any burden; the prosecution must still prove every element of the offence. Options B, A and D are recognised exceptions, together with the case where the accused claims an exemption or qualification under the law creating the offence.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: The maxim ignorantia facti excusat, ignorantia juris non excusat means

options.a: the facts speak for themselves, but the law must be proved
options.b: the ignorance of the judge is the calamity of the innocent
options.c: the burden of proof lies on the one who affirms a fact
options.d: ignorance of fact excuses, but ignorance of law does not

questions.explanation: This maxim separates fact from law: a genuine mistake of fact may excuse, but no one can rely on not knowing the law. Option A mixes res ipsa loquitur with an invented clause, option C translates affirmanti non neganti incumbit probatio, and option B translates ignorantia judicis est calamitas innocentis.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: In a contract case at the Ikeja High Court, neither counsel cites a statutory provision that clearly governs the dispute. Under the principle jura novit curia, what is the position?

options.a: The burden of applying the law shifts to the judge, who must know it
options.b: The judge must decide only on the facts and leave the statute aside
options.c: The case must be struck out because the parties failed to prove the law
options.d: The plaintiff loses automatically because he bears the burden of proof

questions.explanation: Jura novit curia means it is for the court to know the law, so where counsel fail to cite a relevant law, the burden of applying it rests on the judge. Options C and D treat law as if it were a fact the parties must prove, and option B would mean ignoring the applicable law.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: In a debt recovery suit, the defendant's counsel relies on a section of a state law, unaware that it was repealed last year. The plaintiff's counsel knows of the repeal. On whom does the burden of informing the court of the repeal fall?

options.a: On no one, since repealed laws apply until the court discovers the repeal
options.b: On the plaintiff's counsel, who has knowledge of the repeal
options.c: On the court registrar
options.d: On the defendant's counsel, since he cited the law

questions.explanation: Shifting of law arises where a party relies on a law not knowing it has been amended or repealed; the burden of informing the court then shifts to the person who knows of the change. Option D puts the burden on the party who does not know, option C has no basis, and option A is wrong because a repealed law is no longer in force.

questions.topic: Fact Finding and Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Bassef is charged with murder after being found with human remains; he claims they came from accident victims. The prosecution fails to cross-examine him on this defence and does not call a vital witness, and the judge notices this. Which conclusion is most consistent with the adversarial method?

options.a: The case should be sent to mediation because the evidence before the court is incomplete
options.b: The judge cannot call the witness; the unchallenged defence stands and doubt favours Bassef
options.c: Bassef must now prove beyond reasonable doubt that he did not kill anyone at all
options.d: The judge should call the vital witness himself to complete the prosecution's case

questions.explanation: An adversarial judge must not descend into the arena, evidence not challenged in cross-examination is taken as admitted, and the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt with doubts going to the accused. Option D makes the judge take over the prosecution, option C reverses the burden, and option A is not open in a murder trial.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: A principle of law can best be described as

options.a: a comment made by a judge in passing that does not bind later courts
options.b: a prediction of how a particular judge will decide a case
options.c: an established legal truth or proposition that cannot be contradicted except by a clearer proposition, and from which rules are developed
options.d: a specific instruction that applies to one fixed set of facts only

questions.explanation: Principles such as the rule of law, separation of powers and supremacy of the Constitution are broad guideposts by which laws, decisions and arguments are judged, and specific rules grow out of them. Option D describes a rule rather than a principle, Option A describes an obiter dictum, and Option B is the realist view of law.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: The two rules developed from the principle of natural justice are

options.a: ejusdem generis and noscitur a sociis
options.b: audi alteram partem (hear the other side) and nemo judex in causa sua (no one should be a judge in his own cause)
options.c: stare decisis and ratio decidendi
options.d: actus reus and mens rea

questions.explanation: Natural justice is a principle, and these two specific rules apply it: a party must not be condemned unheard, and a judge must not decide his own case. Option A are maxims of statutory interpretation, Option C relate to judicial precedent, and Option D are elements of a crime.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: In the law of negligence, a defendant's conduct is measured against what a reasonable man would have done in the circumstances. This measure is best described as a legal

options.a: maxim of statutory interpretation
options.b: ratio decidendi
options.c: standard
options.d: syllogism

questions.explanation: A legal standard is a flexible measure of conduct, like the reasonable man test, that the judge applies according to the circumstances of each case instead of a fixed, detailed rule. Option B is the binding reason for a particular decision, Option A is a guide for reading statutes, and Option D is a form of deductive argument.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Rhetoric, as used in law, is

options.a: the strict deduction of a conclusion from a major and a minor premise
options.b: the process by which a bill becomes law
options.c: the study of the customs of a people
options.d: the art of persuading another, in speech or writing, to accept one's position or view

questions.explanation: Legal rhetoric is the art of persuasion, which is why lawyers must master language and the use of authorities. Option A describes deductive logic (syllogism), Option C relates to the Historical School, and Option B is the legislative process.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Aristotle distinguished forensic rhetoric from deliberative rhetoric. Broadly, which form do lawyers use when arguing for their clients?

options.a: Deliberative rhetoric
options.b: Forensic rhetoric
options.c: Analogical rhetoric
options.d: Inductive rhetoric

questions.explanation: Lawyers represent their clients' interests and seek to persuade the court, which is forensic rhetoric, while judges broadly use deliberative rhetoric because they must reach a reasoned decision justifiable to the parties and society. Option A is therefore the judges' form, and Option D and Option C are not Aristotle's categories of rhetoric.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: The principal rhetorical device used in law is

options.a: the use of Latin phrases
options.b: personal attacks on the opposing counsel
options.c: the appeal to authority, that is, citing statutes and decided cases to support a position
options.d: appeal to the emotions of the judge

questions.explanation: Lawyers persuade mainly by showing that statutes and judicial decisions support their argument; writers' opinions and foreign decisions are only persuasive. Option D and Option B are not proper legal persuasion, and Option A is a feature of legal language, not the main rhetorical device.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Consider this argument: "Any person under 18 cannot join in forming a company. Seyi is under 18. Therefore Seyi cannot join in forming a company." The statement "Seyi is under 18" is the

options.a: major premise
options.b: ratio decidendi
options.c: conclusion
options.d: minor premise

questions.explanation: In a syllogism, the major premise is the general rule (here, the statutory provision), the minor premise states the facts of the case (Seyi's age), and the conclusion follows from both. So Option A is the age rule, Option C is the final statement, and Option B is a term for the binding reason in a court decision, not a part of a syllogism.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Deductive and inductive logic differ in that

options.a: deductive logic relies on case law, while inductive logic relies only on statutes
options.b: deductive logic reasons from particular cases to a general principle, while inductive logic reasons from the general to the particular
options.c: deductive logic is used only by judges, while inductive logic is used only by legislators
options.d: deductive logic reasons from the general to the particular, while inductive logic reasons from particular cases to a general principle

questions.explanation: Deduction applies a general rule, often a statute, to the facts to reach a conclusion, while induction studies several decided cases to build up a general principle. Option B reverses the two. Option C is wrong because lawyers and judges use both, and Option A is backwards because reasoning from case law is typically inductive.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: A syllogism can be logically valid even though its conclusion is false. This is because

options.a: a valid syllogism always has a true conclusion
options.b: validity and truth mean exactly the same thing
options.c: a syllogism can never contain a false premise
options.d: validity only means the conclusion follows from the premises, while truth depends on whether the premises match the facts

questions.explanation: Logic tests whether a conclusion follows from the premises, not whether the premises are true, so a wrong premise accepted as true will give a valid but false conclusion. This is why a lawyer must spot a witness who is logical but lying. Option A, Option B and Option C all ignore this difference between truth and validity.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: How does practical reasoning differ from formal legal logic?

options.a: It is not tied to deduction or induction; it weighs various considerations, often uses analogy, and its conclusions are judged by society's values
options.b: It ignores the values of society and focuses only on formal validity
options.c: It relies strictly on a major premise, a minor premise and a conclusion
options.d: It can only be used by legislators when drafting bills

questions.explanation: Practical reasoning balances many factors to reach a justifiable conclusion, and whether that conclusion is good or bad depends on the society's prevailing values, which can change over time. Option C describes a syllogism, Option B is the opposite of practical reasoning, and Option D is too narrow because judges and lawyers use it daily.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: The statement "The life of the law has not been logic but experience" is attributed to

options.a: Hans Kelsen
options.b: Jeremy Bentham
options.c: Oliver Wendell Holmes
options.d: John Austin

questions.explanation: Holmes made this point to show that law develops by constantly testing rules against real-life needs and dropping those that can no longer be supported, not by logic alone. Option D, Option A and Option B are known for more formal or utility-based accounts of law.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Apart from appeal to authority, which of the following is NOT a factor judges properly use to justify their decisions?

options.a: Public policy and the view of a reasonable man
options.b: The judge's personal likes and dislikes about the parties
options.c: Whether the consequences of the decision are acceptable in terms of justice
options.d: Coherence of the decision with existing principles and authorities

questions.explanation: A judge must give a reasoned justification, drawing on coherence with existing law (Option D), the justice of the consequences (Option C), and common sense, the reasonable man and public policy (Option A). Personal prejudices are exactly what proper justification is meant to keep out.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Legal reasoning is best defined as

options.a: the memorisation of statutes and decided cases for the purpose of examinations
options.b: systematic, logical, coordinated and persuasive thinking or argument on legal issues
options.c: the personal opinion of a judge about what is fair, without giving reasons
options.d: the use of Latin, French and archaic English words in court proceedings

questions.explanation: Legal reasoning combines 'reasoning' (thinking in a coordinated, orderly and logical way) with 'legal' (connected with law). Option A is mere recall, option D is a feature of legal language, and option C ignores the need for logic and justification.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Section 316 of the Criminal Code makes a person guilty of murder if he unlawfully kills another under listed circumstances, without naming any weapon, so it covers shooting, stabbing, poisoning or strangling. Which feature of legal language does this illustrate?

options.a: Law is always expressed in highly specific language
options.b: Law is usually expressed in general terms
options.c: Law uses argot or jargon
options.d: Law uses archaic English words

questions.explanation: Laws are drafted generally because they must apply to many people in different circumstances, so one provision can cover every method of intentional unlawful killing. Options D and C are other features of legal language not shown here, and option A is the opposite of what the provision does.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Donoghue v Stevenson concerned a snail in a bottle of ginger beer, yet its principle is stated as 'a manufacturer of consumer goods owes a duty of care to the final consumer'. Why is the principle expressed at this higher level of generality?

options.a: Because principles must always be stated as widely as possible, without limits
options.b: Stating it only as snails in ginger beer would hinder the growth of case law
options.c: Because ginger beer is not regarded in law as a consumer good at all
options.d: Because the House of Lords was not sure of the actual facts of the case

questions.explanation: If the case were limited to its exact facts, it could only be a precedent for snails in ginger beer, which would not help future cases such as germs in canned milk. Option D has no basis, option A is wrong because the principle is kept within limits (for example consumable goods and proven health problems), and option C is untrue.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Section 6(5) of the 1999 Constitution does not speak generally of 'superior courts' but lists them one by one: the Supreme Court, the Court of Appeal, the Federal High Court, a State High Court, a Sharia Court of Appeal and a Customary Court of Appeal. This shows that

options.a: law can never be expressed in general terms in a written constitution
options.b: the list is an obiter dictum of the legislature with no binding force
options.c: law can be expressed in highly specific language when no doubt is intended
options.d: the Constitution here uses abstract concepts in order to save words

questions.explanation: Although law is usually general, it can be made highly specific where the lawmaker wants no doubt about its application, as with this list of courts. Option A overstates the point, option D describes a different feature, and option B misuses a term that belongs to judgments.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: What is the main advantage of using abstract legal concepts such as 'rule of law', 'legal personality' or 'possession'?

options.a: They make the law easily understandable to every layman in society
options.b: They allow lawyers to invent any meaning they like for ordinary words
options.c: They achieve economy of words by avoiding a full list of details
options.d: They remove the need for legal reasoning in the interpretation of law

questions.explanation: A single concept, such as 'rule of law' with its components of supremacy of law, equality before the law and fundamental rights, carries a whole set of ideas, saving words. Option A is doubtful because such terms often confuse laymen, option B is wrong because lawyers are not free to use words anyhow, and option D is untrue.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: A lawyer who says 'my brief has not been perfected', meaning 'I have not been paid my professional fee', is using which feature of legal language?

options.a: Argot or jargon meant for those within the profession
options.b: Resonant formal expressions used during court oaths
options.c: Archaic English words such as hereinafter and aforesaid
options.d: Latin and French phrases such as consensus ad idem

questions.explanation: Argot is a special vocabulary not meant to be understood by those outside the legal profession; 'my brief has not been perfected' and 'I am speaking from the bar' are examples. Option B refers to phrases like 'the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth', option D to terms like ultra vires, and option C to words like 'hereinafter'.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: What is the relationship between legal principles and legal rules?

options.a: Rules furnish the basis for principles; principles are specific applications of rules
options.b: Rules are binding on courts, while principles are mere opinions with no legal value
options.c: Principles and rules are exactly the same thing described in different words
options.d: Principles furnish the basis for rules; rules are specific applications of principles

questions.explanation: A principle is a comprehensive legal proposition from which rules develop; for example, the principle of natural justice gives rise to the rules audi alteram partem and nemo judex in causa sua. Option A reverses the relationship, option C ignores the difference in generality, and option B is wrong because arguments against principles are open to attack.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: The rule audi alteram partem, developed from the principle of natural justice, means that

options.a: ignorance of the law is no excuse
options.b: the facts speak for themselves
options.c: no one should be a judge in his own cause
options.d: a party must not be condemned unheard

questions.explanation: Audi alteram partem means 'hear the other side': a judge must hear both parties before reaching a conclusion. Option C is nemo judex in causa sua, the other component of natural justice, option B is res ipsa loquitur, and option A is ignorantia juris non excusat.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: A magistrate in Enugu is assigned a case in which the company being sued for N1,200,000 is owned largely by the magistrate himself. If he hears and decides the case, which rule of natural justice is breached?

options.a: Res ipsa loquitur: the facts speak for themselves
options.b: Nemo judex in causa sua: no one should be a judge in his own cause
options.c: Audi alteram partem: a party must not be condemned unheard
options.d: Stare decisis: let the decision stand

questions.explanation: A magistrate who decides a case in which he has a personal interest is a judge in his own cause, contrary to nemo judex in causa sua. Option C concerns hearing both sides, which is not the problem here, while options D and A are not rules of natural justice.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a well-established principle of constitutional law?

options.a: A particular judge's remark made in passing
options.b: Separation of powers
options.c: The short title of a bill
options.d: A N25,000 fine for failing to renew a vehicle licence

questions.explanation: Rule of law, separation of powers and supremacy of the Constitution are well-established constitutional principles by which legislation, decisions and arguments are judged. Option D is a specific rule, option A is an obiter dictum, and option C is merely part of a bill's form.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: What happens to a line of legal argument that is contrary to an established legal principle?

options.a: It becomes binding on all lower courts in the hierarchy
options.b: It immediately becomes suspect and open to legal attack
options.c: It automatically becomes a new principle of the law
options.d: It must be accepted if it produces a good result in the case

questions.explanation: Principles are guideposts by which arguments and decisions are judged, so an argument against an established principle is suspect even if it seems to produce a good result. Option A confuses it with precedent, option C has no basis, and option D contradicts the role of principles.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Which statement best describes a legal standard such as 'reasonable care' or 'the reasonable man'?

options.a: A rule of evidence that applies only in criminal cases, never in civil cases
options.b: A general measure applied to the circumstances of each case, leaving discretion
options.c: A remark by a judge made in passing that has no legal effect on later cases
options.d: A fixed, detailed rule that gives exactly the same answer in every case

questions.explanation: Standards are flexible: they are applied liberally to the circumstances of each case, and attempts to replace them with hard and fast rules tend to fail. Option D describes a rule rather than a standard, option C describes an obiter dictum, and option A is wrong because the reasonable man standard is central to negligence, a civil wrong.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: A state traffic law contains two provisions: (1) 'No vehicle shall be driven within a school zone at more than 30 km/h', and (2) 'Every driver shall drive with reasonable care for other road users'. Which statement is correct?

options.a: Provision (1) is a rule and provision (2) is a standard
options.b: Provision (1) is a standard and provision (2) is a rule
options.c: Both provisions are principles of constitutional law
options.d: Both provisions are obiter dicta

questions.explanation: Provision (1) fixes a precise limit that applies the same way every time, which makes it a rule; provision (2) requires the court to judge what reasonable care means in each situation, which makes it a standard. Option B reverses them, option C confuses them with principles such as separation of powers, and option D misuses a term for judicial remarks.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Who defined rhetoric as 'the art of winning men's minds with words'?

options.a: Aristotle
options.b: Roscoe Pound
options.c: Plato
options.d: John Austin

questions.explanation: Plato described rhetoric as the art of winning men's minds with words. Aristotle (option A) is associated with the distinction between forensic and deliberative rhetoric, while Austin (option D) and Pound (option B) are jurists known for theories about the nature and functions of law.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Following Aristotle's distinction, what type of rhetoric do lawyers and judges broadly use?

options.a: Lawyers use forensic rhetoric, while judges use deliberative rhetoric
options.b: Both lawyers and judges use only forensic rhetoric
options.c: Lawyers use deliberative rhetoric, while judges use forensic rhetoric
options.d: Neither lawyers nor judges use rhetoric

questions.explanation: Lawyers represent their clients and try to persuade the court to accept their view, which is forensic rhetoric; judges aim at a reasoned decision justifiable in the interests of the parties and society, which is deliberative rhetoric. Option C reverses them, option B ignores the judge's different goal, and option D is wrong.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: What is the principal rhetorical device used in law?

options.a: An emotional appeal to the sympathy and feelings of the trial judge
options.b: Questioning the character and competence of the opposing counsel
options.c: The use of archaic English words to impress the court and the public
options.d: The appeal to authority by citing judicial or statutory authorities

questions.explanation: Although legal argument is made in words, its main persuasive tool is appeal to authority: citing statutes and decided cases. Option A and option B are not recognised legal techniques of persuasion, and option C is merely a feature of legal language.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: In a Nigerian High Court, counsel supports his argument by citing (i) a section of a Nigerian statute, (ii) a decision of the Nigerian Supreme Court and (iii) a passage from a respected textbook writer together with a decision of a Ghanaian court. How should the court treat item (iii)?

options.a: As binding in the same way as the Supreme Court decision
options.b: As having only persuasive effect
options.c: As overriding the Nigerian statute
options.d: As inadmissible in any Nigerian court

questions.explanation: Statutes and decisions of Nigerian courts are primary authorities, while the writings of learned authorities and decisions of other jurisdictions have only persuasive effect. Options A and C give item (iii) far too much weight, and option D is wrong because such writings and foreign decisions may be referred to.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: The statement 'There is nothing like a born lawyer' expresses the view that

options.a: only the children of lawyers can grow up to become good courtroom advocates
options.b: lawyers do not need to master language since judges decide on facts alone
options.c: legal rhetoric is an acquired skill developed through training and practice
options.d: persuasion is a natural gift at birth and cannot be learned by anyone

questions.explanation: Skill in legal persuasion is acquired through academic and professional training and practical experience; lawyers are made by diligence, patience and application. Options A and D treat it as inborn, and option B contradicts the importance of words to a lawyer.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Which of the following is a stated value of logic to the lawyer?

options.a: It replaces the need for him to know the statutes and decided cases
options.b: It guarantees that every conclusion he reaches is factually true and correct
options.c: It allows him to ignore the facts of the case and argue on law alone
options.d: It helps him reason clearly, express himself precisely and spot bad arguments

questions.explanation: Logic helps a lawyer think clearly, state his position firmly and spot defective arguments that might mislead the court. Option B is wrong because logic deals with validity, not truth, and options A and C are wrong because the lawyer must still master both the facts and the authorities.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: A syllogism is best described as

options.a: an inductive argument that builds a general principle from several decided cases
options.b: a comparison of two cases based on their points of resemblance to each other
options.c: a remark made by a judge in passing that does not bind any later court
options.d: a deductive argument whose conclusion follows from a major and a minor premise

questions.explanation: A syllogism is a set of three connected propositions in which the conclusion necessarily follows from the major and minor premises. Option A describes inductive reasoning, option C describes an obiter dictum, and option B describes analogical reasoning.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts deductive and inductive reasoning?

options.a: Deductive reasoning moves from the particular to the general, while inductive reasoning moves from the general to the particular
options.b: Deductive reasoning moves from the general to the particular, while inductive reasoning moves from the particular to the general
options.c: Both move from the general to the particular
options.d: Deductive reasoning is used only by judges, while inductive reasoning is used only by lawyers

questions.explanation: Deduction starts from a general proposition, such as a statute, and applies it to particular facts; induction examines particular decisions to arrive at a general principle. Option A reverses them, option C ignores the difference, and option D is wrong because both lawyers and judges use both forms.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Consider this argument: 'Any trader who sells in Oyingbo market without a permit shall pay a fine of N20,000. Mama Bisi sold in Oyingbo market without a permit. Therefore Mama Bisi shall pay a fine of N20,000.' Which part is the minor premise?

options.a: Mama Bisi sold in Oyingbo market without a permit
options.b: Any trader who sells in Oyingbo market without a permit shall pay a fine of N20,000
options.c: The permit system of Oyingbo market
options.d: Therefore Mama Bisi shall pay a fine of N20,000

questions.explanation: In a legal syllogism the minor premise states the facts of the particular case, here what Mama Bisi did. Option B is the major premise, the general rule taken from the law, option D is the conclusion, and option C is not one of the three propositions.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: A client asks his lawyer whether a new Lagos tenancy law applies to his N900,000 rent dispute. The lawyer reads the relevant section, finds that the client's facts fall within it, and concludes how the section applies to him. Which form of reasoning has the lawyer used?

options.a: Rhetoric based on appeal to emotion
options.b: Inductive reasoning, building a principle from several cases
options.c: Deductive reasoning, with the statute as the major premise
options.d: Analogical reasoning between two unrelated statutes

questions.explanation: When advising on a detailed statutory provision, the lawyer treats the statute as the major premise, fits the client's facts in as the minor premise and deduces the conclusion. Option B applies when the authority is case law rather than a clear statute, option D does not describe what he did, and option A is not legal logic.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: A key limitation of syllogism as a method of legal reasoning is that

options.a: it is concerned with validity rather than with the truth of the premises
options.b: it can be used only in criminal cases and never in civil disputes
options.c: it always requires a jury to decide whether the premises are correct
options.d: it can never produce a firm conclusion from the premises given to it

questions.explanation: A syllogism is valid when the conclusion necessarily follows from the premises, but that says nothing about whether the premises are true; for example, 'Every good man goes to heaven; John died a good man; therefore John is in heaven' is valid but its truth cannot be verified. Options D, B and C are not limitations of syllogism at all.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Counsel argues: 'Section 12 of the State Revenue Law imposes a N50,000 penalty on late filers; my client filed late; so my client must pay N50,000.' In fact, section 12 was repealed before the client filed. What does this show about syllogistic reasoning?

options.a: A repealed law remains a valid major premise until the court formally rules on it
options.b: Deductive reasoning cannot be used at all when the major premise is a statute
options.c: A wrong premise accepted as true leads to a wrong conclusion, though the form is valid
options.d: A syllogism is invalid whenever it involves money penalties or fines of any amount

questions.explanation: The argument is logically valid in form, but its major premise is false because the section no longer exists, so the conclusion is wrong. Option D has no basis, option A is wrong because a repealed provision is no longer law, and option B contradicts the fact that statutes are the usual major premise in deduction.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Why must a lawyer carefully distinguish between truth and validity when dealing with witnesses?

options.a: A witness may be logical but untruthful, and counsel must expose it
options.b: Because only valid testimony is admissible in a Nigerian court of law
options.c: Because witnesses are not allowed to reason logically while testifying
options.d: Because testimony that is logical is always true and must be believed

questions.explanation: A witness can be perfectly logical while lying; if counsel or the judge does not see the difference between truth and validity, undeserved weight may be given to such evidence. Option D confuses validity with truth, option B invents an admissibility rule, and option C is untrue.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: The argument 'A man is a human being; a woman is a human being; therefore a man is a woman' illustrates which limitation of logic?

options.a: Inductive reasoning can never be used by judges in deciding any case
options.b: A statement may be logical in one context and illogical in another
options.c: Analogy is a perfect form of induction that always gives a true result
options.d: Rhetoric in law depends mainly on appeal to judicial or statutory authority

questions.explanation: The pattern 'things equal to the same thing are equal to one another' works in mathematics but produces nonsense when transferred to men and women, showing that logic valid in one context may fail in another. Options A, D and C are unrelated or false statements.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: When the conclusion of an argument does not necessarily follow from its premises, the fallacy committed is called

options.a: non sequitur
options.b: per incuriam
options.c: obiter dictum
options.d: stare decisis

questions.explanation: Non sequitur ('it does not follow') is the fallacy where the conclusion does not follow from the premises, making the argument invalid. Option B describes a decision given through carelessness, option C a remark made in passing, and option D the doctrine of precedent.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Why is inductive reasoning usually needed when a lawyer bases his argument on case law rather than on a statute?

options.a: Statutes are always too vague to support deductive reasoning by a lawyer
options.b: Case law cannot be used as legal authority in any Nigerian court or tribunal
options.c: Judges are not allowed to use deductive reasoning when case law is cited
options.d: One decision may not yield a clear major premise, so several cases must be examined

questions.explanation: Deduction requires a clear major premise; with case law, the lawyer must reason from particular decisions to the general principle they establish, which then serves as the major premise. Option B is false, option A overstates the problem of vagueness, and option C is false because judges use both forms.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: To show that a negligent driver must pay damages to her client, counsel cites three earlier cases in which negligent defendants were held liable, shows that they share common features with her client's case, and argues that they establish a general rule that applies. Which form of reasoning is this?

options.a: Inductive reasoning
options.b: Forensic rhetoric based on emotion
options.c: Deductive reasoning from a statute
options.d: Reasoning per incuriam

questions.explanation: Building a general proposition from several particular decisions with common features is inductive reasoning, moving from the particular to the general. Option C would start from a statute as the major premise, option B is not what counsel did, and option D refers to a decision given in ignorance of a binding authority.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Lord Diplock in the Dorset Yacht case described how a court decides whether a duty of care exists. How did he describe the two stages of the process?

options.a: The first stage is analytical and inductive; the second is deductive and analytical
options.b: The first stage is mediation between the parties; the second stage is arbitration
options.c: Both stages are purely inductive, moving from particular cases to a general rule
options.d: The first stage is deductive and analytical; the second is rhetorical and persuasive

questions.explanation: The court first analyses previous decisions to find the characteristics common to cases where a duty of care was held to exist (induction), then applies that proposition to the facts before it (deduction). Options D, C and B misdescribe the two stages.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Analogical reasoning in law is best described as

options.a: comparing the issue with closely similar earlier decisions; a loose, not strictly logical, form of reasoning
options.b: a strictly formal argument whose conclusion follows necessarily from a major and a minor premise
options.c: the rule that a lower court must always follow the decision of a higher court on the same point
options.d: reasoning that ignores all previous decisions and relies only on the judge's own sense of fairness

questions.explanation: Analogical reasoning categorises the issue and compares it with closely similar earlier decisions; it is regarded as not strictly logical but a looser form of reasoning. Option B describes syllogism, option C describes binding precedent, and option D is the opposite of reasoning by analogy.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Farrar described English case law as the product of practical reasoning emerging from decision-making. Which attributes does it combine?

options.a: Legislation and the codification of custom
options.b: Syllogism and the old trial by ordeal
options.c: Reasoning by analogy and reasoning by rules
options.d: Forensic rhetoric and mediation by the judge

questions.explanation: Case law combines reasoning by analogy, comparing points of resemblance between cases, with reasoning by rules, classifying categories and stating principles. Options D, B and A pair terms that do not describe how case law is built.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: What is meant by the statement 'The life of the law has not been logic but experience'?

options.a: Only old precedents should ever be followed, since they represent the experience of the law
options.b: Logic is only part of legal reasoning; rules are reshaped by experience and changing values
options.c: Logic has no place at all in legal reasoning and should be avoided by judges and lawyers
options.d: Judges should decide cases on experience alone without giving any reasons for decisions

questions.explanation: The statement means that logic is only part of the story; the common law has stayed relevant by constantly supporting rules with reasons and modifying or discarding them when they no longer fit. Option C overstates the point, option D contradicts the need for justification, and option A ignores how rules are changed.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Why is litigation sometimes described as 'a gamble'?

options.a: Because judges weigh factors beyond authority, so outcomes can be hard to predict
options.b: Because the burden of proof shifts randomly from one party to the other during trial
options.c: Because courts never follow precedent, so earlier decisions give no guidance at all
options.d: Because judgments are decided by casting lots when the evidence is evenly balanced

questions.explanation: Since decisions involve logic, authority, justice, public policy and common sense, it can be difficult to predict how a court will resolve some cases. Option D is false, option B is wrong because the burden shifts with the pleadings and the evidence, and option C ignores stare decisis.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Which principle is associated with the case of Chinwendu v Mbamali?

options.a: A lower court must follow a higher court even if the decision was per incuriam
options.b: Justice delayed is justice denied
options.c: Justice should not be sacrificed on the altar of technicalities
options.d: The burden of proof lies on the one who affirms

questions.explanation: In Chinwendu v Mbamali the court warned that justice must not be sacrificed on the altar of technicalities and that disputes should be decided on their merits. Option B is a general saying about delay, option A is a rule of precedent, and option D is a rule on the burden of proof.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: On appeal, a party asks the court to set aside a judgment for N3,000,000 only because the respondent's counsel misnumbered two paragraphs of his brief, although the case was fully argued on its merits. Which approach is most consistent with modern legal reasoning?

options.a: Allow the appeal, because strict technical rules always override the demands of justice
options.b: Refer the whole matter to mediation, because the brief contains technical errors
options.c: Decide on the merits, since technicality must not cause a miscarriage of justice
options.d: Decide according to its personal sympathy for whichever party seems more deserving

questions.explanation: Rhetoric and logic are the technical parts of adjudication, but courts may depart from strict technicality where the interest of justice demands. Option A is the very approach the courts have rejected, option B has no basis, and option D would replace reasoned justification with personal feeling.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: A judge is trying an officer under a law that prescribes death for coup plotting. Pardons have been granted only once before, and international bodies are urging mercy. The judge reasons that a lighter sentence would better serve justice, public policy and what a reasonable man would do. Which aspect of legal reasoning is the judge relying on?

options.a: Strict syllogism, ignoring every factor except the exact wording of the statute
options.b: The rule that the opinions of foreign bodies are binding on Nigerian courts
options.c: Shifting of the burden of proof to the accused to show that there was no coup
options.d: Justifying the decision by justice, public policy and common sense, beyond authority

questions.explanation: Modern judges justify decisions not only by citing authority but by considering justice, public policy, common sense and the reasonable man. Option A describes the strictly technical approach the judge is moving away from, option B is wrong because foreign views are at most persuasive, and option C is unrelated.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: The doctrine of judicial precedent, also known as stare decisis, means that

options.a: a court may ignore the decisions of higher courts whenever it disagrees with them
options.b: the legislature must approve every judgment before it can bind any other court
options.c: every remark made by any judge binds all other courts in the country in later cases
options.d: a decision on a point of law binds the same court and lower courts in similar cases

questions.explanation: Stare decisis requires the same question of law to be decided the same way by the court and the courts below it. Option C is wrong because only the ratio decidendi binds, not passing remarks, option A contradicts the doctrine, and option B has no basis.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: In an earlier case with facts A, B, C and D, the court treated A, B and C as the material facts, discarded D, and gave decision Y. A later case in a lower court has material facts A, B and C, plus a different fact E that the court considers immaterial. Under the doctrine of precedent, the lower court should

options.a: give a decision opposite to Y
options.b: treat the earlier case as overruled
options.c: refuse to decide until fact D is proved
options.d: give decision Y

questions.explanation: Precedent binds through the essential facts and the decision based on them: where the essential facts are again A, B and C, the decision must also be Y. Option A contradicts the doctrine, option C is wrong because D was discarded as irrelevant, and option B is wrong because a lower court cannot overrule a higher court.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Counsel before the Oyo State High Court relies on a decision of the Lagos State High Court on the same point of law. How should the Oyo State High Court treat that decision?

options.a: As binding only if the Lagos judge was more senior than the Oyo judge
options.b: As persuasive only, since the courts are of coordinate jurisdiction
options.c: As irrelevant, since High Court decisions are never cited in other states
options.d: As binding, since every State High Court binds every other High Court

questions.explanation: Decisions of courts of coordinate or concurrent jurisdiction are only persuasive, so one State High Court is not bound by another. Option D overstates their effect, option C is wrong because such decisions may be cited and can persuade, and option A is wrong because seniority of judges does not make a decision binding.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: A judge of the Osun State High Court refuses to follow a Supreme Court decision because he thinks it was wrongly decided, and instead treats a contrary House of Lords decision as binding on him. Which statement is correct?

options.a: He erred twice: the Supreme Court decision binds him, and a House of Lords decision is at most persuasive in Nigeria
options.b: He was right on both points, since a High Court may choose which authority to follow
options.c: He was right to follow the House of Lords, since English decisions bind Nigerian courts
options.d: He was right to reject the Supreme Court decision, since the Supreme Court cannot bind State High Courts

questions.explanation: Supreme Court decisions bind all lower courts, and since foreign courts are outside the Nigerian court hierarchy, their decisions are only persuasive. Options B, C and D each misstate how binding and persuasive precedent work in Nigeria.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: The ratio decidendi of a case means

options.a: the final order of the court, such as the amount of damages awarded
options.b: a decision reached through ignorance or neglect of a binding statute
options.c: a statement of opinion made by the judge in passing, by the way
options.d: the reason for the decision: the legal rule on which the decision rests

questions.explanation: Only the ratio decidendi of a case, its essential legal reason, constitutes a binding precedent for later cases. Option C is an obiter dictum, option A is the order or outcome rather than its legal basis, and option B describes a per incuriam decision.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: According to Goodhart, how is the principle (ratio) of a case found?

options.a: From the reasons given in the opinion, considered without the facts
options.b: From the rule of law stated in the judgment, read on its own terms
options.c: By choosing among many possible levels of generality of the facts
options.d: From the facts the judge treated as material and his decision on them

questions.explanation: Goodhart held that the ratio is found in the facts the judge treated as essential, together with his decision on them, and also in what he held to be irrelevant. Options B and A are approaches Goodhart expressly rejected, and option C is Stone's approach, which criticised Goodhart.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Julius Stone, disagreeing with Goodhart, saw the process of finding the ratio decidendi as basically one of

options.a: reading the headnote prepared by the editor of the law report for the case
options.b: choosing an appropriate level of generality among many potential rationes
options.c: counting the number of judges who agreed with the leading judgment delivered
options.d: applying the rule that ignorance of the law is no excuse to the parties

questions.explanation: Stone argued that facts can be stated at different levels of generality, so a case holds several possible rationes and a later court must choose among them. Option A is not a method of finding the ratio, option C relates to appellate courts with several judges, and option D is unrelated.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: An obiter dictum is

options.a: the binding legal reason on which the decision of the case rests
options.b: a final and binding order made by an arbitrator after a hearing
options.c: a remark made by a judge 'by the way' that is not binding
options.d: a decision given in ignorance of a relevant and binding statute

questions.explanation: Obiter dictum means 'something said in passing': words of an opinion not necessary for deciding the case, which do not bind later courts. Option A is the ratio decidendi, option D is per incuriam, and option B is an award.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: In deciding a breach of contract case over the supply of bags of cement worth N700,000, the judge adds: 'Had the goods been perishable foodstuffs, I would have applied a different rule.' The goods were not perishable. That additional statement is

options.a: a standard of proof
options.b: the ratio decidendi
options.c: a per incuriam decision
options.d: an obiter dictum

questions.explanation: The statement concerns facts that were not before the court, so it was not necessary for the decision and is a remark made in passing. Option B is wrong because the ratio rests on the facts actually found, option C refers to decisions that overlook binding authority, and option A is unrelated.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: On what does the weight given to an obiter dictum mainly depend?

options.a: The level of the court and the learning of the judge who made it
options.b: Whether both parties to the case agreed with it at the time
options.c: The amount of money involved in the case in which it was made
options.d: The total length of the judgment in which the remark appears

questions.explanation: Obiter dicta do not bind, but their persuasive weight depends on the court's place in the hierarchy and the eruditeness of the judge; statements of the Supreme Court made after asking counsel to address it on the law are likely to be followed. Options C, B and D are not the factors that give obiter weight.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: A decision described as reached per incuriam is one that

options.a: was reached by the parties themselves through mediation outside the regular courts
options.b: was made by a judge in passing on facts that were not actually before the court
options.c: was given through carelessness, overlooking a relevant statute or binding precedent
options.d: was given by the highest court in the land and therefore binds every other court

questions.explanation: Per incuriam literally means 'through carelessness'; it applies where a relevant statute or binding precedent was not brought to the court's attention and was overlooked. Option D describes a binding Supreme Court decision, option B an obiter dictum, and option A an ADR settlement.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: A Chief Magistrate in Ilorin believes that a High Court decision binding on her was given per incuriam because it overlooked a statute. What should she do?

options.a: Declare the High Court decision overruled and apply the statute directly
options.b: Follow the High Court decision, though she may express doubt as obiter
options.c: Refer the question of law to an arbitrator for a binding determination
options.d: Refuse to follow it, since per incuriam decisions bind no court at all

questions.explanation: No court is bound by its own per incuriam decision, but a lower court remains bound by a higher court's decision even if it was reached per incuriam. Option D states the rule too widely, option A is beyond a magistrate's jurisdiction, and option C has no basis.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: 'Distinguishing' a case means

options.a: transferring the case to a higher court because the earlier decision appears to be inconsistent
options.b: following the earlier case exactly in every detail, even where the facts are clearly different
options.c: showing an essential factual difference, so the earlier case is not followed but remains good law
options.d: declaring that the earlier case was wrongly decided and is therefore no longer good law at all

questions.explanation: A court distinguishes a precedent when it finds a significant factual difference that justifies not applying it, while accepting that it is still good law. Option D describes overruling, which is open only to a court not bound by the earlier decision, option B is following, and option A is a transfer.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Glanville Williams classified distinguishing into restrictive and non-restrictive. What is non-restrictive distinguishing?

options.a: The court cuts down the ratio of the earlier case by treating extra facts as essential
options.b: The court leaves the earlier ratio intact but finds the facts materially different
options.c: The court follows the earlier case automatically without examining the facts
options.d: The court declares the earlier case wrongly decided and overrules it completely

questions.explanation: In non-restrictive distinguishing the earlier ratio is left intact and the present case is simply shown to be different on its facts. Option A describes restrictive distinguishing, which narrows the earlier ratio, option D is overruling, and option C is not distinguishing at all.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a factor affecting the weight of a precedent?

options.a: The status and composition of the court that decided it
options.b: Whether the decision was unanimous or had a dissent
options.c: The number of pages in the judgment
options.d: The age of the precedent

questions.explanation: The weight of a precedent depends on its age, the status of the court, the adequacy of its law report, its history in later cases, and whether the court was unanimous; the length of the judgment is not one of them. Options D, A and B are recognised factors.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the attitude of the Supreme Court of Nigeria to its own previous decisions?

options.a: It respects them but may overrule one reached on a wrong principle
options.b: It is absolutely bound by all its previous decisions without any exception
options.c: It must follow decisions of State High Courts that conflict with its own
options.d: It treats its previous decisions as merely persuasive obiter dicta

questions.explanation: As the court of last resort, the Supreme Court respects its precedents but, as held in cases such as Bronik Motors v Wema Bank, may depart from them on grounds such as injustice and public policy. Option B overstates the binding effect, option D understates it, and option C reverses the hierarchy.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Under the rule in Young v Bristol Aeroplane Co., followed by the Court of Appeal, the court is bound by its own previous decisions subject to exceptions. Which of the following is NOT one of those exceptions?

options.a: Where the court considers its earlier decision unpopular with the public
options.b: Where its earlier decision was given per incuriam
options.c: Where its earlier decision cannot stand with a decision of a higher court
options.d: Where there are two conflicting decisions of its own, it may choose which to follow

questions.explanation: The three exceptions are conflicting decisions of its own, a decision that cannot stand with a decision of a higher court, and a decision given per incuriam. Unpopularity of a decision is not an exception, while options D, C and B are the recognised exceptions.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Where an appellate court is equally divided, the practice is to dismiss the appeal on the principle semper praesumitur pro negante. What does this mean?

options.a: Let the earlier decision of the court stand
options.b: The facts of the accident speak for themselves
options.c: Justice must not only be done but be seen to be done
options.d: The presumption is always in favour of the negative

questions.explanation: Semper praesumitur pro negante means the presumption is always in favour of the negative, so an equally divided court dismisses the appeal and the decision below stands. Option C restates the dictum that justice must be seen to be done, option B paraphrases res ipsa loquitur, and option A translates stare decisis.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: On the old controversy whether judges make law, what is now the settled position?

options.a: Judges make law only in criminal matters and never in civil or equitable matters
options.b: Judges never make law; they only declare law that already existed before the case
options.c: Judges do make law, though retrospectively, where no statute or precedent applies
options.d: Only the legislature can create any rule of law, so case law does not really exist

questions.explanation: Judges must decide cases even where no statute or precedent clearly applies, so they make new law; it has been said that the rules of equity and nine-tenths of the common law were made by judges. Option B is the old declaratory view now set aside, option D ignores case law, and option A has no basis.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: To curb the crime of obtaining money by false pretences, popularly called '419', the government enacted the Advance Fee Fraud law. Which reason for new legislation does this best illustrate?

options.a: Arrest of anti-social behaviour
options.b: Global shifts in value systems
options.c: Scientific and technological breakthroughs
options.d: Change from a military to a civilian regime

questions.explanation: Governments legislate to arrest reckless or anti-social practices that harm the public or the country's image; the Advance Fee Fraud law is given as an example. Option B concerns changing values such as women's and children's rights, option D concerns a change of regime, and option C concerns new technology.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: Following a transition from military to civilian rule, the new government abolished an agency the previous regime had created and made new laws to pursue its own programmes. Which reason for new legislation does this illustrate?

options.a: Scientific and technological breakthroughs in the country
options.b: Global shifts in value systems on rights and the environment
options.c: Arrest of anti-social behaviour such as fraud and cultism
options.d: Change in the political and economic ideologies of government

questions.explanation: When the baton of governance changes, political goals change and changes in the law become inevitable; the abolition of the Petroleum Trust Fund at the start of civilian rule is an example. Options A, C and B are other reasons for legislation that do not fit these facts.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: How does a vague statutory provision differ from an ambiguous one?

options.a: Vagueness is always less serious than ambiguity, because context easily resolves a vague provision
options.b: An ambiguous provision has no meaning at all, while a vague provision has exactly two meanings
options.c: Ambiguity offers two or more meanings; vagueness leaves a cloudy meaning context can hardly cure
options.d: There is no difference, because both terms describe a provision that has been badly punctuated

questions.explanation: Ambiguity offers two or more mutually exclusive meanings, often resolvable by context; vagueness leaves the meaning indeterminate and is worse because context rarely cures it. Option B misdescribes both, option A reverses their seriousness, and option D ignores the distinction.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: In answering law problem questions, the acronym IRAC stands for

options.a: Issue, Ratio, Argument, Citation
options.b: Introduction, Rule, Analysis, Comment
options.c: Introduction, Definition, Body, Conclusion
options.d: Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion

questions.explanation: IRAC means identify the Issue, state the Rule (or Principle, in the IPAC variant), Apply it to the facts and reach a Conclusion. Options B and A are invented versions, and option C is IDBC, the structure used for essay questions.

questions.topic: Legal Reasoning: Logic, Rhetoric, Principles and Standards
questions.question: A student is given this question: 'Mr. Ade sued Mr. Ola in the Ibadan High Court and cited only an English House of Lords decision. Advise Mr. Ola.' Which approach is most suitable for answering it?

options.a: Listing all the Latin maxims and English cases known to the student
options.b: IRAC: identify the issue, state the rule, apply it, and conclude
options.c: IDBC: introduction, definition, body and conclusion, as for an essay
options.d: Writing a general essay on the history of English law in Nigeria

questions.explanation: This is a problem question, because it gives facts and asks for advice, so it is answered with IRAC (or IPAC). Option C is the structure for essay questions, and options D and A would not address the issue raised by the facts.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Under which rule of statutory interpretation must the court give the words of a statute their natural, ordinary and plain meaning, as stated by Tindal C.J. in the Sussex Peerage case?

options.a: The literal rule
options.b: The mischief rule
options.c: The ejusdem generis rule
options.d: The golden rule

questions.explanation: The literal rule says that where the words are precise and unambiguous, the words themselves best declare the legislature's intention, so the court simply applies their ordinary meaning. Option D allows a departure from that meaning to avoid absurdity, Option B looks at the defect the statute was meant to cure, and Option C narrows general words that follow a list.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: The golden rule of interpretation allows a court to

options.a: depart from the ordinary meaning of words where it would lead to absurdity, inconsistency or repugnance, but no further than needed
options.b: refuse to apply any statute it considers unjust
options.c: apply the ordinary meaning of words even where the result is absurd
options.d: look at the debates in the legislature to find what members intended

questions.explanation: The golden rule starts from the ordinary meaning but modifies it just enough to avoid a manifest absurdity or repugnance that the legislature could not have intended. Courts cannot simply refuse to apply a statute (Option B), and the use of legislative debates (Option D) is not part of this rule. Option C describes a strict literal approach.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: The mischief rule of statutory interpretation was laid down in

options.a: the Sussex Peerage case
options.b: Donoghue v. Stevenson
options.c: Heydon's case
options.d: Salomon v. Salomon & Co. Ltd

questions.explanation: Heydon's case (1584) set out the mischief rule, which asks what the law was before the statute and what defect the statute was passed to remedy. Option A is associated with the literal rule, while Option D (company law) and Option B (negligence) are not about statutory interpretation.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: When applying the mischief rule, the court mainly asks

options.a: what the words mean in their ordinary dictionary sense alone
options.b: what defect or mischief in the earlier law the statute was meant to remedy
options.c: how a reasonable man would vote on the statute
options.d: whether the statute agrees with natural law

questions.explanation: The mischief rule looks at the state of the law before the enactment and the shortcoming the new law came to cure, then interprets the words to suppress that mischief. Option A describes the literal rule, and Option D and Option C are not tests the court uses to interpret statutes.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Awolowo v. Shagari, which arose from the 1979 presidential election, is often used to show the weakness of the literal rule because

options.a: the court refused to interpret the Constitution at all
options.b: Supreme Court justices applying the literal rule to the same words reached opposing conclusions
options.c: the court relied entirely on the debates of the legislature
options.d: the court applied the ejusdem generis rule to reach an absurd result

questions.explanation: The dispute over 'two-thirds of all the States' (the famous 12 two-thirds argument) showed that words do not always have one plain meaning, since judges using the same literal approach disagreed. Option A and Option C did not happen, and Option D names the wrong rule.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: In Adegbenro v. Akintola, the Privy Council interpreted the provision that the Governor could remove the Premier "if it appears to him" that the Premier no longer commanded majority support. The court held that

options.a: the Governor could act only after a formal vote in the House of Assembly
options.b: the provision was void for vagueness
options.c: only the courts could decide whether the Premier had lost support
options.d: the Governor could reach that view without any limit on the material he relied on

questions.explanation: Reading the words literally, the Privy Council held that the Governor was not limited in the material on which he formed his view, so it could, as critics put it, even 'appear to him in a dream'. This is often cited to show how the literal rule can give surprising results. Option A, Option B and Option C were not the holding.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A statute refers to "bread, meat pie, cake, doughnut, sausage and other snacks". Under the ejusdem generis rule, "other snacks" will be read to cover

options.a: only things of the same class as those listed, such as pastries and confectioneries
options.b: only the items specifically named
options.c: main meals and drinks but not pastries
options.d: any food or drink whatsoever

questions.explanation: Ejusdem generis means that general words following a list of specific items are limited to things of the same kind as the list. So 'other snacks' covers similar pastries but not main food items or drinks (Option D and Option C). Option B would make the general words meaningless.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A rule states that a Principal or Vice-Principal absent from office without excuse shall be sanctioned. A court holds that it does not apply to ordinary teachers. Which maxim has it applied?

options.a: Ut res magis valeat quam pereat
options.b: Expressio unius est exclusio alterius
options.c: Lex non cogit ad impossibilia
options.d: Noscitur a sociis

questions.explanation: Expressio unius est exclusio alterius means that expressly mentioning one thing excludes others, so naming the Principal and Vice-Principal leaves other staff out. Option D means a word takes its meaning from the words around it. Option C means the law does not compel the impossible, and Option A means a provision should be read so that it works rather than fails.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: The maxim noscitur a sociis means that

options.a: the express mention of one thing excludes others
options.b: a provision should be interpreted so that it is effective rather than void
options.c: a word takes its meaning from the other words with which it is associated
options.d: the law does not compel the doing of impossibilities

questions.explanation: Noscitur a sociis literally means 'it is known by its companions': the meaning of a doubtful word is gathered from its context. Option A is expressio unius est exclusio alterius, Option D is lex non cogit ad impossibilia, and Option B is ut res magis valeat quam pereat.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Which of the following is a presumption courts use as a guide to legislative intention?

options.a: A presumption against ousting the jurisdiction of the courts
options.b: A presumption that every new Act silently changes all existing law
options.c: A presumption that statutes operate retrospectively
options.d: A presumption in favour of criminal liability without fault

questions.explanation: Courts presume that the legislature does not intend to shut people out of the courts, so a clause ousting jurisdiction must be clear and is construed strictly. The real presumptions are the opposite of Option C and Option D: against retrospective operation and against liability without fault. Option B is also wrong, since an Act is presumed not to alter existing law unless it says so.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Which of the following is an intrinsic aid to the interpretation of a statute?

options.a: The Interpretation Act
options.b: A law dictionary
options.c: The preamble or long title of the statute
options.d: A textbook by a recognised author

questions.explanation: Intrinsic aids are found inside the statute itself, such as the long title, preamble, definition or interpretation sections and schedules. A dictionary (Option B), a writer's book (Option D) and the Interpretation Act (Option A) all come from outside the statute, so they are extrinsic aids.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A statute that applies to everyone and everywhere within the state, such as the Criminal Code, is

options.a: a public general Act
options.b: a local Act
options.c: a private Act
options.d: a consolidating Act

questions.explanation: A public general Act has general application throughout the country to all persons. Option B applies only to a particular area or community, Option C applies to a particular person or body, and Option D describes a re-enactment of earlier statutes, which is about form rather than scope.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A law imposing a curfew in one part of the federation, or a law establishing a particular university, is best classified as

options.a: a public general Act
options.b: a consolidating Act
options.c: a code
options.d: a local Act

questions.explanation: A local Act applies to a particular locality or community, or deals with a particular regional problem or institution. Option A applies everywhere in the state, Option C gathers statute, common law and equity on a subject into one document, and Option B re-enacts earlier statutes as a coherent whole.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A statute granting a state pardon to a named convicted person, or proscribing a particular union, is

options.a: a private Act
options.b: a local Act
options.c: a code
options.d: a public general Act

questions.explanation: A private Act is even narrower than a local Act: it is made in respect of a particular person or body of persons. Option D applies to everyone, Option B applies to a particular place, and Option C brings together all the law on a subject.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
