questions.question: A newly passed statute that re-enacts the contents of earlier related statutes, with necessary modifications, to produce one coherent whole is

options.a: a private Act
options.b: a code
options.c: subsidiary legislation
options.d: a consolidating Act

questions.explanation: A consolidating Act brings scattered statutes on a subject together into a single enactment. It is different from Option B, which goes further by also gathering common law principles and doctrines of equity. Option A applies to a particular person, and Option C is made by a body other than the legislature.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: What distinguishes a code from an ordinary consolidating Act?

options.a: A code applies only to one locality
options.b: A code applies only to a particular named person
options.c: A code brings together existing statutes and also the principles of common law and doctrines of equity on a subject
options.d: A code is made by a minister under delegated powers

questions.explanation: A code, such as the Criminal Code, aims to state all the law on a subject in one document, including rules that came from common law and equity, while consolidation only re-enacts statutes. Option A describes a local Act, Option D subsidiary legislation, and Option B a private Act.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Bye-laws of local governments, regulations of public corporations and statutory instruments made by ministers are examples of

options.a: subsidiary (delegated) legislation
options.b: Acts of the National Assembly
options.c: codes
options.d: judicial precedents

questions.explanation: Subsidiary or delegated legislation is law made by persons or bodies other than the legislature, under powers conferred by a statute. Option B are made by the legislature itself, Option C are comprehensive statutes, and Option D are court decisions, not legislation.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: The statute under which a subsidiary legislation is made is known as

options.a: the private statute
options.b: the consolidating statute
options.c: the enabling statute
options.d: the interpretation statute

questions.explanation: The enabling statute (or parent Act) confers the power to make the subsidiary legislation and sets its limits. Option B re-enacts earlier statutes, Option A applies to a particular person, and Option D refers to the Interpretation Act, which defines common words used in legislation.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Subsidiary legislation that goes beyond the limits of the power conferred by its enabling statute is

options.a: valid until the legislature expressly repeals it
options.b: ultra vires, null and void
options.c: automatically converted into an Act of the National Assembly
options.d: valid if it was published in the Gazette

questions.explanation: Delegated power must be exercised within its limits; anything beyond them is ultra vires (beyond power) and void. Option A and Option D are wrong because publication or the absence of repeal cannot cure a lack of power, and Option C is simply not how delegated legislation works.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Which of the following is a main reason for the use of delegated legislation?

options.a: It allows the courts to make laws without any statutory authority
options.b: The Constitution forbids the legislature from making detailed laws
options.c: The legislature cannot make detailed rules for every aspect of life, and many areas need technical expertise
options.d: Delegated legislation is always superior to statutes

questions.explanation: The legislature usually sets out the general framework and leaves specialists and agencies to fill in technical details and respond to changing circumstances. Option B is false, Option D is the reverse of the truth because delegated legislation is inferior to its enabling statute, and Option A misdescribes it since it always rests on a statute.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: In Nigerian legislative terminology, an enactment made by a State Military Governor or Administrator during military rule is called

options.a: a Decree
options.b: a Law
options.c: an Act
options.d: an Edict

questions.explanation: Under military rule, the Federal Military Government made Decrees while State military governors made Edicts. In civilian times, the National Assembly makes Acts and a State House of Assembly makes Laws. So Option A, Option C and Option B are the names for enactments by other law makers.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Strictly speaking, legislation as a source of law refers to law made by which of the following?

options.a: Superior courts when they lay down principles in decided cases
options.b: The legislature, the body whose primary duty is to make law
options.c: A community whose customs are accepted by its members as binding
options.d: Any ministry, university or public corporation that issues rules

questions.explanation: In the strict sense, legislation is law made by the legislature, the organ whose main job is law-making, as B states. Option D describes the wider sense in which many agencies make rules, and A describes judicial precedent. Option C is customary law, not legislation.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: The formal and express promulgation or declaration of legal rules, proscriptions or directions into statutes on the subjects to which they relate best describes:

options.a: Judicial precedent
options.b: Legislation
options.c: Customary law
options.d: Doctrines of equity

questions.explanation: Legislation is the formal, express declaration of legal rules into statutes, so B is right. Judicial precedent (A) comes from court decisions, while customary law (C) and equity (D) grew from usage and the Chancery courts rather than from formal enactment.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Section 4(2) of the 1999 Constitution empowers the National Assembly to make laws for the:

options.a: Peace, order and good government of the Federation
options.b: Welfare, security and prosperity of the Federation
options.c: Unity, faith and progress of the Federation
options.d: Justice, equity and good conscience of the Federation

questions.explanation: Section 4(2) gives the National Assembly power to make laws for the peace, order and good government of the Federation, which is A. Option D borrows the wording of the repugnancy test for customary law, and C and B are invented phrases that only sound constitutional.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the reasons for making new legislation or changing old laws?

options.a: Change in the political and economic ideologies of government
options.b: The need to preserve every existing custom whatever the change in values
options.c: Scientific and technological breakthroughs
options.d: The dynamic nature of society

questions.explanation: New laws are made because society changes, so a wish to freeze every custom regardless of change (B) is not a reason for legislation; many customs have in fact been set aside as repugnant. Options D, C and A are all recognised reasons, along with global shifts in value and the arrest of anti-social behaviour.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: The spread of computers and the Internet creates new problems about private information being shared with everyone and about copyright in broadcast music, so the National Assembly begins work on information technology laws. Which reason for new legislation does this illustrate?

options.a: Change in the political ideology of a new government
options.b: Scientific and technological breakthroughs
options.c: Global shifts in value systems
options.d: The transition from a military to a civilian regime

questions.explanation: Laws prompted by new inventions such as computers, satellites and the Internet are made to cope with scientific and technological breakthroughs, so B is correct. Option A and D concern changes of government, and C concerns changing ideas of justice such as women's and children's rights, not new technology.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: After a military regime hands over to an elected government, the new administration repeals several Decrees and abolishes an agency created by the old regime in order to pursue its own policies. Which reason for legislation is at work?

options.a: The need to codify customary law
options.b: Global shifts in value systems
options.c: Change in the political and economic ideologies of government
options.d: Scientific and technological breakthroughs

questions.explanation: When the baton of governance changes, new goals and ideologies make changes in the law inevitable, as in the abolition of the Petroleum Trust Fund after the return to civil rule; that is C. Options D and B are different reasons, and A is about codification rather than a change of government.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Nigeria joins several international organisations and, influenced by them, passes laws on the rights of women and children and on the protection of endangered species. Which reason for legislation does this best illustrate?

options.a: Global shifts in value systems
options.b: Arrest of anti-social behaviour
options.c: Change in the political ideology of government
options.d: Scientific and technological breakthroughs

questions.explanation: Laws on women's and children's rights and on conservation that reflect international standards come from global shifts in value systems, so A is right. Option D concerns new technology, C concerns a change of government, and B concerns curbing harmful conduct such as fraud.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: As people adopt new attitudes about public health, a State enacts a law forbidding the dumping of refuse in public places and the indiscriminate slaughtering of animals. Which reason for legislation does this best illustrate?

options.a: The need to consolidate existing statutes
options.b: Scientific and technological breakthroughs
options.c: Change in the political ideology of government
options.d: The dynamic nature of society

questions.explanation: Because human beings and their values keep changing, the law must also change, and laws on refuse dumping and slaughtering are given as examples of this, so D is right. Option B concerns new inventions, C concerns a change of government, and A describes a type of Act rather than a reason for new law.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Which of the following statements about who may initiate a proposal for legislation is correct?

options.a: Only the President or a State Governor may initiate a proposal
options.b: Proposals may come from citizens, interest groups, NGOs, communities, ministries or legislators
options.c: Only a serving member of the National Assembly may initiate a proposal
options.d: Only the Law Reform Commission may initiate a proposal

questions.explanation: Legislative proposals can be instigated by citizens, interest groups, communities, private persons, NGOs, government ministries or legislators, as B says. Options A, C and D each wrongly limit the right to one body; for example, a private person's idea can be presented through a member of the National Assembly.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Which statement about the form of a legislative proposal is correct?

options.a: It must be a fully drafted bill with long title and enacting clause
options.b: It must be written in English, Hausa, Igbo and Yoruba before submission
options.c: It must follow a form prescribed in the Second Schedule to the Constitution
options.d: It need not take a stereotyped form but should be logically and structurally presented

questions.explanation: A legislative proposal need not assume any fixed form, although it makes sense to present it logically and to state the subject matter it relates to, so D is right. Option A confuses a proposal with a finished bill, which comes later, and C and B invent formal requirements that do not exist.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: In what order should a well-structured legislative proposal usually present its contents?

options.a: Suggested changes, present position, concrete proposals for the law, anomalies
options.b: Present position, anomalies, suggested changes, concrete proposals for the law
options.c: Concrete proposals for the law, present position, anomalies, suggested changes
options.d: Anomalies, concrete proposals for the law, present position, suggested changes

questions.explanation: A proposal first describes the present position, then the anomalies or problems, then suggestions for change, and lastly concrete proposals and a framework for the law, which is the order in B. The other options put the concrete framework or the suggestions before the problem has been shown, which reverses the logic of the proposal.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a usual channel through which legislative proposals are expressed or submitted?

options.a: Memoranda submitted to the Law Reform Commission
options.b: A judgment of the Supreme Court addressed to the parties
options.c: Opinions expressed in the print and electronic media
options.d: Memoranda submitted to the relevant committee of the legislature

questions.explanation: A court judgment settles a dispute between parties; it is not a channel for proposing new legislation, so B is the odd one out. Proposals are normally expressed in memoranda to government departments, the legislature or its committees (D) or the Law Reform Commission (A), and may also appear in the media (C) or come through pressure groups.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A national teachers' union writes newspaper articles and submits memoranda urging a law to make teaching a regulated profession. In legislative terms, the union is:

options.a: Making delegated legislation under an enabling statute
options.b: Channelling a legislative proposal as a pressure group
options.c: Presenting a bill for its first reading
options.d: Promulgating a Decree on behalf of the executive

questions.explanation: Professional, economic and other pressure groups often channel legislative proposals through memoranda and the media, as the Nigerian Union of Teachers did on professionalising teaching, so B is right. A union has no power to make delegated legislation (A) or Decrees (D), and only a bill already before a House can have a first reading (C).

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A legislative draftsman should receive detailed instructions before drafting. Which of the following is NOT one of the items the instructions should state?

options.a: The names of the judges who will later interpret the law
options.b: The object of the legislation and background information
options.c: The mischief or need the law is meant to cure or meet
options.d: The implementation bodies, procedures and possible exemptions

questions.explanation: Drafting instructions should state the object, background, the mischief or need to be met, the implementing bodies, procedures and instruments, and possible exemptions, which covers B, C and D. Who will later interpret the law (A) is not something a draftsman is told or needs; interpretation is for whichever court hears a case.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a quality expected of a good legislative draftsman?

options.a: Familiarity with the socio-cultural and political peculiarities of the country
options.b: High intellectual competence and an analytical, diagnostic mind
options.c: Patience, care and close attention to detail
options.d: Firmness in refusing corrections and criticisms of his draft

questions.explanation: A good draftsman must be amenable to corrections, suggestions and criticisms, so refusing them (D) is the opposite of what is expected. Options B, A and C are all listed qualities, because the draftsman writes for legislators, lawyers, judges and ordinary citizens alike.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: The chairman of a local government council plans to appoint any Arts graduate as the council's legislative draftsman because 'drafting is only about good English'. What is the best advice?

options.a: Let the councillors draft bills themselves, since they will vote on them
options.b: Appoint any Arts graduate, since mastery of English is the only skill needed
options.c: Appoint a professional linguist, since bills are judged mainly on grammar
options.d: Appoint a lawyer, because knowledge of law is an indispensable quality of a draftsman

questions.explanation: Drafting a bill free of ambiguity, vagueness and textual defects needs legal training, so the council should engage a lawyer with the other qualities of a draftsman, as D says. Good English matters, but B and C ignore the legal technicalities, and A ignores that drafting is a specialist skill separate from voting.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Section 55 of the 1999 Constitution provides that the business of the National Assembly shall be conducted in:

options.a: English only, with no provision for any Nigerian language
options.b: English and Nigerian Pidgin, whichever members prefer
options.c: English, and in Hausa, Ibo and Yoruba when adequate arrangements have been made
options.d: Hausa, Ibo and Yoruba only, with English used for records

questions.explanation: Section 55 names English, and Hausa, Ibo and Yoruba once adequate arrangements are made, which is C; in practice English remains the language of the law in Nigeria. Option A ignores the three indigenous languages the section mentions, while D and B misstate which languages are listed.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Under the drafting principle of mastery and familiarity of language, which practice should a draftsman follow?

options.a: Use expressions peculiar to each ethnic group so all feel included
options.b: Prefer Latin phrases such as pari passu because they are more precise
options.c: Use technical legal jargon so that only lawyers can apply the law
options.d: Use common, familiar English words and avoid tribal or Latin expressions

questions.explanation: The draftsman should stick to common, familiar words so that people do not need a lawyer or a linguist to know what the law says, and should avoid tribal expressions and even assimilated Latin like inter alia or pari passu, so D is right. Options B, A and C each recommend exactly the kind of language the principle warns against.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A draft reads: 'where the borrower fails, refuses, neglects, omits or avoids repayment ... in breach of his obligation, undertaking, agreement or promise'. Which drafting principle does it most clearly break?

options.a: Economy of language
options.b: Consistency of terms
options.c: Orderliness
options.d: Correct punctuation

questions.explanation: The clause piles up words that do the same work, which is the verbosity that economy of language forbids, so A is right; one word from each list would do. Consistency of terms (B) is about using one word for one idea throughout, orderliness (C) concerns arrangement of sections, and D concerns punctuation marks.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A draft provides: 'Only courts specified in section 6 above shall exercise the powers hereinafter contained in this section.' Which drafting fault does the use of 'above' and 'hereinafter' show?

options.a: Lack of orderliness
options.b: Ambiguity
options.c: Archaism
options.d: Inconsistency of terms

questions.explanation: Words such as 'hereinafter', 'hereinbefore' and 'above mentioned' are archaic and can be removed without any damage to the meaning, so the fault is archaism, C. The sentence has only one meaning, so it is not ambiguous (B), it does not switch terms (D), and its arrangement is not in issue (A).

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: In a draft Tenancy Law, section 2 refers to 'the lessor' and section 5 refers to 'the landlord', although both mean the same person. Which drafting principle is breached?

options.a: Direct and explicit expression
options.b: Avoidance of archaism
options.c: Consistency of terms
options.d: Economy of language

questions.explanation: Once a draftsman picks a word for an idea he must use it throughout, and 'lessor' and 'landlord' should not be used interchangeably for the same person, so C is right. Economy (D) is about cutting redundant words, B is about old-fashioned words, and A is about avoiding winding sentences.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A drafter replaces a long, winding clause on self-defence with the simple sentence 'Every person has a right to defend himself when attacked.' Which drafting principle is being applied?

options.a: Consistency of terms
options.b: Use of an interpretation clause
options.c: Use of schedules
options.d: Direct and explicit expression

questions.explanation: Replacing a clumsy, intricate clause with a short sentence that carries the same meaning applies the principle of direct and explicit expression, so D is right. Consistency of terms (A) is about using one word per idea, while schedules (C) and interpretation clauses (B) are separate structural devices.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Why must a draftsman be careful with connective words such as 'from' and 'to' in a time provision?

options.a: They are archaic words that should never appear in a statute
options.b: They may either include or exclude the stated periods
options.c: They are defined in the same way in every Nigerian statute
options.d: They always oblige the reader to count only working days

questions.explanation: Connective and definitive words can carry more than their everyday meaning; 'from' and 'to' may include or exclude stated periods, just as 'shall' may signal duty or discretion and 'or' may join or offer alternatives, so B is right. They are not archaic (A), and D and C invent fixed rules that do not exist.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Writers and drafters are advised to avoid certain pitfalls of style. Which of the following is NOT such advice?

options.a: Use the same word always for the same idea
options.b: Be wary of using metaphors in a draft
options.c: Avoid repetitions and needless duplications
options.d: Vary words for the same idea to add elegance

questions.explanation: The advice is to use the same word for the same idea, because elegant variation is confusing in a statute, so D reverses the rule. Options B, A and C are the three pitfalls a drafter is warned about; a statute is not a literary masterpiece or an experiment in synonyms.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A statute whose language affords two or more mutually exclusive meanings, each of which can be deduced from the text, is said to be:

options.a: Ultra vires
options.b: Ambiguous
options.c: Vague
options.d: Archaic

questions.explanation: Ambiguity exists when a provision is capable of two or more mutually exclusive meanings, each deducible from the text, so B is right. Vagueness (C) is a cloudy, indeterminate meaning rather than competing clear ones, A refers to subsidiary law made beyond its powers, and D refers to old-fashioned words.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Ambiguity in statutes is often classified into three types. Which of the following is NOT one of them?

options.a: Syntactic ambiguity
options.b: Lexical ambiguity
options.c: Procedural ambiguity
options.d: Contextual ambiguity

questions.explanation: The three usual classes are lexical, syntactic and contextual ambiguity, which are B, A and D. 'Procedural ambiguity' (C) is not one of the recognised classes.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Why is vagueness in a statute regarded as worse than ambiguity?

options.a: A vague provision can hardly be resolved by reference to the context of the statute
options.b: Vagueness affects only marginal notes, not the operative sections
options.c: An ambiguous provision can never be resolved by any court
options.d: A vague provision always has exactly two possible meanings

questions.explanation: A vague provision is cloudy and indeterminate, and unlike an ambiguous one it can hardly be cured by looking at the context of the statute, so A is right. Option D actually describes ambiguity, B is invented, and C is wrong because ambiguity can often be resolved from context.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A State Law bans 'large gatherings' without a permit but does not say how many people make a gathering 'large'. Officials cannot say whether a meeting of 40 people is covered. This defect is best described as:

options.a: Archaism caused by old-fashioned legal words
options.b: Vagueness, creating borderline cases with no definite answer
options.c: Lexical ambiguity between two clear dictionary meanings
options.d: Inconsistency of terms across different sections

questions.explanation: Where a provision creates borderline cases in which there is no definite answer whether it applies, the defect is vagueness, so B is right. The word 'large' does not offer two competing clear meanings, so C does not fit, and there are no archaic words (A) or switched terms (D) in the provision.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A statute requires every 'bank' within a river basin to be registered. One party argues it means financial institutions; another argues it means riverbanks. Each reading fits the words. This is an example of:

options.a: Ambiguity
options.b: Economy of language
options.c: Open texture deliberately built in
options.d: Vagueness

questions.explanation: The word 'bank' here yields two mutually exclusive meanings, each deducible from the text, which is ambiguity, A; it is lexical ambiguity because it arises from a single word. Vagueness (D) is an indeterminate meaning rather than two clear rivals, C is intended flexibility, and B is a drafting virtue, not a defect.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: In legislative drafting, 'open texture' refers to:

options.a: Built-in generality or flexibility, since no statute can foresee every future case
options.b: The rule that all bills must be gazetted before second reading
options.c: A drafting error in which two sections contradict each other
options.d: The practice of opening each statute with a long title and preamble

questions.explanation: Because a drafter must make a rule general enough to cover unforeseen cases while keeping it clear, and no statute can settle all future situations in advance, flexibility or open texture is built into legislation, so A is right. Option D describes preliminary parts, C describes inconsistency, and B confuses open texture with gazetting.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: The observation that 'breadth of scope and precision are not always compatible objectives' describes which dilemma of the drafter?

options.a: Deciding whether to use marginal notes or schedules
options.b: Deciding whether a bill should start in the Senate or the House
options.c: Choosing between drafting in English and in an indigenous language
options.d: Making a rule general enough to cover all foreseeable cases yet detailed and clear

questions.explanation: The drafter must make a rule broad enough to cover all foreseeable instances within the policy of the statute and also detailed enough to be clear, and these two aims pull against each other, so D is right. Options C, B and A are practical choices, not the generality-versus-precision dilemma behind open texture.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: In what order do the parts of a Commonwealth-style statute usually appear?

options.a: Preliminary, final, principal, executive endorsement, miscellaneous
options.b: Principal, preliminary, final, miscellaneous, executive endorsement
options.c: Executive endorsement, preliminary, principal, miscellaneous, final
options.d: Preliminary, principal, miscellaneous, final, executive endorsement

questions.explanation: The usual order is preliminary parts, principal parts, miscellaneous parts, final parts and then the executive endorsement where the bill is signed, as in D. The other options misplace the endorsement, which comes last, or put substantive provisions ahead of the long title and enacting clause.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A draftsman is placing a clause that repeals an earlier Act, saves certain rights under it and makes transitional arrangements. In which part of the statute does this clause usually belong?

options.a: Preliminary parts
options.b: Principal parts
options.c: Final parts
options.d: Executive endorsement part

questions.explanation: Final parts provide for savings, transitional provisions, repeals, schedules and possibly an interpretation section, so C is right. Preliminary parts (A) hold the long title, preamble, short title, enacting and commencement clauses, principal parts (B) hold the substantive and administrative provisions, and D is where the bill is signed.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Which of the following belongs to the preliminary parts of a statute?

options.a: The offences and other supplementary provisions
options.b: The substantive provisions and the administrative provisions
options.c: The savings, transitional provisions and repeals
options.d: The long title, short title, enacting clause and commencement clause

questions.explanation: Preliminary parts comprise the long title, the preamble (usually but not always), the short title or citation, the enacting clause and the commencement clause, so D is right. Option B describes the principal parts, A the miscellaneous parts, and C the final parts.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: The part of a statute that contains its substantive provisions and its administrative provisions naming the enforcing agencies is called the:

options.a: Final parts
options.b: Principal parts
options.c: Miscellaneous parts
options.d: Preliminary parts

questions.explanation: The principal parts contain the substantive provisions, which are the main business of the law, and the administrative provisions stating the enforcing instruments and agencies, so B is right. Preliminary parts (D) introduce the law, miscellaneous parts (C) hold offences and supplementary provisions, and final parts (A) hold savings, repeals and schedules.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: In the structure of a statute, 'schedules' are used to:

options.a: Record the votes cast at the third reading of the bill
options.b: Contain the President's signature and the date of assent
options.c: State the long title and the date of commencement
options.d: Set out elaborate technical information that cannot conveniently go in the main text

questions.explanation: Schedules carry more elaborate, technical or explicit information that could not conveniently be included in the main text of the legislation, so D is right. Votes (A) are not part of the statute's text, the signature belongs to the executive endorsement (B), and the long title and commencement are preliminary parts (C).

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Why must a legislative draftsman pay particular attention to punctuation?

options.a: Punctuation is ignored by courts, so errors in it are harmless
options.b: Punctuation decides which House of the legislature must pass the bill
options.c: Punctuation marks may only be used in schedules, not in sections
options.d: Changing punctuation alone can alter the meaning of a passage without changing a word

questions.explanation: The effect of punctuation is so far-reaching that the meaning of a paragraph can be changed by tinkering with it without altering any word, so D is right. Option A is wrong because courts take punctuation into account when construing an enactment, and C and B are invented rules.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Under the 1999 Constitution, the National Assembly is a bicameral legislature made up of:

options.a: The Senate and the House of Representatives
options.b: The Senate and the State Houses of Assembly
options.c: The House of Representatives and the Federal Executive Council
options.d: The Senate and the Council of State

questions.explanation: Nigeria's federal legislature is bicameral, with the Senate and the House of Representatives together forming the National Assembly, so A is right. State Houses of Assembly (B) are separate State legislatures, and the Federal Executive Council (C) and Council of State (D) are executive or advisory bodies.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: What happens at the first reading of a bill in the House where it originates?

options.a: The final draft is voted on by a simple or two-thirds majority
options.b: The Clerk reads it to inform members of its subject; no questions are asked on it
options.c: A committee goes through it clause by clause and word by word
options.d: Members debate its general principles and ask questions on it

questions.explanation: The first reading, done by the Clerk or a designated person, merely introduces members to the subject matter, and the bill is not questioned at that stage, so B is right. Debate on general principles (D) happens at second reading, clause-by-clause scrutiny (C) at committee stage, and the final vote (A) at third reading.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: At which stage of a bill are its general principles and import debated and questions asked on it for the first time?

options.a: Report stage
options.b: Committee stage
options.c: Second reading
options.d: First reading

questions.explanation: After printing and distribution, the second reading is when the general principles of the bill are discussed and questions asked, so C is right. The first reading (D) is only an introduction, the committee stage (B) is detailed clause-by-clause work, and the report stage (A) presents the amended bill back to the House.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: The function of the committee stage of a bill is best described as:

options.a: Voting on the final draft by the required majority
options.b: Reading the long title aloud so members know the bill exists
options.c: Obtaining the President's signature on the passed bill
options.d: Going through the text clause by clause, even word by word, to make it more acceptable

questions.explanation: At committee stage the bill goes through the text clause by clause and, if necessary, word by word, and may undergo drastic amendment, so D is right. Option B describes the first reading, C describes assent, and A describes the third reading.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: The House of Representatives sets up a committee to investigate a specific crisis in the aviation sector, and the committee is dissolved once it submits its report. This committee is:

options.a: A joint finance committee
options.b: A committee of the whole Senate
options.c: An ad hoc committee
options.d: A standing committee

questions.explanation: Committees set up from time to time to look into specific issues and dissolved after completing their assignment are ad hoc committees, so C is right. Standing committees (D) are permanent committees on subjects such as education, health and aviation, the joint finance committee (A) deals with disputed money bills, and B concerns the other House.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: The stage at which a bill is put before the House in its amended or revised form after committee work, when its likely success or failure becomes evident, is the:

options.a: Second reading
options.b: First reading
options.c: Assent stage
options.d: Report stage

questions.explanation: After the committee stage comes the report stage, when the amended bill is laid before the House for further consideration, so D is right. The second reading (A) comes before committee work, the first reading (B) is only an introduction, and assent (C) follows passage by both Houses.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Which sequence correctly shows the stages of a bill in its House of origin?

options.a: First reading, second reading, committee stage, report stage, third reading
options.b: First reading, committee stage, second reading, third reading, report stage
options.c: Second reading, first reading, report stage, committee stage, third reading
options.d: First reading, second reading, report stage, committee stage, third reading

questions.explanation: A bill is introduced at first reading, debated in principle at second reading, examined in detail at committee stage, returned to the House at report stage, and then read a third time and voted on, which is A. Option D reverses the committee and report stages, and the other options put debate or reporting in the wrong place.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: At the third reading, by what majority is a bill passed?

options.a: By a simple majority or a two-thirds majority, depending on its subject matter
options.b: By the Speaker or Senate President alone if members are divided
options.c: Always by unanimous vote of all members present
options.d: Always by a three-quarters majority of the whole House

questions.explanation: At the third reading the bill in its final draft is voted on and passed by a simple majority or by a two-thirds majority depending on its subject matter, so A is right. No rule requires unanimity (C) or three-quarters (D) for ordinary bills, and a presiding officer cannot pass a bill alone (B).

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: After a bill has been passed by the House in which it originated, what happens next?

options.a: It becomes law at once if it was passed by two-thirds
options.b: It goes straight to the President for assent
options.c: It is sent to the other House and goes through a similar procedure
options.d: It is sent to the Supreme Court to confirm its validity

questions.explanation: Because the National Assembly is bicameral, a bill passed in its House of origin is sent to the other House, where it passes through a similar procedure before going to the President, so C is right. It does not go straight to the President (B), courts play no part in passing bills (D), and a two-thirds vote in one House alone does not make law (A).

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Under section 58(5) of the 1999 Constitution, what is the effect when the President withholds assent to a bill?

options.a: It becomes law if passed again by a simple majority of a joint sitting
options.b: It becomes law without assent if passed again by two-thirds majority in each House
options.c: It becomes law automatically after the President's term ends
options.d: It is dead and can never be reintroduced in the National Assembly

questions.explanation: Where the President withholds assent and the bill is again passed by each House by a two-thirds majority, it becomes law and his assent is not required, so B is right. A veto does not kill the bill forever (D), there is no automatic law at the end of a term (C), and a simple majority (A) is not enough.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: The President withholds assent to a Road Safety Bill. The Senate passes it again by a two-thirds majority, but the House of Representatives passes it again by only a simple majority. What is the position?

options.a: It does not become law, because each House must re-pass it by two-thirds
options.b: It becomes law, because a simple majority in both Houses is enough
options.c: It becomes law, because the Senate's two-thirds vote is enough
options.d: It becomes law once the Clerk reads its long title a third time

questions.explanation: Section 58(5) requires the bill to be passed again by each House by a two-thirds majority before it can become law without assent, so a simple majority in the House of Representatives is not enough, as A says. Options C and B each ignore the requirement in one of the Houses, and D invents a rule.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: What is the effect of the assent of the President or a State Governor on a bill?

options.a: It makes the bill a Decree of the National Assembly
options.b: It sends the bill to the Senate for its first reading
options.c: It sends the bill back to the committee stage for amendment
options.d: It turns the passed bill into an Act (federal) or a Law (State)

questions.explanation: Unless the bill is assented to (or the veto is overridden), it cannot become an Act or a Law; assent by the President produces an Act if federal, and by a Governor a Law if State, so D is right. Assent ends the process rather than restarting it (C, B), and Decrees (A) belong to military regimes.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Why is a bill published in the Gazette after it has been introduced?

options.a: To make it binding law immediately on publication
options.b: To give the public notice so that people can weigh in for or against it
options.c: To show that the President has already assented to it
options.d: To obtain the approval of the Chief Justice of Nigeria

questions.explanation: Bills are gazetted to give the public notice that legislation is being considered so that people can make their views known, for or against, so B is right. Gazetting a bill does not make it law (A), the judiciary is not part of the process (D), and assent comes at the end, not at gazetting (C).

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: How does law-making under a military regime differ from law-making under a civilian regime in Nigeria?

options.a: Military Decrees require a two-thirds vote of the State Houses of Assembly
options.b: Military Decrees must pass three readings in both the Senate and the House
options.c: Military law-making is slower because each Decree goes to the Supreme Court
options.d: Legislative and executive powers are fused, so Decrees are made without readings or debates

questions.explanation: Under military rule the legislature and executive are fused, and a Decree is made by typing and signing a text by the Head of the Federal Military Government without readings, debates or voting, so D is right. This ease explains the many shortcomings and endless amendments in military laws. Options B, A and C describe procedures that did not apply to Decrees.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: During a military regime, the Military Governor of a State signs a short typed text banning street trading in the State capital. That enactment is called:

options.a: A Law
options.b: A Decree
options.c: An Edict
options.d: An Act

questions.explanation: An enactment made by a State Military Governor or Administrator is an Edict, so C is right. A Decree (B) is made by the Federal Military Government, an Act (D) by the National Assembly, and a Law (A) by an elected State House of Assembly.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: What is a major weakness of legislation made under military regimes?

options.a: The involvement of the judiciary, which makes Decrees unconstitutional
options.b: The need for a two-thirds vote, which blocks most Decrees
options.c: Lack of rigorous scrutiny, which leads to shortcomings and endless amendments
options.d: Excessive public consultation, which delays every Decree for years

questions.explanation: Because Decrees and Edicts are made so easily, they escape rigorous criticism and scrutiny, which accounts for their many shortcomings and the endless amendments that follow, so C is right. Options D, B and A describe features of the civilian process or invented rules, not the military process.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: The National Assembly passes an Act setting up a commission to tackle environmental and economic problems in one particular region of Nigeria. This Act is best classified as a:

options.a: Private Act
options.b: Local Act
options.c: Public General Act
options.d: Code

questions.explanation: A Local Act applies to a particular locality or community, and laws made to combat environmental or economic problems of a particular region, such as the Niger Delta Development Commission Act, are given as examples, so B is right. It is not a Public General Act (C) because it targets one region, not a Private Act (A) because it is not about particular persons, and not a Code (D).

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A statute is passed solely to grant a state pardon to one named convicted person and to return property earlier confiscated from him. This is a:

options.a: Local Act
options.b: Private Act
options.c: Public General Act
options.d: Consolidating Act

questions.explanation: A Private Act is made in respect of a particular person or body of persons, for example a statute granting a state pardon to a convicted person or restoring confiscated property, so B is right. A Local Act (A) concerns a place, a Public General Act (C) applies to everyone, and a Consolidating Act (D) re-enacts earlier statutes.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A Consolidating Act is best described as a statute that:

options.a: Is made by a Minister under powers given by an enabling statute
options.b: Applies only to one named person or body of persons
options.c: Combines existing statutes, common law and equity on a subject into one document
options.d: Re-enacts the contents of earlier related statutes, with necessary changes, as one coherent whole

questions.explanation: A Consolidating Act is a newly passed statute that re-enacts the content of an earlier statute or related statutes, with such modifications as are necessary, to produce a coherent whole, so D is right. Option B describes a Private Act, C describes a Code, which goes further by including common law and equity, and A describes subsidiary legislation.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A statute that puts together in one document the existing legislation, the principles of common law and the doctrines of equity on a stated subject is a:

options.a: Code
options.b: Private Act
options.c: Local Act
options.d: Consolidating Act

questions.explanation: A Code attempts to put existing legislation, common law principles and equitable doctrines on a subject into one comprehensive document, with the Criminal Code, Penal Code and Companies and Allied Matters Act as examples, so A is right. A Consolidating Act (D) re-enacts only earlier statutes, while Local (C) and Private (B) Acts are defined by their limited reach.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: What is the main difference between a Consolidating Act and a Code?

options.a: Consolidation re-enacts statutes only; a Code also takes in common law and equity
options.b: Consolidation applies only to States; a Code applies only to the Federation
options.c: Consolidation is made by the military; a Code is made by the legislature
options.d: Consolidation needs no assent; a Code needs a two-thirds majority

questions.explanation: A Consolidating Act brings together and re-enacts earlier statutes, while a Code sums up the existing legislation together with the principles of common law and doctrines of equity on a subject, so A is right. Options B, C and D invent differences of level, regime and voting that do not define either type.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: The National Assembly repeals four separate statutes on civil aviation and re-enacts their provisions, with minor changes, in a single new Act. No common law or equitable rules are added. The new Act is a:

options.a: Local Act
options.b: Consolidating Act
options.c: Private Act
options.d: Code

questions.explanation: Re-enacting the contents of several related statutes, with necessary modifications, into one coherent statute is consolidation, so B is right. It is not a Code (D) because no common law or equity is being brought in, and it is not limited to particular persons (C) or to one locality (A).

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Reformers propose a single statute on land in Nigeria that would bring together the Land Use Act, conveyancing statutes, common law rules and customary land tenure. This proposal is an example of:

options.a: Delegated legislation
options.b: A Private Act
options.c: Consolidation of a single statute
options.d: Codification

questions.explanation: Pulling scattered statutes, common law and customary rules on land into one comprehensive law that states all the law on the subject is codification, so D is right. Consolidation (C) re-enacts statutes only, delegated legislation (A) is made under an enabling statute, and a Private Act (B) concerns particular persons.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an argument in favour of codification?

options.a: It simplifies the work of judges and makes the law more accessible
options.b: It preserves the flexibility and adaptability of customary law
options.c: It reconciles scattered sources of law on a single subject
options.d: It eliminates overlapping provisions and encourages reform

questions.explanation: Loss of flexibility is in fact a major objection to codifying customary law, because flexibility and adaptability are its strengths, so B is not an argument in favour. Options C, D and A are the main benefits claimed for codification.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Which jurist opposed codification because he believed in the unconscious, evolutionary growth of law rather than drastic change?

options.a: John Austin
options.b: Jeremy Bentham
options.c: Von Savigny
options.d: Hans Kelsen

questions.explanation: Von Savigny, of the historical school, saw law as growing gradually and unconsciously with the people and opposed codification, arguing a code cannot provide in advance for all future cases, so C is right. Bentham (B) was a famous champion of codification, while Austin (A) and Kelsen (D) are known for positivist theories of law, not for this objection.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Which is a reason given against codifying customary law in Nigeria?

options.a: Customary law is too rigid to change, so a code adds nothing
options.b: Customary law has been fully replaced by received English law
options.c: Ethnic diversity and the near irreconcilable differences among customary systems
options.d: Customary law already applies uniformly across the whole country

questions.explanation: Codifying customary law is said to be impracticable because of Nigeria's ethnic diversity, the near irreconcilable differences in customary practices, and the threat to flexibility, so C is right. Option D is false since each ethnic group has its own system, A reverses the point that flexibility is customary law's strength, and B is false.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: To answer the fear that codification fossilises the law, what safeguard is suggested?

options.a: A rule that judges may ignore the code where it seems outdated
options.b: A standing provision that the code be reviewed every ten or twenty years
options.c: A rule that the code can never be amended once enacted
options.d: A requirement that each code be re-enacted as a military Decree

questions.explanation: A standing provision for review of the code, say every ten or twenty years, lets reform keep pace with changing times and answers the fear of fossilisation, so B is right. Option C would cause the very fossilisation feared, A would destroy certainty, and D is unrelated.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of subsidiary (delegated) legislation?

options.a: The Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999
options.b: An Act passed by the Senate and House of Representatives
options.c: Bye-laws made by a local government under powers given by a statute
options.d: A Law passed by a State House of Assembly

questions.explanation: Subsidiary or delegated legislation is law made under powers conferred by a statute, such as local government bye-laws, regulations of public corporations and statutory instruments by ministers, so C is right. Options B and D are statutes made by the legislature itself, and A is the supreme law from which other laws derive validity.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: An Act empowers the Minister of Health to make regulations on drug labelling. The Minister makes regulations that also create a new tax on pharmacies, which the Act does not authorise. The tax provision is most likely:

options.a: Valid, because any regulation becomes an Act once published
options.b: Valid until the President formally assents to it
options.c: Ultra vires and void, for exceeding the delegated power
options.d: Valid, because ministerial regulations rank above statutes

questions.explanation: Delegated legislation must not exceed the limits of the power granted by the enabling statute, otherwise it is ultra vires, null and void, so C is right. Subsidiary legislation is inferior to statutes, so D is wrong, publication does not turn a regulation into an Act (A), and presidential assent applies to bills, not regulations (B).

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Which of the following is a reason why delegated legislation has become inevitable in modern governance?

options.a: The legislature cannot provide for every detail and lacks technical expertise in many areas
options.b: Delegated legislation ranks higher than Acts of the National Assembly
options.c: The Constitution forbids the legislature from making detailed rules
options.d: Courts refuse to apply statutes that contain technical details

questions.explanation: It is practically impossible for the legislature to legislate for every aspect of life, and many areas need technical expertise, so it lays down a general framework and leaves details to specialists, as A says. There is no constitutional ban on detail (C), delegated legislation is inferior to statutes (B), and D is invented.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: In a classification that divides legislation into municipal, primary, judicial, executive and subordinate legislation, a practice direction issued by the Chief Judge of a State to regulate proceedings in the State High Court is an example of:

options.a: Municipal legislation
options.b: Primary legislation
options.c: Judicial legislation
options.d: Executive legislation

questions.explanation: In this classification, judicial legislation refers to the rule-making role of the courts, and practice directions issued by the Chief Judge of a State or the Chief Justice of Nigeria are its example, so C is right. Executive legislation (D) refers to bills initiated by the executive, such as the EFCC Act, municipal legislation (A) to bye-law powers, and primary legislation (B) to foundational laws like the Constitution.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Which section of the 1999 Constitution provides interpretations of key words and expressions used in the Constitution?

options.a: Section 58
options.b: Section 318
options.c: Section 4
options.d: Section 55

questions.explanation: Section 318 is the interpretation section of the 1999 Constitution, and section 318(4) applies the Interpretation Act to the Constitution, so B is right. Section 4 (C) vests legislative powers, section 55 (D) deals with the language of National Assembly business, and section 58 (A) sets out how bills become law.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A Lagos State Law provides that 'In this Law, money means paper currency (notes) only'. A trader is charged under the Law for hoarding N50 coins. How does the definition affect the case?

options.a: The coins are 'money', because definitions cannot narrow the ordinary meaning of words
options.b: The coins are 'money', because the Interpretation Act overrides any definition in a Law
options.c: The coins are not 'money' under the Law, because the definition narrows the ordinary meaning
options.d: The court must ignore the definition, because definitions belong only in schedules

questions.explanation: Definition sections and interpretation clauses may delimit, extend or narrow the ordinary meaning of words, and here 'money' has been narrowed to paper currency, so coins fall outside it, as C says. Option A denies a power definitions clearly have, the Interpretation Act is a fallback where a statute gives no definition of its own (B), and definitions may sit in the section itself or at the start or end of a statute (D).

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: "The primary duty of the courts in interpreting statutes ... is to find the intention of the legislature." Which statement best reflects how courts approach this task?

options.a: Courts ask the legislators who passed the Act what they meant
options.b: Courts may replace a statute with their own policy where it is unclear
options.c: Courts apply whatever meaning best suits the party with the stronger case
options.d: Courts seek the lawmakers' intention as expressed in the statute, though they were not present when it was made

questions.explanation: Judges seek to discover the intention of the legislature as contained in the statute and give effect to it, even though they were not there when the law was made, so D is right. Option C abandons neutrality, A is not how courts work, and B would be usurping the legislative function.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: The rule that the intention of the law must be found on its face, so that courts apply the natural and ordinary meaning of the words whatever the consequences, is called:

options.a: The literal rule
options.b: The ejusdem generis rule
options.c: The golden rule
options.d: The mischief rule

questions.explanation: The literal or plain meaning rule requires courts to apply the natural, ordinary meaning of the words notwithstanding the implications, so A is right. The golden rule (C) allows departure from that meaning to avoid absurdity, the mischief rule (D) looks at the defect the statute was meant to cure, and ejusdem generis (B) concerns general words after a list.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: In the Sussex Peerage case, Tindal C.J. said that where the words of a statute are precise and unambiguous, nothing more is needed than to expound them in their natural and ordinary sense. This statement is a classic expression of:

options.a: The golden rule
options.b: The rule in Heydon's case
options.c: The literal rule
options.d: The mischief rule

questions.explanation: Tindal C.J.'s statement that clear words should be given their natural and ordinary sense, because the words themselves best declare the lawgiver's intention, is the classic statement of the literal rule, C. The golden rule (A) qualifies this to avoid absurdity, and the mischief rule (D) is the same thing as the rule in Heydon's case (B).

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a recognised criticism of the literal rule?

options.a: Applying the literal meaning may lead to inconvenient or absurd results
options.b: It is ill-suited to modern social legislation in a developing society
options.c: It allows judges too much freedom to rewrite statutes to suit their own views
options.d: Words have no ordinary meaning except in the context in which they are used

questions.explanation: The literal rule is criticised for being too rigid, not for giving judges too much freedom, so C is not a criticism of it; that charge is usually aimed at gap-filling approaches. Options D, A and B are the standard weaknesses: words take meaning from context, literalism can produce absurdity, and it fits poorly with changing social needs.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: In Council of the University of Ibadan v Adamolekun (1967), the Supreme Court declared a Western Nigeria Edict void for inconsistency with a Federal Military Government Decree, rejecting a literal reading of an ouster provision that would have left the void Edict standing. Which rule of interpretation does the case illustrate?

options.a: The expressio unius rule
options.b: The golden rule
options.c: The ejusdem generis rule
options.d: The literal rule

questions.explanation: The court refused a literal reading that would let a void, inconsistent law coexist with the superior law, because that would be absurd and legally anomalous, which is the golden rule at work, B. The literal rule (D) was the argument rejected, and C and A are maxims about lists and express mention that were not in issue.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A State Law provides that 'no person shall hawk goods in the vicinity of the State Secretariat'. A hawker is caught selling goods inside the Secretariat premises and argues that 'in the vicinity of' means only the area near or around the Secretariat, not the premises themselves. The court rejects this argument as absurd and holds that the Law covers the premises too. Which rule has the court applied?

options.a: The golden rule
options.b: The rule against retrospective laws
options.c: The literal rule
options.d: The expressio unius rule

questions.explanation: The court departs from a strict literal reading because it would produce an absurd result the lawmakers could not have intended, and modifies the meaning only as far as needed, which is the golden rule, A. The hawker was relying on the literal rule (C), expressio unius (D) concerns things expressly listed, and B concerns laws reaching back in time.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: The rule of interpretation that considers the statutory purpose and the history of a statute by looking at the state of the law before it was passed, to find the defect it was meant to cure, is the:

options.a: Noscitur a sociis rule
options.b: Golden rule
options.c: Mischief rule
options.d: Literal rule

questions.explanation: The mischief rule, also called interpretation by reference to the statutory purpose, looks at the law before the statute to see what shortcoming the new law came to cure, so C is right. The literal rule (D) applies plain meaning, the golden rule (B) avoids absurdity, and noscitur a sociis (A) reads a word with its neighbours.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Under the rule in Heydon's case, a court considers several matters when interpreting a statute. Which of the following is NOT one of them?

options.a: What the judge personally thinks the best policy on the subject would be
options.b: What remedy Parliament adopted and the true reason for it
options.c: What mischief or defect the earlier law did not provide for
options.d: What the law was before the Act was passed

questions.explanation: Heydon's case directs the court to ask what the law was before the Act, what mischief or defect it did not provide for, what remedy Parliament resolved on, and the true reason for that remedy, which covers D, C and B. The judge's own view of good policy (A) is not one of these questions; the inquiry is about Parliament's purpose.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Before 2025, traders in a State evaded a market levy by registering stalls in relatives' names. A 2025 State Law was passed to stop this evasion. A trader now uses a newly formed company to hold his stalls. The court asks what defect the old law had and holds that the Law covers the company scheme because it is the very evil the Law was passed to cure. Which approach has the court used?

options.a: The ejusdem generis rule
options.b: The literal rule
options.c: The presumption against ousting jurisdiction
options.d: The mischief rule

questions.explanation: Looking at the law before the statute, identifying the mischief it was meant to cure and interpreting the words to suppress that mischief is the mischief rule, so D is right. The literal rule (B) would look only at the words, ejusdem generis (A) concerns general words after a list, and C concerns statutes that try to shut out the courts.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: What is a main limitation of the mischief rule?

options.a: It requires a two-thirds vote of the legislature before use
options.b: It can be used only for constitutions, not ordinary statutes
options.c: It forbids the court from looking at anything except the bare words
options.d: It assumes statutes cure defects, yet many modern laws meet new social or technological needs

questions.explanation: The mischief rule assumes every statute is made to correct an existing defect, but many modern laws respond to social, economic, political or technological needs rather than curing a defect, and the rule gives no clear test for construing the words used, so D is right. Option C describes the literal rule's narrowness, and B and A are invented limits.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: What is the status of the literal, golden and mischief rules?

options.a: They are convenient rules of practice to assist courts, not principles of law
options.b: They are customary rules applicable only in customary courts
options.c: They are binding rules of law laid down in the Constitution
options.d: They are provisions of the Interpretation Act that courts must apply in order

questions.explanation: The canons are not principles of law but convenient rules of practice developed over time to help courts interpret statutes, and their helpfulness is open to doubt, so A is right. They are not laid down in the Constitution (C) or listed in a fixed order in the Interpretation Act (D), and they are not customary rules (B).

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: In Awolowo v Shagari, Fatayi-Williams CJN remarked that a common feature of most canons of interpretation is that they:

options.a: Are binding only on the Supreme Court and not on lower courts
options.b: Always lead to the same answer whichever canon is chosen
options.c: Are of little practical assistance in settling doubts in particular cases
options.d: Must be applied in a fixed order beginning with the mischief rule

questions.explanation: Fatayi-Williams CJN observed that many canons take the form of broad general principles and so are of little practical help in settling doubts about interpretation in particular cases, so C is right. Option B is contradicted by the opposing conclusions in Awolowo v Shagari itself, and D and A invent rules.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: "There is no golden rule nor is there a mischief rule or a literal rule or any other rule at all; instead, there are a thousand and one interpretative criteria." What does this statement suggest?

options.a: Interpretation draws on many criteria rather than a few fixed rules
options.b: The literal rule is the only true rule of statutory interpretation
options.c: Courts should never interpret statutes and must leave it to the legislature
options.d: The golden rule should always be preferred over the other canons

questions.explanation: The statement denies that there are a few fixed rules and says interpretation in fact uses a great many criteria, so A is right. It rejects the golden rule (D) and the literal rule (B) as rules just as much as the mischief rule, and it does not say courts should stop interpreting statutes (C).

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: The principle that 'an Act must be read as a whole' means that:

options.a: Every section of an Act must be interpreted literally and separately
options.b: Words take their meaning from the context in which they are used, not in isolation
options.c: Courts must read all Acts passed in the same year together
options.d: Only the long title of an Act may be used to interpret it

questions.explanation: Reading an Act as a whole means that words derive their meaning from their context and must be interpreted by reference to it, not in isolation, so B is right. Option D is too narrow, A is the opposite of reading in context, and C confuses context with date of enactment.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an intrinsic (internal) aid to the interpretation of a statute?

options.a: A recognised law dictionary such as Black's Law Dictionary
options.b: The preamble of the statute
options.c: The interpretation section of the statute
options.d: The long title of the statute

questions.explanation: Intrinsic aids are found inside the statute itself, such as the preamble, long title, definition and interpretation sections, schedules and appendixes, which covers B, D and C. A dictionary (A) is outside the statute, so it is an extrinsic aid.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: In interpreting the word 'premises' in a Federal Act, a judge looks first at the Act's long title and preamble, and then consults a leading textbook on property law. Which statement correctly classifies these aids?

options.a: All three are extrinsic aids because none is an operative section
options.b: The long title and preamble are extrinsic aids; the textbook is an intrinsic aid
options.c: The long title and preamble are intrinsic aids; the textbook is an extrinsic aid
options.d: All three are intrinsic aids because the judge relies on them

questions.explanation: Intrinsic aids come from within the statute, such as the long title and preamble, while extrinsic aids come from outside it, such as dictionaries, the Interpretation Act and leading works by recognised authors, so C is right. Option B reverses the classes, and D and A ignore the inside-versus-outside test.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Section 318(4) of the 1999 Constitution provides that:

options.a: English dictionaries shall be binding on courts interpreting the Constitution
options.b: The Constitution may be interpreted only by the National Assembly
options.c: Customary law shall apply to interpret words not defined in the Constitution
options.d: The Interpretation Act shall apply for the purposes of interpreting the Constitution

questions.explanation: Section 318(4) states that the Interpretation Act shall apply for the purposes of interpreting the provisions of the Constitution, which is D; this applies unless the context otherwise requires. Interpretation is a judicial task, not a legislative one (B), and C and A invent rules not in the section.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: What is one main purpose of an Interpretation Act?

options.a: To avoid needless and burdensome repetition of common definitions in every statute
options.b: To set out the stages a bill passes through before assent
options.c: To transfer the power to interpret statutes from courts to ministers
options.d: To list the cases in which the literal rule must be used

questions.explanation: An Interpretation Act gives general definitions of common words and phrases, so each statute need not repeat them; its main purpose is to avoid needless and burdensome repetition, so A is right. It does not rank the canons (D), does not take interpretation away from courts (C), and the stages of a bill are in the Constitution and House rules (B).

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a presumption courts use as an indicator of legislative intention?

options.a: A presumption against ousting the jurisdiction of the courts
options.b: In criminal law, a presumption against imposing liability without fault
options.c: A presumption in favour of statutes operating retrospectively
options.d: A presumption against interference with vested rights

questions.explanation: Courts presume against retrospective operation of statutes, not in favour of it, so C reverses the real presumption. Options D, A and B are recognised presumptions, along with the presumption that a new Act does not alter existing law unless it says so expressly.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A Federal Act provides that 'no court shall entertain any action' arising from the decisions of a new tax tribunal. The words can reasonably mean either that all court review is barred or only that fresh suits on the merits are barred, leaving judicial review open. How should the court construe the provision?

options.a: Strictly, adopting the meaning that preserves the jurisdiction of the courts
options.b: Liberally, adopting the meaning that ousts the courts most widely
options.c: By applying whichever meaning the tax tribunal prefers
options.d: By declining to interpret it until the National Assembly amends it

questions.explanation: There is a presumption against ousting the jurisdiction of the courts, and a statute that ousts it must be construed strictly, so if it reasonably bears two meanings, the one preserving the courts' jurisdiction is taken, as A says; Fatayi-Williams JSC stated this in Barclays Bank of Nigeria Ltd v CBN. Option B reverses the presumption, and D and C abandon the court's duty to interpret.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A 2026 Act creates a new offence of failing to register a business name, but says nothing about whether guilty knowledge is required and does not state that the offence is one of strict liability. A trader who honestly could not have known of the duty is charged. Which presumption is most relevant?

options.a: The presumption against imposing criminal liability without fault
options.b: The presumption that general words follow a list of specific words
options.c: The presumption that a new Act does not alter existing law
options.d: The presumption against ousting the jurisdiction of the courts

questions.explanation: In criminal law there is a presumption against imposing liability without fault, although an express provision can make an offence one of strict liability, so where the Act is silent this presumption is the relevant one, A. Option D concerns attempts to shut out courts, C concerns changes to earlier law, and B is the ejusdem generis maxim rather than a presumption about fault.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A Lagos State Law passed in March 2026 imposes a new levy on hotel bookings. Although the Law is silent on the point, the State revenue service tries to collect the levy on bookings made in 2024. Which presumption works against the revenue service?

options.a: The maxim lex non cogit ad impossibilia
options.b: The presumption against retrospective operation of statutes
options.c: The presumption against ousting the jurisdiction of the courts
options.d: The presumption against liability without fault in criminal law

questions.explanation: Courts presume that a statute does not operate retrospectively or interfere with vested rights unless it says so in clear terms, so a silent 2026 Law should not reach 2024 bookings, as B says. Option D concerns criminal fault, C concerns ouster clauses, and A concerns impossible commands.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
