questions.question: The ejusdem generis rule means that:

options.a: The express mention of one thing excludes all others not mentioned
options.b: A statute should be read so that it is valid rather than void
options.c: The law does not compel a person to do the impossible
options.d: General words following a list of specific words are limited to things of the same class

questions.explanation: Under ejusdem generis, where specific words of one class are followed by general words, the general words are restricted to things of the same class as the specific ones, so D is right. Option A is expressio unius est exclusio alterius, B is ut res magis valeat quam pereat, and C is lex non cogit ad impossibilia.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A State Law provides: 'It shall not be lawful for makers of bread, meat pie, cake, doughnut, sausage and other snacks to display such except in places provided.' Applying the ejusdem generis rule, which of the following is most likely covered by 'other snacks'?

options.a: Chin-chin, a fried pastry snack
options.b: Plates of jollof rice
options.c: Fresh fish
options.d: Bottled zobo drink

questions.explanation: The listed items are all confectionery or pastry, so under ejusdem generis 'other snacks' is limited to that class and covers a pastry snack such as chin-chin, A. Jollof rice (B) is a main food item and zobo (D) is a drink, both outside the class, and fresh fish (C) is not a pastry at all.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A State Education Law provides that 'the Principal and/or Vice-Principal of any school who is absent from office without due excuse' shall be liable to a penalty. A classroom teacher is absent without excuse. Which maxim shows that the teacher is not caught by this provision?

options.a: Expressio unius est exclusio alterius
options.b: Ut res magis valeat quam pereat
options.c: Lex non cogit ad impossibilia
options.d: Ejusdem generis

questions.explanation: Expressio unius est exclusio alterius means the express mention of one thing excludes others, so naming only the Principal and Vice-Principal excludes teachers and other staff, making A right. Ejusdem generis (D) needs general words after a list, which this provision lacks, while C and B concern impossibility and validity.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: The maxim that a word takes its meaning from the other words with which it is associated is:

options.a: Expressio unius est exclusio alterius
options.b: Lex non cogit ad impossibilia
options.c: Noscitur a sociis
options.d: Stare decisis

questions.explanation: Noscitur a sociis means a word is known by its companions, so it is read in the light of the words around it, which is C. Expressio unius (A) is about express mention excluding others, lex non cogit ad impossibilia (B) is about impossible commands, and stare decisis (D) is the doctrine of judicial precedent.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: A provision in an Act is capable of two mutually exclusive interpretations: one makes the provision valid and effective, the other makes it invalid and ineffective. Which maxim tells the court which to adopt?

options.a: Expressio unius est exclusio alterius, so the invalid interpretation is adopted
options.b: Noscitur a sociis, so the court chooses whichever reading is shorter
options.c: Lex non cogit ad impossibilia, so the provision is ignored
options.d: Ut res magis valeat quam pereat, so the valid interpretation is adopted

questions.explanation: Under ut res magis valeat quam pereat a statute is construed so that it may have effect rather than be destroyed, so the interpretation that keeps the provision valid is adopted, as D says. Lex non cogit ad impossibilia (C) is about impossible commands, and A and B misapply maxims that concern express mention and context.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: The maxim lex non cogit ad impossibilia means that:

options.a: A statute is construed to have effect rather than be destroyed
options.b: A statute is construed so as not to command what is humanly impossible
options.c: A statute must always be construed against the government
options.d: General words take their meaning from the specific words before them

questions.explanation: Lex non cogit ad impossibilia means the law does not compel the doing of impossibilities, so a statute is read in a way that does not require what is humanly impossible, which is B. Option A is ut res magis valeat quam pereat, D is ejusdem generis, and C is not a recognised maxim of interpretation.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: In Carter v Bradbeer, Lord Diplock cautioned that in questions of statutory construction, a ratio decidendi on the meaning of words in one statute:

options.a: Binds every court that later interprets the same words in any statute
options.b: Has no more than persuasive influence when the same words appear in another statute
options.c: Overrides the words of any later statute that uses different language
options.d: Has no value at all and must never be cited in another case

questions.explanation: Lord Diplock said the strict doctrine of precedent has only narrow application in statutory construction, and a ruling on words in one provision can have no more than persuasive influence on the same words in another provision, so B is right. Option A overstates precedent, D understates it, and C would put a judgment above a statute.

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: In Magor and St Mellons RDC v Newport Corporation, Lord Simonds criticised the idea that judges should fill gaps in statutes by describing it as:

options.a: A naked usurpation of the legislative function under the thin disguise of interpretation
options.b: The correct method of applying the ejusdem generis rule
options.c: A necessary use of the rule in Heydon's case
options.d: The proper application of the literal rule in modern conditions

questions.explanation: When the case reached the House of Lords, Lord Simonds rejected Lord Denning's view that judges should fill in gaps, calling it 'a naked usurpation of the legislative function under the thin disguise of interpretation', so A is right. Gap-filling is not the literal rule (D), and Lord Simonds was not endorsing it as an application of the mischief rule (C) or ejusdem generis (B).

questions.topic: Legislation: Process, Types and Statutory Interpretation
questions.question: Which approach to statutory interpretation is considered most appropriate overall?

options.a: Following previous interpretations of similar words in any other statute
options.b: Exclusive use of the mischief rule, ignoring the words of the statute
options.c: A combination of the canons and aids, read against the legislative purpose
options.d: Strict use of the literal rule in every case, whatever the result

questions.explanation: No single canon is reliable on its own, so a combination of the canons and aids should be used, giving effect to the ordinary and contextual meaning against the background of the legislative purpose, as C says. Option D can produce absurdity, B ignores the text, and A overstates precedent, which is only persuasive across different statutes.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: In the study of Nigerian legal method, the expression 'sources of Nigerian law' refers to:

options.a: The government agencies responsible for printing and distributing copies of statutes
options.b: The moral and religious beliefs that individual judges bring to the cases before them
options.c: The historical events that led to the amalgamation of Northern and Southern Nigeria in 1914
options.d: The materials through which a lawyer, court or judge finds reliable authorities for a particular legal question

questions.explanation: The expression refers to where a lawyer or judge goes to find reliable authority on a legal question, such as statutes, case law and customary law. Option C describes history, not where the law is located. Options A and B describe publishers and personal beliefs, neither of which is an authority a court relies on.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Which of the following is a PRIMARY source of Nigerian law?

options.a: Law digests summarising decided cases
options.b: Customary law, including Islamic law where applicable
options.c: Legal dictionaries such as Stroud's Judicial Dictionary
options.d: Legal textbooks written by Nigerian professors

questions.explanation: The primary category covers the authorities that can bind a Nigerian court: received English law, Nigerian legislation, judicial precedent and customary law (including Islamic law). Options A, C and D are all secondary works, which only help to find or explain the law and can at most persuade a court.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a primary source of Nigerian law?

options.a: Nigerian case law or judicial precedent
options.b: Nigerian legislation and subsidiary enactments
options.c: Articles in legal periodicals and journals
options.d: Received English law

questions.explanation: Legal periodicals and journals fall in the secondary category: they discuss the law but are not the law itself. Options A, B and D are all in the primary category of Nigerian law, which is capable of binding a court.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: What is the main difference in legal effect between primary and secondary sources of Nigerian law?

options.a: Secondary sources bind lower courts while primary sources bind only the Supreme Court
options.b: Only primary sources can bind a Nigerian court; secondary sources are merely persuasive
options.c: Primary sources are always written while secondary sources are always unwritten
options.d: Both bind the courts equally, but primary sources are older than secondary sources

questions.explanation: Primary authorities such as legislation and case law carry binding force, while secondary works such as law books and periodicals can only persuade, usually where no primary authority exists. Option C is wrong because customary law is primary yet largely unwritten. Options A and D wrongly give binding force to secondary works.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Gboga, a newly qualified lawyer, must address a Lagos court on a novel point. There is no statute or reported decision on it, only a textbook by a leading professor in the field. What is the correct position on citing the textbook?

options.a: He may cite it only if the professor is called to give evidence as an expert witness
options.b: He may cite it and the court is bound to follow it, since no primary authority exists
options.c: He may cite it as persuasive authority, and its weight will depend on the standing of the author and the significance of the subject
options.d: He may not cite it at all, because only primary sources may be mentioned in a Nigerian court

questions.explanation: Where judicial decisions are scanty or absent, reputable law books can be cited as persuasive authority, and their weight depends on who wrote them and the importance of the subject. Option B is wrong because a secondary authority never becomes binding just because nothing else exists. Option D is wrong because courts do accept such works for persuasion.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Received English law in Nigeria consists of:

options.a: The doctrines of equity and the decisions of English courts given after 1 October 1960
options.b: The common law of England and all Acts of the UK Parliament passed before Nigeria's independence in 1960
options.c: The common law of England, the doctrines of equity and the statutes of general application in force in England on 1 January 1900
options.d: The statutes of general application in force in England on 1 October 1954 and English customary law

questions.explanation: The reception provisions bring in three things: the common law, the doctrines of equity, and statutes of general application in force in England on 1 January 1900. Option B is wrong because not every pre-independence Act was received, only statutes of general application up to the 1900 date. Option D uses the wrong date, which is the date federalism began, not the reception date.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Statutes of general application are received into Nigeria if they were in force in England on which date?

options.a: 1 October 1954
options.b: 1 January 1914
options.c: 1 January 1900
options.d: 1 October 1960

questions.explanation: The cut-off date for statutes of general application is 1 January 1900, as stated in the Interpretation Act and the Supreme Court Ordinance 1914. Option B is the year of amalgamation and of the Supreme Court Ordinance itself, not the reception date. Options A and D are the dates federalism began and Nigeria became independent.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three components of received English law under the reception provisions?

options.a: English statutes of general application passed after 1 January 1900
options.b: Statutes of general application in force in England on 1 January 1900
options.c: The doctrines of equity
options.d: The common law of England

questions.explanation: Only statutes of general application that were already in force in England on 1 January 1900 are received; an English statute passed after that date is not part of received English law. Options B, C and D are exactly the three components named in the reception provisions.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: How does the application of the English common law and doctrines of equity in Nigeria differ from that of statutes of general application?

options.a: Common law and equity are applied as they stand in England when applied, while statutes of general application are tied to the 1 January 1900 date
options.b: Common law and equity apply only in Lagos, while statutes of general application apply in every State
options.c: Common law and equity must be re-enacted by the National Assembly each year, while statutes of general application need not
options.d: Common law and equity are frozen as at 1 January 1900, while statutes of general application apply as they stand today

questions.explanation: Nigerian courts apply common law and equitable principles as they stand in England on the day of application, so their application is not limited by time. Statutes of general application, by contrast, are received only if in force in England on 1 January 1900. Option D reverses the two rules.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: An English statute of general application was in force in England on 1 January 1900 and was later repealed in England in 1960. It has never been repealed in Nigeria. What is its status in Nigeria?

options.a: It became customary law and must pass the repugnancy test
options.b: It applies in Nigeria only if the UK Parliament re-enacts it
options.c: It remains in force in Nigeria despite its repeal in England
options.d: It ceased to apply in Nigeria automatically on its repeal in England

questions.explanation: Statutes of general application received into Nigeria remain in force here even if they have since been repealed in England, unless a Nigerian legislature removes them. Option D is the common mistake of assuming English repeal carries over to Nigeria. Options B and A have no basis since Nigeria is sovereign and the statute is not customary law.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Which of the following correctly states where the meaning of 'statute of general application' is found?

options.a: In section 1 of the 1999 Constitution
options.b: In case law, because the reception enactments do not define the phrase
options.c: In a schedule to the Interpretation Act listing all such statutes
options.d: In the definition section of the Supreme Court Ordinance 1914

questions.explanation: Neither the Supreme Court Ordinance, the Interpretation Act nor other reception enactments define 'statute of general application', so its meaning has been worked out by the courts. Options D and C are wrong because those enactments use the phrase without defining it or listing the statutes. Option A is about constitutional supremacy, not reception.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: In Attorney General v John Holt & Co Ltd, Osborne CJ proposed a 'rough but not infallible test' for a statute of general application. The test asks:

options.a: By what courts the statute is applied in England, and to what classes of the community in England it applies
options.b: Whether the statute is repugnant to natural justice, equity and good conscience, and whether it is contrary to public policy
options.c: Whether the statute was expressly extended to Nigeria by name, and whether it was published in the Nigeria Gazette
options.d: Whether the statute was passed before or after Nigeria's independence, and whether it is still in force in England

questions.explanation: Osborne CJ asked two preliminary questions: by what courts the statute is applied in England, and to what classes of the community it applies. A statute applied by all courts to all classes is likely to be of general application. Option B is a trap: those are the validity tests for customary law, not for English statutes.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Suppose an English Act in force on 1 January 1900 merely regulated procedure in certain English courts. Under the test in Attorney General v John Holt & Co Ltd, it would most likely be:

options.a: Held to be a statute of general application, because all English Acts in force in 1900 were received
options.b: Held to be a statute of general application, because procedural Acts apply to every litigant
options.c: Held not to be a statute of general application, because it was applied only by certain courts
options.d: Held to be customary law, because procedure is a matter of local custom

questions.explanation: Under Osborne CJ's test, a statute applied only by certain courts, such as one regulating procedure, is probably not locally applicable. Option A is wrong because only statutes of general application are received, not every Act. Option B misreads the test, which uses a procedural statute as the example of one that would not qualify.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: An English Act in force on 1 January 1900 was applied by all the civil courts of England to all classes of the community. Applying Osborne CJ's test, what is the likely conclusion?

options.a: It is unlikely to apply because it regulated the affairs of ordinary people
options.b: There is a strong likelihood that it is a statute of general application in force in Nigeria
options.c: It cannot be a statute of general application because it was applied by civil courts only
options.d: It is certain to be in force in Nigeria, because the test is conclusive

questions.explanation: Where a statute was applied by all civil or criminal courts, as the case may be, to all classes of the community, there is a strong likelihood it is in force. Option D overstates the test, which Osborne CJ himself called 'rough but not infallible'. Option C is wrong because the test speaks of all civil or criminal courts 'as the case may be'.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: In Dede v African Association Ltd, the court took which view of statutes of general application?

options.a: That they include only statutes passed after 1 January 1900
options.b: That they must be statutes applicable throughout the United Kingdom, not those in force in England only
options.c: That they cease to apply in Nigeria once repealed in England
options.d: That they must be statutes applied by all courts to all classes of the community in England

questions.explanation: In Dede, Webber J ruled that statutes of general application must mean those applicable throughout the United Kingdom, a view criticised because the Ordinance itself speaks of statutes 'in force in England'. Option D is the test later proposed by Osborne CJ in Attorney General v John Holt & Co Ltd, a different case.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: In Lawal v Younan, the Federal Supreme Court held which English statutes to be statutes of general application?

options.a: The Land Transfer Act 1897
options.b: The Fraudulent Conveyances Act 1571
options.c: The Statute of Frauds 1677
options.d: The Fatal Accidents Acts of 1846 and 1864

questions.explanation: Lawal v Younan held that the Fatal Accidents Acts 1846 and 1864, which applied to all classes of the community in England, were statutes of general application. Option A was the statute considered in Young v Abina, and option B the one in Braithwaite v Folarin.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: In Young v Abina, the West African Court of Appeal held that which statute was of general application because it applied quite generally to the estates of all persons dying in England after 1 January 1898?

options.a: The Land Transfer Act 1897
options.b: The Fraudulent Conveyances Act 1571
options.c: The Trustees Act 1888
options.d: The Fatal Accidents Act 1846

questions.explanation: Young v Abina concerned the Land Transfer Act 1897, which the court said could hardly be of more general application since it applied to the estates of all persons dying after 1 January 1898. Option D was the subject of Lawal v Younan, and option B of Braithwaite v Folarin.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: In Braithwaite v Folarin, which statute was held to be of general application because it applied generally to the ordinary affairs and dealings of men?

options.a: The Infant Relief Act 1874
options.b: The Fatal Accidents Act 1864
options.c: The Fraudulent Conveyances Act 1571
options.d: The Land Transfer Act 1897

questions.explanation: Braithwaite v Folarin held the Fraudulent Conveyances Act 1571 to be a statute of general application, since it applied to the ordinary affairs of men without any special restriction. Options D and B were the statutes in Young v Abina and Lawal v Younan respectively.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Statutes of general application have NOT been received into some Nigerian States for matters within State legislative competence. In which of the following States do they still apply to such matters?

options.a: Edo State
options.b: Ogun State
options.c: Ondo State
options.d: Lagos State

questions.explanation: Statutes of general application apply in all Nigerian jurisdictions except Edo, Delta, Ekiti, Osun, Ondo, Ogun and other States carved from the former Western and Mid-Western regions, for matters within their competence. Lagos is not among the excepted States. Options A, B and C are all named among the States where they have not been received.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Counsel in an Abuja High Court cites an English Court of Appeal decision given in 1995 on a point of contract law. What is the status of that decision before the Nigerian court?

options.a: It must be ignored completely, because foreign decisions cannot be cited
options.b: It is binding, because English common law is part of received English law
options.c: It is binding only if it was decided before 1 January 1900
options.d: It is only persuasive, because foreign decisions do not bind Nigerian courts

questions.explanation: As an independent and sovereign nation, Nigeria is not bound by foreign laws, including English decisions; they serve only as persuasive authority. Option B confuses the reception of common law principles with a duty to follow particular English courts. Option A goes too far, since persuasive foreign decisions are regularly cited.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Which local enactments brought the received English law into force in Nigeria?

options.a: The African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights
options.b: The Legitimacy Act and the Marriage Act
options.c: The Interpretation Act and the Supreme Court Ordinance 1914, among others
options.d: The Penal Code and the Criminal Code

questions.explanation: English law applies in Nigeria because Nigerian enactments, such as the Interpretation Act and section 14 of the Supreme Court Ordinance 1914, received it in general terms. Option A is an international treaty incorporated into Nigerian law and has nothing to do with reception. Options B and D are substantive statutes, not reception provisions.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Nigerian legislation, as a source of law, consists of:

options.a: Customary law and Islamic law
options.b: Textbooks and law reports
options.c: Statutes and judicial decisions
options.d: Statutes and subsidiary legislation

questions.explanation: Nigerian legislation is made up of statutes, which are enacted by the legislature, and subsidiary legislation, which is made under powers given by a statute. Option C adds judicial decisions, which are case law, a separate category. Option A is customary law, and option B lists secondary works that only record or explain the law.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: A law passed by the Nigerian central legislature before 1 October 1954, when federalism became a constitutional feature, is called:

options.a: A Decree
options.b: An Act
options.c: An Edict
options.d: An Ordinance

questions.explanation: Ordinances were laws passed by the central legislature before 1 October 1954, when the Lyttleton Constitution introduced federalism. Option B is a law of the elected National Assembly in a civilian regime. Options C and A are military-era enactments of a State military government and the Federal Military Government respectively.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: In Nigerian legislative terminology, a 'Decree' is:

options.a: An enactment made by the National Assembly in a civilian regime
options.b: An enactment made by the Federal Military Government during military rule
options.c: An enactment made by a Military Governor or Administrator of a State
options.d: An enactment made by a State House of Assembly in a civilian regime

questions.explanation: A Decree was the enactment of the Federal Military Government during military rule. Option C describes an Edict, the State-level military counterpart. Options D and A describe a Law and an Act, made by civilian legislatures.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: In 2015, the Lagos State House of Assembly passed an enactment regulating tenancy in the State. What is such an enactment called?

options.a: A Law
options.b: An Act
options.c: An Edict
options.d: An Ordinance

questions.explanation: An enactment made by an elected State legislature, the House of Assembly, in a civilian regime is called a Law. Option B is the name for an enactment of the National Assembly. Option C applies only to State enactments under military rule, and option D only to central laws made before 1 October 1954.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: In 1976, during military rule, the Military Governor of a Nigerian State made an enactment regulating markets in that State. What is the correct name for it?

options.a: A Decree
options.b: An Edict
options.c: A Law
options.d: A bye-law

questions.explanation: An enactment made by a State Military Governor or Administrator during military rule is an Edict. Option A is wrong because Decrees were made by the Federal Military Government, not by States. Option C is the civilian State equivalent, and option D is subsidiary legislation such as a local government rule.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: A statute was enacted in 1950 by the Nigerian central legislature. A student describing it correctly would call it:

options.a: An Ordinance
options.b: A Decree
options.c: An Act
options.d: A Law

questions.explanation: Laws passed by the central legislature before 1 October 1954 are called Ordinances, and 1950 falls before that date. Option C is the name for National Assembly enactments in a civilian regime, which did not exist in 1950. Options B and D are military federal enactments and civilian State enactments.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Which of the following pairings of enactment and law-maker is INCORRECT?

options.a: Ordinance - central legislature before 1 October 1954
options.b: Act - National Assembly
options.c: Law - State House of Assembly
options.d: Edict - Federal Military Government

questions.explanation: The Federal Military Government made Decrees; Edicts were made by State Military Governors or Administrators, so pairing an Edict with the Federal Military Government is wrong. Options A, B and C are all correct pairings.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Why is 1 October 1954 the dividing line between Ordinances and later forms of Nigerian legislation?

options.a: It was when Nigeria became independent
options.b: It was when federalism was introduced by the Lyttleton Constitution
options.c: It was when statutes of general application were received
options.d: It was when Nigeria became a republic

questions.explanation: The Lyttleton Constitution introduced federalism on 1 October 1954, and laws of the central legislature before that date are Ordinances. Options A and D are 1 October 1960 and 1 October 1963 respectively. Option C is wrong because the reception date for statutes of general application is 1 January 1900.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an example of subsidiary (delegated) legislation?

options.a: A bye-law made by a local government
options.b: Regulations made by a public corporation
options.c: A statutory instrument made by a minister
options.d: An Act passed by the National Assembly

questions.explanation: Subsidiary legislation is made by persons or bodies other than the legislature under powers conferred by a statute. An Act of the National Assembly is itself a statute made by the legislature. Options A, B and C are the standard examples of delegated legislation.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: A State Law empowers a local government to make bye-laws fixing fines of up to N5,000 for illegal dumping. The local government makes a bye-law fixing a fine of N50,000. What is the legal effect of the bye-law's fine?

options.a: It becomes customary law and must be tested for repugnancy
options.b: It is valid, because the local government is the law-maker for its area
options.c: It is valid until the State House of Assembly passes a resolution against it
options.d: It is ultra vires and liable to be declared null and void, because it exceeds the power delegated

questions.explanation: Delegated legislation must stay within the limits of the power granted by the enabling statute; exceeding those limits renders it ultra vires, meaning beyond power, and void. Option B ignores that the local government's power comes only from the State Law. Option A confuses written delegated legislation with customary law.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a reason given for the use of delegated legislation?

options.a: Specialists and those involved in specific activities can deal with particular cases
options.b: Many areas of public affairs require technical expertise the legislature may lack
options.c: To allow administrative bodies to override the provisions of the enabling statute
options.d: It is practically impossible for the legislature to make laws for every aspect of life

questions.explanation: Delegated legislation exists because the legislature cannot foresee every detail and lacks technical expertise, so it lays down the framework and leaves details to specialists. It never permits a body to override its enabling statute; doing so would be ultra vires. Options A, B and D are the genuine reasons.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: The Laws of the Federation of Nigeria revised and published in 2004 were printed in loose-leaf format mainly in order to:

options.a: Reduce the number of federal statutes in force
options.b: Replace the 1999 Constitution as the highest law
options.c: Make it easy to incorporate future amendments or revisions
options.d: Allow States to remove federal laws they disagree with

questions.explanation: The loose-leaf format allows new amendments and revisions to be slotted in without reprinting the whole collection. Option A is wrong because the format does not repeal anything. Options D and B are wrong because States cannot remove federal laws and the Constitution remains supreme.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Which source of law is described as the most important in a modern nation and the 'measuring scale' for the efficacy of other legal sources?

options.a: Customary law
options.b: Legislation
options.c: Received English law
options.d: Judicial precedent

questions.explanation: Legislation is the most important form of law in the modern world because it can validate, alter or abolish the content of the others. For example, customary law is applied only as statute directs, and received English law operates through local reception statutes. Options A, C and D are all subject to legislation.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: On what date did the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999 come into force?

options.a: 1 January 1999
options.b: 1 October 1999
options.d: 12 June 1999

questions.explanation: The 1999 Constitution came into force on 29 May 1999, the date civilian rule returned. Option B confuses it with Independence Day, 1 October. Options A and D are not the commencement date.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Which section of the 1999 Constitution proclaims its supremacy over all other laws, authorities and persons in Nigeria?

options.a: Section 12
options.b: Section 1
options.c: Section 4
options.d: Section 36

questions.explanation: Section 1 of the 1999 Constitution declares the Constitution supreme and makes any other law that is inconsistent with it void to the extent of the inconsistency. Option C deals with legislative powers, option A with the implementation of treaties, and option D with the right to fair hearing.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: A State House of Assembly passes a Law that conflicts with a provision of the 1999 Constitution. What is the effect of the conflict?

options.a: The Law is void to the extent of its inconsistency with the Constitution
options.b: The Law prevails within that State because States are autonomous
options.c: The Law prevails because it is more recent than the Constitution
options.d: Both remain equally valid and the court chooses the fairer one

questions.explanation: The Constitution is the highest law of the land, from which all other laws derive their validity, so any inconsistent law is void to the extent of the inconsistency. Option C wrongly applies the idea that a later law prevails; that does not hold against the Constitution. Option B ignores that the Constitution binds every State.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Customary law, as a source of Nigerian law, consists of:

options.a: The decisions of customary courts that bind all higher courts
options.b: English common law principles adapted to Nigerian conditions
options.c: Rules made by local governments under an enabling Law
options.d: The customs accepted by members of a community as binding among them

questions.explanation: Customary law is made up of customs that the members of a community accept as binding on them, and acceptance as an obligation is one of its main features. Option C describes subsidiary legislation. Option B describes received English law, which is a separate body of law.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Nigerian customary law is usually classified into:

options.a: Ethnic (non-Moslem) customary law and Moslem (Islamic) law
options.b: Criminal customary law and constitutional customary law
options.c: Written customary law and English customary law
options.d: Federal customary law and State customary law

questions.explanation: Customary law in Nigeria is commonly divided into ethnic or non-Moslem customary law and Moslem law, which is Islamic law. Option C is wrong because 'English customary law' is not a category of Nigerian customary law. Options B and D are invented divisions.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts ethnic customary law with Islamic law in Nigeria?

options.a: Ethnic customary law applies only in the North, while Islamic law applies only in the South
options.b: Both are fully written and identical across all ethnic groups
options.c: Ethnic customary law is written in the Quran, while Islamic law is unwritten
options.d: Ethnic customary law is unwritten and varies between ethnic groups, while Islamic law is largely in written form

questions.explanation: Ethnic customary law is indigenous, unwritten and diverse from one ethnic group to another, while Islamic law is largely written, drawing on the Quran and other recorded authorities. Option C reverses the two. Option B is wrong because the diversity of ethnic customary law is a major obstacle to uniformity.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the sources of Islamic law?

options.a: The consensus of Islamic scholars
options.b: Decisions of the English Court of Chancery
options.c: The practice of the Prophet (the Sunna)
options.d: The Holy Quran

questions.explanation: Islamic law is derived from the Holy Quran, the Sunna, the consensus of Islamic scholars, and analogical deductions from the holy writ. The English Court of Chancery developed equity, which is part of received English law, not Islamic law. Options A, C and D are genuine foundations of the Sharia.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: The predominant version (school) of Islamic law applied in Nigeria is that of the:

options.a: Hanbali school
options.b: Shafi'i school
options.c: Hanafi school
options.d: Maliki school

questions.explanation: The Maliki school is the predominant version of Islamic law in Nigeria. Options A, B and C are other recognised Sunni schools, but they are not the dominant one in Nigeria.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: In Lewis v Bankole, the court described which feature as one of the most striking features of West African native custom?

options.a: Its flexibility and adaptability to altered circumstances without entirely losing its character
options.b: Its being written down in codes kept by traditional rulers
options.c: Its rigidity and resistance to change over the centuries
options.d: Its identity with the rules of English common law

questions.explanation: Lewis v Bankole stressed that native custom is flexible and adapts to changing circumstances without losing its character. Option C is the opposite. Option B is wrong because ethnic customary law is largely unwritten, and option D because customary law is distinct from English law.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Before a Nigerian court enforces a rule of customary law, the rule must NOT be:

options.a: Unwritten; older than 1900; or different from English law
options.b: Repugnant to natural justice, equity and good conscience; contrary to public policy; or incompatible with any law for the time being in force
options.c: Contrary to Islamic law; unknown outside its community; or more than one hundred years old
options.d: Inconsistent with English law; not recorded in a law report; or applied by a customary court

questions.explanation: The three statutory validity tests are repugnancy to natural justice, equity and good conscience; being contrary to public policy; and incompatibility, directly or by implication, with any law in force. Options A and D wrongly treat difference from English law as a ground of invalidity, which Dawodu v Danmole rejected.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the statutory tests of validity of customary law in Nigeria?

options.a: The rule must not be contrary to public policy
options.b: The rule must not be repugnant to natural justice, equity and good conscience
options.c: The rule must not be incompatible directly or by implication with any law in force
options.d: The rule must be consistent with the principles of English law

questions.explanation: Consistency with English law is not a test; a customary rule does not become invalid merely because it differs from English legal principles. Options A, B and C are the three validity tests laid down by statute.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Where are the tests of validity of customary law prescribed?

options.a: In the rules of the Maliki school of Islamic law
options.b: In statutes, such as the High Court Laws of the States and of the Federal Capital Territory
options.c: In the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights
options.d: Only in the unwritten traditions of each community

questions.explanation: The validity tests are laid down by statute: the High Court Laws of all the States and the FCT direct courts to enforce customary law only if it passes them. Option D is wrong because communities cannot set the limits on their own custom. Options C and A are not where the tests come from.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: In Esugbayi Eleko v Officer Administering the Government of Nigeria, Lord Atkin explained the repugnancy test by saying that:

options.a: A barbarous custom must be rejected as repugnant to natural justice, equity and good conscience
options.b: Any custom differing from English law must be rejected
options.c: A custom becomes valid once accepted by a majority of the community
options.d: Customary law must give way to statutes of general application

questions.explanation: Lord Atkin held in Eleko that a barbarous custom must be rejected on the ground of repugnancy. Option B is wrong because difference from English law alone does not make a custom invalid. Option C ignores that even widely accepted custom must pass the validity tests.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: In Dawodu v Danmole, the Privy Council held that the Yoruba idi-igi custom of distributing a deceased person's estate:

options.a: Was repugnant because it denied equality among the children
options.b: Was incompatible with the Marriage Ordinance
options.c: Was contrary to public policy and therefore void
options.d: Was not repugnant to natural justice, equity and good conscience

questions.explanation: The Privy Council rejected Jibowu J's view that idi-igi was repugnant, noting that natural justice in a society that accepts polygamy should not be equated with that of a monogamous society. Option A is the trial judge's view, which was overturned. Options C and B were not the grounds considered.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Under Yoruba customary law of succession, the idi-igi method distributes the estate of a deceased man:

options.a: Per stirpes, according to the branches of the family (each wife's children as a unit)
options.b: Per capita, equally among all the children as individuals
options.c: Entirely to the eldest son as heir
options.d: Entirely to the surviving wives

questions.explanation: Idi-igi is distribution per stirpes, by branches of the family, while ori-ojori is distribution per capita, by the number of children. Option B describes ori-ojori, which the trial judge in Dawodu v Danmole preferred as more equal. Options C and D are not idi-igi.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Justice Dede of a Kogi State High Court invalidates every customary rule he finds inconsistent with English legal principles. Is his approach correct?

options.a: No; customary law can never be declared invalid by a High Court
options.b: Yes; the repugnancy test means the same thing as inconsistency with English law
options.c: No; inconsistency with English law is not a ground of invalidity, and the custom must be judged only by the statutory validity tests
options.d: Yes; customary law is valid only where it agrees with English common law

questions.explanation: A customary rule is not invalid merely because it differs from English law; Dawodu v Danmole made this clear. The judge should apply only the three statutory tests. Option B wrongly equates repugnancy with difference from English law. Option A goes too far, since High Courts do strike down customs that fail the tests.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: In Re Effiong Okon Atta, the court held which customary rule to be repugnant?

options.a: A rule distributing an estate per stirpes among the wives' children
options.b: A rule legitimising a child born outside a statutory marriage
options.c: A rule entitling the former owner of a slave to administer the slave's personal estate after the slave's death
options.d: A rule denying a person accused of highway robbery the right to defend himself

questions.explanation: Re Effiong Okon Atta struck down, as repugnant, a custom allowing a former slave owner to administer the deceased slave's estate. Option D is Guri v Hadejia Native Authority. Option B is Cole v Akinyele, decided on public policy. Option A is the idi-igi rule upheld in Dawodu v Danmole.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Afar, a native of Agbor, is tried for robbery in the Delta State High Court. The judge convicts him without letting him present a defence, saying that under Agbor custom a robbery suspect is not entitled to be heard. How should the customary rule be assessed?

options.a: It is invalid only because it differs from English criminal procedure
options.b: It is valid, because customary law is a primary source of Nigerian law
options.c: It is valid, because courts must apply the custom of the accused's community
options.d: It is invalid as repugnant to natural justice, equity and good conscience, as in Guri v Hadejia Native Authority

questions.explanation: A custom denying an accused person the right to defend himself fails the repugnancy test; Guri v Hadejia Native Authority rejected such a rule in a case of highway robbery (hiraba). Options B and C ignore that customary law applies only if it passes the validity tests. Option A gives the wrong reason, since difference from English law is not itself a ground of invalidity.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: In Cole v Akinyele, the Federal Supreme Court invalidated a customary rule on legitimacy on which ground?

options.a: Incompatibility with the Constitution
options.b: Inconsistency with English common law
options.c: Public policy
options.d: Repugnancy to natural justice, equity and good conscience

questions.explanation: In Cole v Akinyele, Brett FJ held invalid on grounds of public policy a custom that made an acknowledged child born out of wedlock legitimate, sharing equally with children of a marriage under the Marriage Ordinance. Option D is the ground in cases such as Guri and Effiong Okon Atta. Option B is not a ground of invalidity at all.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Chief Ade is married under the Marriage Act. He acknowledges paternity of a child born outside that marriage and claims that, under his custom, the child is legitimate and shares equally with the children of the statutory marriage. Following Cole v Akinyele, which validity test is the custom most likely to fail?

options.a: Repugnancy to natural justice
options.b: Public policy
options.c: Incompatibility with the 1999 Constitution
options.d: Consistency with English law

questions.explanation: These facts match Cole v Akinyele, where a custom legitimising an acknowledged child born out of wedlock so that the child shared equally with children of a marriage under the Marriage Ordinance was struck down as contrary to public policy. Option A is the test in Guri and Eleko. Option D is not a validity test.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: A State Law expressly prohibits a practice that a particular customary rule permits. A litigant relies on the customary rule in a State High Court. Which validity test does the rule fail?

options.a: Repugnancy to natural justice, equity and good conscience
options.b: Incompatibility, directly or by implication, with a law for the time being in force
options.c: Inconsistency with English common law
options.d: Public policy, because all customs are against public policy

questions.explanation: A customary rule that conflicts with an existing statute fails the incompatibility test, because customary law yields to written law in force. Option A concerns customs that are inherently barbarous or unjust, which is a different test. Option C is not a test, and option D is false because most customs are valid.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Which statement best describes the meaning of the repugnancy clause as developed by Nigerian courts?

options.a: It applies only to Islamic law and not to ethnic customary law
options.b: It has not received a detailed and settled explanation, and its meaning is gathered from decided cases
options.c: It has been precisely defined in section 1 of the 1999 Constitution
options.d: It means any rule that differs from English law

questions.explanation: Nigerian courts have not given the repugnancy clause a detailed and settled meaning; its content is drawn from cases such as Eleko, Dawodu v Danmole and Guri. Option D is wrong because difference from English law is not repugnancy. Option C is wrong because the clause comes from the High Court Laws, not section 1 of the Constitution.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Why can a person no longer be convicted in Nigeria for an offence known only to unwritten customary law?

options.a: Because customary criminal law fails the incompatibility test only in the North
options.b: Because customary law was abolished entirely as a source of Nigerian law
options.c: Customary criminal law has been displaced, and offences must now be defined in written law such as the Criminal Code and Penal Code
options.d: Because customary law applies only in Lagos State

questions.explanation: Customary law today operates in civil matters; customary criminal law has been displaced by written codes such as the Criminal Code and Penal Code. Option B is wrong because customary law remains a primary authority in civil matters such as succession and marriage. Options D and A are invented limits.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: The doctrine of judicial precedent means:

options.a: The practice whereby the earlier decision of a court is followed in later similar cases, with lower courts bound to follow higher courts
options.b: The rule that customary courts must follow the decisions of English courts
options.c: The rule that the most recent statute always prevails over an earlier one
options.d: The practice whereby each judge decides every case afresh without regard to earlier decisions

questions.explanation: Judicial precedent is the practice of following earlier decisions in later similar cases; where the later court is lower than the earlier one, it must follow the earlier decision. Option D is the opposite of precedent. Option C is a rule about statutes, not case law.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: The Latin maxim stare decisis, which expresses the rule that lower courts must follow earlier decisions of higher courts, means:

options.a: Let the decision stand
options.b: Beyond the powers
options.c: The thing speaks for itself
options.d: Something said in passing

questions.explanation: Stare decisis means 'let the decision stand', the principle behind binding precedent. Option C is res ipsa loquitur, option B is ultra vires, and option D is obiter dictum.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: A judge of the Kaduna State High Court is faced with facts materially similar to those of a Supreme Court decision. Under the doctrine of judicial precedent, the High Court judge:

options.a: May ignore it if he considers it unfair
options.b: May follow either it or a contrary decision of another High Court
options.c: Must follow the ratio decidendi of the Supreme Court decision
options.d: Must follow it only if it was reported in the NWLR

questions.explanation: Decisions of higher courts bind lower courts, so the High Court must follow the Supreme Court's ratio decidendi on facts that are similar in all important respects. Option A would defeat stare decisis. Option B is wrong because a coordinate High Court decision cannot displace a binding Supreme Court decision.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes ratio decidendi from obiter dictum?

options.a: Both bind later courts equally, but only the ratio is reported
options.b: The ratio decidendi is the legal principle necessary for the decision and binds later courts, while an obiter dictum is a remark made in passing that does not bind
options.c: The ratio decidendi is a remark made in passing, while an obiter dictum is the binding principle
options.d: The ratio decidendi is the judge's summary of the facts, while an obiter dictum is the final order

questions.explanation: The ratio decidendi, the 'reason for the decision', is the rule of law on which the decision rests and is what binds future cases. An obiter dictum, 'something said in passing', is not binding, though it may persuade and can later be adopted as a ratio. Option C reverses the two terms.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of judicial precedent as a source of Nigerian law?

options.a: It enables lawyers and litigants to predict the outcome of disputes
options.b: It provides ready solutions to legal problems
options.c: It promotes uniformity, consistency and certainty in the law
options.d: It allows each judge to depart freely from higher court decisions he dislikes

questions.explanation: Precedent is valued because it gives ready solutions and makes the law uniform, certain and predictable. Allowing judges to depart freely from higher decisions would destroy those benefits. Options A, B and C are the advantages of judicial precedent.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: A Nigerian court extends an existing rule by analogy to cover a new situation that the earlier case did not deal with. This type of precedent is called:

options.a: Per incuriam precedent
options.b: Declaratory precedent
options.c: Derivative precedent
options.d: Original precedent

questions.explanation: A derivative precedent extends an existing rule analogically to a new situation. Option D is a wholly new decision with no similar earlier case. Option B simply restates an existing rule. Option A is not a type of precedent; per incuriam describes a decision reached in ignorance of a binding authority.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: A declaratory precedent is one that:

options.a: Simply declares or restates an existing rule, giving it added weight and authority
options.b: Extends an existing rule by analogy to a new situation
options.c: Creates a completely new rule where no earlier similar case exists
options.d: Is reached through ignorance of a binding statute

questions.explanation: A declaratory precedent re-echoes an existing rule, which strengthens it and helps weed out conflicting decisions. Option C describes an original precedent, and option B a derivative precedent. Option D describes a decision given per incuriam.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Without which two things would the principle of stare decisis be impracticable?

options.a: A hierarchy of courts and an efficient system of law reporting
options.b: A codified customary law and an Islamic court
options.c: A written constitution and a military government
options.d: A Law Commission and a loose-leaf statute book

questions.explanation: Stare decisis depends on knowing which courts are higher and binding, and on reliable reports of their decisions. Options B, C and D are not preconditions for binding precedent.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: The branch of law known historically as jus gentium, which recognises that no nation can exist in isolation, is:

options.a: Customary law
options.b: Constitutional law
options.c: Islamic law
options.d: International law (the law of nations)

questions.explanation: Jus gentium means the law of nations, the basis of international law, which governs relations among States through treaties, conventions and similar instruments. Options A, B and C are domestic categories of law.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Under the Nigerian constitutional system, when does a treaty that Nigeria has signed become operative as law in Nigeria?

options.a: When the National Assembly has enacted it into law
options.b: When any State High Court applies it in a case
options.c: As soon as the President signs it
options.d: As soon as it is published in a foreign gazette

questions.explanation: Section 12(1) of the 1999 Constitution provides that a treaty has no force of law in Nigeria until the National Assembly enacts it into law. Option C is a common mistake: signature or ratification by the executive alone is not enough. Option B is wrong because courts cannot domesticate a treaty.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: In Sani Abacha v Gani Fawehinmi, the Supreme Court held that the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights:

options.a: Applies only in the States that signed it individually
options.b: Is superior to the 1999 Constitution
options.c: Having been incorporated into Nigerian law, is enforceable in Nigerian courts
options.d: Is not enforceable in Nigeria because it is a foreign document

questions.explanation: Because the African Charter was enacted into Nigerian law, the Supreme Court in Abacha v Fawehinmi held it enforceable in Nigerian courts. Option D ignores its domestication. Option B is wrong because the Constitution remains supreme over every other law.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Nigeria ratified an international trade convention in 2020, but the National Assembly has not enacted it into law. A Kano trader sues, relying solely on a right granted by the convention. What is the likely outcome?

options.a: The convention is enforceable because ratification by the executive is enough
options.b: The convention is enforceable because international law binds all courts automatically
options.c: The convention is enforceable only in the Kano State High Court
options.d: The convention cannot be enforced as law in Nigeria until the National Assembly enacts it

questions.explanation: Under section 12(1) of the 1999 Constitution, a treaty becomes operative in Nigeria only after the National Assembly enacts it into law. Option A is the common mistake of treating ratification as domestication. Option B is wrong because Nigeria requires an enactment before a treaty has the force of law.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: A law digest, such as the Digest of Supreme Court Cases, is best described as:

options.a: A journal of academic articles on law reform
options.b: An abridgement of cases giving summaries of the facts, issues, arguments and decisions
options.c: A dictionary of foreign legal terms
options.d: A collection of statutes arranged in loose-leaf form

questions.explanation: Digests abridge cases, giving useful summaries of the facts, issues, arguments and decisions in judicial proceedings. Option D describes a statute compilation such as the Laws of the Federation. Options C and A describe legal dictionaries and periodicals.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Why are law reports described as essential in a country such as Nigeria that operates judicial precedent?

options.a: Law reports replace the need for legislation
options.b: Only by reference to reported cases can courts and lawyers ascertain the position of the law
options.c: Law reports record only customary law
options.d: Law reports are themselves binding statutes

questions.explanation: Where precedent operates, the law is partly contained in decided cases, and lawyers and judges can only know those decisions through reports. Option D is wrong because a law report is a secondary work that records decisions, not a statute. Options A and C misstate its role.

questions.topic: Sources of Nigerian Law
questions.question: Under the division of legislative powers in the 1999 Constitution, which statement is correct?

options.a: All matters may be legislated on by both levels equally, so there is no division
options.b: Matters on the Exclusive List are for the States only, and residual matters are for the federal legislature only
options.c: Matters on the Exclusive List are for the federal legislature only, matters on the Concurrent List may be legislated on by both levels, and residual matters are left to the States
options.d: The Concurrent List is for local governments, and the Exclusive List for the States

questions.explanation: The Exclusive Legislative List is reserved to the National Assembly, the Concurrent List is shared by the National Assembly and State Houses of Assembly, and residual matters, which appear on neither list, fall to the States. Option B reverses the federal and State roles. Option A ignores the constitutional division altogether.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: In the context of legal method, 'research' means:

options.a: Interviewing witnesses in order to prove facts in court
options.b: The use of library resources to seek recorded information on a legal problem in order to authoritatively determine the rights, duties and liabilities of the parties
options.c: Drafting a bill for presentation to the National Assembly
options.d: Memorising lecture notes so as to pass law examinations

questions.explanation: Legal research is the use of library resources to find recorded information that settles the rights, duties and liabilities of the parties to a legal problem. Option D is mere examination preparation, which is not the same as finding the law. Option A is fact-gathering for evidence, and option C is legislative drafting.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a reason why a lawyer needs to carry out legal research?

options.a: Research findings may help persuade a court to adopt the lawyer's reasoning
options.b: The law is static, so research is needed only once at the start of a career
options.c: Diligent research may persuade a court to adopt a new position or even reverse its earlier decision
options.d: The law is dynamic and developing, so current rules must be determined

questions.explanation: Research is needed precisely because law is dynamic, not static, so a lawyer must keep checking the current rules. Options A, C and D are all genuine reasons: law keeps developing, research supports persuasion, and good research can even lead a court to change its position.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: The saying that 'lawyers do not know much more law than other people, but they know better where to find it' emphasises the importance of:

options.a: Having a large private collection of novels
options.b: Courtroom advocacy skills
options.c: Memorising every statute word for word
options.d: Legal research and the effective use of the library

questions.explanation: The saying stresses that a lawyer's real advantage is knowing where and how to find the law, which is the skill of legal research. Option C is wrong because the point is precisely that lawyers need not carry all the law in memory. Option B is a different skill.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: What is the great disadvantage of a law student confining himself to lecture notes and law textbooks?

options.a: Textbooks are always more up to date than law reports
options.b: He takes all his law at second hand, because the law itself is contained in statutes and judicial decisions
options.c: He will be unable to read the Constitution
options.d: He will learn too many cases to remember

questions.explanation: The law is contained in statutes and judicial decisions; what a text writer thinks is not itself law and may misread the authorities. Relying only on secondary works means taking the law at second hand. Option A is wrong because books often lag behind the latest reports.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: Why is a competent law librarian described as an important research aid?

options.a: Once the subject area is identified, he can assemble the relevant primary and secondary authorities for the researcher
options.b: He writes the legal opinion for the lawyer
options.c: He decides which party should win a case
options.d: He removes the need for the researcher to know how to use the library

questions.explanation: A good law librarian specialises in knowing what is relevant to a subject and can assemble both primary and secondary authorities, and it helps if he is legally trained. Option D is wrong because such librarians are rare, so the researcher must still know how to use the library himself.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: Most books are identified by six elements. Which of the following is NOT one of them?

options.a: The place and date of publication
options.b: The name of the library that owns the book
options.c: The author's name
options.d: The publisher

questions.explanation: The six identifying elements are the cover, the author's name, the publisher, the title, the place of publication and the date of publication. The owning library is not one of them. Options A, C and D are among the six, and apart from the cover they all appear on the title page.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: Tobi pulls a book from a library shelf and sees the call mark K108.7. Another library's books have call marks such as 642.13. Which classification systems do these indicate?

options.a: K108.7 indicates the Dewey Decimal system; 642.13 indicates the Library of Congress system
options.b: Both indicate the Dewey Decimal system
options.c: Both indicate the Library of Congress system
options.d: K108.7 indicates the Library of Congress system; 642.13 indicates the Dewey Decimal system

questions.explanation: A call mark beginning with a letter shows the Library of Congress classification, while one beginning with numbers shows the Dewey Decimal system. Option A reverses the two, which is the usual slip. Options C and B ignore the difference between letters and numbers.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: Four books in a Library of Congress library have the call numbers B358.C54, B200.C57, K146.O2 and B200.A18. Which of them will be shelved FIRST?
questions.explanation: Books are shelved alphabetically by the subject letter, then numerically by the subject number, then by the author letter and number. B comes before K, 200 comes before 358, and author letter A comes before C, so B200.A18 is first. Option D has the same subject number but a later author letter.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: Why is the library catalogue a better approach than browsing the shelves, even in a library with open stacks?

options.a: Browsing may miss books that are borrowed, reserved or on the reserve shelf, while the catalogue lists all the library's books
options.b: The catalogue contains the full text of every book
options.c: The catalogue arranges books by the colour of their covers
options.d: Browsing is forbidden in all Nigerian law libraries

questions.explanation: The catalogue tells the researcher about every book the library holds, including those a browser would miss because they are borrowed or reserved. It is especially important in libraries with closed stacks. Option B overstates what a catalogue contains; it gives entries, not the full text.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: Jumar, a visiting law student with little time before the library closes, must find a contract book by a named new author but is unsure of its exact title. What is her best approach?

options.a: Search the Words and Phrases section of a law report index
options.b: Browse the shelves one by one until she finds it
options.c: Check the author's entry in the catalogue, note the call number and go to the shelf
options.d: Check the periodical index

questions.explanation: With limited time, browsing is ill advised; she should use the catalogue, and the author's entry is the main entry and the best route when the author is known. Option B wastes time. Option D is for journal articles, and option A is for judicially defined words.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: A lawyer is applying for bail for an accused person in the Ogun State High Court. Under which law will the application be brought?

options.a: The law of whichever State the lawyer practises in most often
options.b: The Laws of Lagos State, because Lagos is the former federal capital
options.c: English law only, as received in 1900
options.d: The relevant law of Ogun State, since each State has its own system of law and courts

questions.explanation: Each Nigerian State has its own system of law and courts, so an application in a State High Court is brought under that State's law. Options B and A pick the wrong State's law. Option C ignores that local State law governs procedure in that State's courts.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT usually contained in a modern law report?

options.a: A headnote and an outline of the facts
options.b: The reporter's own verdict on which party should have won
options.c: The name of the case, its date, the court and the judges
options.d: A verbatim copy of the judgment

questions.explanation: A modern law report gives the case name, date, court and judges, a headnote, an outline of the facts, counsel's names, sometimes a summary of arguments, and always a verbatim copy of the judgment. The reporter does not substitute his own verdict. Options A, C and D are standard contents.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: A reported case is usually cited by stating:

options.a: The names of the judges, the counsel and the court registry number
options.b: The headnote, the ratio decidendi and the final order
options.c: The names of the parties, the year, the volume, the name of the law report and the page
options.d: The date of filing, the suit number and the trial judge only

questions.explanation: A case citation gives the parties' names, the year (or month), the volume, the name of the law report and the page where the case begins. Options A and D describe court records rather than a law report citation. Option B describes parts of a judgment, not a citation.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: What is the significance of square brackets, as against round brackets, around the year in a case citation?

options.a: Square brackets show that the year is essential for locating the case; round brackets show that it is not
options.b: Square brackets show that the case was decided by the Supreme Court; round brackets show a High Court case
options.c: Square brackets show that the year is not essential; round brackets show that it is
options.d: Square brackets show a foreign case; round brackets show a Nigerian case

questions.explanation: When the year is in square brackets, it is an essential part of finding the case, because the reports are arranged by year. When it is in round brackets, the volume number is what locates the case and the year is not essential. Option C reverses the rule, which is the common slip.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: In the citation Marina Nominees Ltd v FBIR [1986] 2 NWLR (Pt 20) 40, what does 'Pt 20' refer to?

options.a: Page 20 of the judgment
options.b: Paragraph 20 of the headnote
options.c: Part 20 of the Nigerian Weekly Law Reports, a part number that is never duplicated
options.d: The 20th case decided by the Supreme Court in 1986

questions.explanation: The Nigerian Weekly Law Reports identifies each issue by a part number, and no part number is ever repeated, so the part and the page are the most useful details for tracing the case. Here 2 is the volume, Pt 20 is part 20 and 40 is the page. Option A confuses the part with the page.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: Jumar's supervisor gives her the citation Adeolu v Mabamiye (1985) 2 NWLR p.5, which omits the part number. What is a sensible way to find the full citation?

options.a: Look for it in the periodical index
options.b: Look in the Dewey Decimal section of the library
options.c: Check the list of cases in a standard book on the subject, or an index, to obtain the full citation including the part
options.d: Give up, because a case cannot be traced without the part number

questions.explanation: Because the NWLR is traced mainly by part and page, a missing part is a problem, but it can be solved by checking the list of cases in a standard book on the subject or an index, or by going through the volumes. Option D is too pessimistic. Option A is for journal articles, not law reports.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: A researcher wants to see all the reported cases on locus standi, and also how the courts have judicially defined the phrase 'reasonable cause'. Where should she look?

options.a: In the periodical index under both headings
options.b: In a case index: under L for locus standi, and in the 'Words and phrases' section for 'reasonable cause'
options.c: In the catalogue's author entries
options.d: In a general dictionary of the English language

questions.explanation: A case index, arranged alphabetically by subject, is the best tool for finding all the authorities on an issue, so locus standi appears under L. Judicially defined expressions are listed under 'Words and phrases'. Option A finds journal articles, not cases. Option D gives ordinary meanings, not judicial definitions.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: How do the Nigerian Weekly Law Reports (NWLR) and the Supreme Court of Nigeria Judgments (SCNJ) differ in coverage?

options.a: The SCNJ is published weekly, while the NWLR appears once a year
options.b: The NWLR reports only High Court cases, while the SCNJ reports Court of Appeal cases
options.c: The NWLR reports decisions of both the Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court, while the SCNJ reports only Supreme Court cases
options.d: Both report only customary court decisions

questions.explanation: The NWLR comes out weekly and reports cases of the Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court, while the SCNJ reports only Supreme Court cases and usually appears every month or two. Option A reverses their frequency. Options B and D misstate which courts they cover.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: Which of the following is a Nigerian law report?

options.a: Weekly Law Reports (WLR)
options.b: Nigerian Weekly Law Reports (NWLR)
options.c: Appeal Cases (AC)
options.d: All England Law Reports (All ER)

questions.explanation: The Nigerian Weekly Law Reports, published since 1985, is one of the main Nigerian law reports. Options A, C and D are United Kingdom reports, although Nigerian lawyers may cite them as persuasive authority.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: Which of the following is a way in which periodicals (journals) differ from books?

options.a: Periodicals appear at intervals and contain briefer articles by different writers
options.b: Periodicals are always written by a single author
options.c: Periodicals contain longer treatments than books
options.d: Periodicals always discuss one subject completely in a single edition

questions.explanation: Periodicals appear at intervals (weekly, monthly, quarterly and so on), their articles are briefer so the essentials are reached quicker, and they contain contributions by different writers. Option D describes a book, whose author treats the subject in one complete edition. Options B and C are the opposite of the true position.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: Amaka is researching recent developments in Nigerian banking law. She has no particular article in mind and no citation. What is the best tool for finding relevant journal articles?

options.a: The library's card catalogue of books
options.b: A periodical index
options.c: A case index under 'Words and phrases'
options.d: Browsing the journal section one journal at a time

questions.explanation: A periodical index does for journal articles what the catalogue does for books: it lists published articles by subject and author so the citation can be noted. Option D is slow and may prove futile. Options A and C are for books and cases respectively.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: Reference books in a library are distinguished from regular books in that they:

options.a: Can be borrowed for longer periods than other books
options.b: Contain only primary legislation
options.c: Do not circulate and are marked with 'R' or 'REF' above the call number
options.d: Have no call number at all

questions.explanation: Reference books, such as dictionaries and encyclopedias, give quick, brief information, do not circulate, and can only be used in the reference section. They are marked with R or REF above the call number. Option A is the opposite of the rule, and option D is wrong because they do carry call numbers.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: A student needs only the meaning of the legal term 'locus standi' and the date of a historical event for his assignment. What is the most efficient resource?

options.a: The Dewey Decimal classification table
options.b: The periodical index
