options.c: A full treatise read from cover to cover
options.d: A reference book, such as a law dictionary, used in the reference section

questions.explanation: Reference books exist for brief, concise information such as the meaning of a word or the date of an event, and can be consulted without reading a whole book. A subject reference book such as Black's Law Dictionary suits a legal term. Option C is inefficient. Option B locates articles, not definitions.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: Which work is described as the most comprehensive legal encyclopedia, covering all areas of English law and serving as the take-off point for legal research?

options.a: Stroud's Judicial Dictionary
options.b: Black's Law Dictionary
options.c: Halsbury's Laws of England
options.d: The Digest of Supreme Court Cases

questions.explanation: Halsbury's Laws of England is the most comprehensive legal encyclopedia, covering all areas of English law, and is a natural starting point for research. Legal encyclopedias are also more current than ordinary law books. Options B and A are law dictionaries, and option D is a digest of cases.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: Lexis and Westlaw are examples of:

options.a: Legal databases making recent judicial decisions and legislation available electronically
options.b: Library classification systems
options.c: Types of argumentative essay
options.d: Nigerian law reports published weekly

questions.explanation: Lexis and Westlaw are electronic legal databases giving access to recent decisions and legislation from the Commonwealth, Europe and the United States. Information technology lets a computer find in seconds what a manual search might take days to find. Option B describes systems like Dewey and Library of Congress.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: An essay titled 'Constitutional Development in Nigeria' traces events in order from 1914 to the present day. Which type of essay is it most likely to be?

options.a: A narrative essay
options.b: An argumentative essay
options.c: A descriptive essay
options.d: An expository essay

questions.explanation: A narrative essay presents details about events in the order in which they occurred, so a chronological account of constitutional development from 1914 is narrative. Option B would require taking and defending a position. Option C would focus on how something looks or feels.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: A student is asked to write on 'The Abolition of the Death Penalty: To Be or Not to Be?' and must take a stand, persuade the reader and demolish the opposing arguments. This calls for:

options.a: A descriptive essay
options.b: A narrative essay
options.c: An expository essay
options.d: An argumentative essay

questions.explanation: An argumentative essay requires the writer to support or oppose a position, give reasons for his claims and demolish the arguments for the opposing view. Option C explains and clarifies without necessarily taking sides. Options B and A recount or describe.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: A good essay topic is said to possess which three attributes?

options.a: It is correct, complete and concise
options.b: It is long, technical and controversial
options.c: It is popular, foreign and historical
options.d: It is vague, broad and open-ended

questions.explanation: A good topic is correct because it gives adequate information about the subject, complete because it is clearly understandable to everyone in the field, and concise because it states the content in the shortest efficient way. Options B and D describe topics that are hard to manage.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: When rethinking a chosen topic, a writer who has difficulty raising questions on it is advised to use which words?

options.a: Correct, complete and concise
options.b: Issue, rule, application and conclusion
options.c: Introduction, definition, body and conclusion
options.d: What, who, where, when, how and why

questions.explanation: Questioning the topic with what, who, where, when, how and why throws light on it and opens up new ideas. Option C is the IDBC structure for answering essay questions, and option B is IRAC for problem questions. Option A lists the attributes of a good topic.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: A writer is deemed to have made a definite choice of thesis when it:

options.a: Avoids taking any position on the topic
options.b: Repeats the title of the essay word for word
options.c: Lists every question that can possibly be asked about the topic
options.d: Makes a restricted and organised assertion about the topic and clearly reveals the writer's attitude towards it

questions.explanation: The thesis turns the basic question into a basic answer: a restricted, organised assertion that announces the major points and the writer's attitude. Option C describes the earlier questioning stage, not the thesis. Option A is the opposite of a thesis.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: Before writing, Kunle gives his essay idea to a classmate who has researched the same topic and asks her to criticise it as ruthlessly as possible. Which test of the idea is he applying?

options.a: The writing test
options.b: The possibility test
options.c: The credibility test
options.d: The friendly colleague test

questions.explanation: The friendly colleague test involves getting someone, preferably a person who has researched the topic, to critique the idea so it is thoroughly 'sieved' before writing. Option C asks whether the idea is current and plausible. Option B asks whether the task can be completed in the time available. Option A involves trying the idea out on paper.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the preliminary tests for an essay idea?

options.a: The repugnancy test
options.b: The writing test
options.c: The credibility test
options.d: The possibility test

questions.explanation: The preliminary tests of an essay idea are the writing test, the credibility test, the friendly colleague test and the possibility test. The repugnancy test belongs to the validity of customary law, not essay writing. Options B, C and D are genuine idea tests.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: When choosing works to rely on, why may a writer still cite an old work such as Obilade's The Nigerian Legal System?

options.a: Recent journals are never relevant to legal writing
options.b: Old works are always more accurate than new ones
options.c: Some works are classics in their field and remain relevant as guideposts to the development of the law
options.d: Only works over forty years old may be cited in legal writing

questions.explanation: Some older works are classics that remain relevant despite later developments, so they can be cited for the impact they have had. Option B is wrong because currency is also vital, which is why the latest editions should be used. Option A contradicts that need for currency.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: While reading an article for her essay, Ngozi asks herself whether the writer's conclusions are justified by his evidence, whether his reasoning is faulty and whether the work will command respect when cited. She is:

options.a: Organising her reading time
options.b: Reading responsibly
options.c: Reading selectively
options.d: Reading critically

questions.explanation: Reading critically means analysing what you read: testing the writer's arguments and evidence, checking the reasoning and deciding whether the work will command respect. Option C means reading only what will be used. Option B means reading methodically and in context. Option A means scheduling your reading.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: The advice 'Don't get it right, get it written' applies to which stage of essay writing?

options.a: The first draft, where the whole paper is written without stopping to correct anything
options.b: The second draft, where omitted words and details are added
options.c: The outline, where major divisions are planned
options.d: The third draft, where repetition and verbosity are cut

questions.explanation: At the first draft the writer should get the whole paper down without stopping to correct, because until it is written there is nothing to revise. Option B adds missing words and details. Option D trims deadwood and moves the text towards a reader-oriented work.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: At which drafting stage does the writer cut off the 'dead wood' of repetition and verbosity and move from a writer-oriented draft towards a finished reader-oriented work?

options.a: The second draft
options.b: The first draft
options.c: The preliminary reading stage
options.d: The third draft

questions.explanation: The third draft trims repetition and verbosity and addresses content, organisation, logic and coherence, turning a writer-oriented draft into a reader-oriented work. Option B is for getting everything written without correction. Option A is for adding missing words and details.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: For an essay introduction to be effective, it must:

options.a: Be the longest part of the essay
options.b: Contain all the main arguments of the body
options.c: Always be written before anything else
options.d: Identify the subject, arouse interest and be brief

questions.explanation: An effective introduction identifies the subject, arouses interest and is brief; it may take the form of a question, a problem or an illustration. Option C is wrong because writing the introduction may be put off until the body is organised. Option B is a common mistake, since starting the body in the introduction loses the marks for the introduction.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: The use of the thoughts and ideas belonging to others without acknowledgement is called:

options.a: Paraphrase
options.b: Plagiarism
options.c: Citation
options.d: Brevity

questions.explanation: Plagiarism is using other people's thoughts and ideas without acknowledging them, and good legal writing must avoid it by giving credit and expressing independent views. Option C is the proper way of acknowledging another writer. Option D means saying much in few words.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: Bisi ends her essay on cybercrime by predicting what the problem may look like in Nigeria in ten years and warning of what could happen if nothing is done. Her conclusion is best described as:

options.a: A looking-ahead conclusion
options.b: A reflective conclusion
options.c: An introduction in disguise
options.d: A straightforward conclusion

questions.explanation: A looking-ahead conclusion makes a prediction or sounds a warning about what may happen to the subject in future. Option B highlights related issues and questions for further inquiry. Option D states that the work has ended and then makes suggestions and recommendations.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: Why should an essay proposing a legal solution to cultism in Nigerian universities also consider psychological, social, economic and political factors?

options.a: Because a multidimensional approach, not a strictly legal solution, is needed to put such issues in perspective
options.b: Because brevity requires ignoring the law
options.c: Because only sociologists may write about cultism
options.d: Because legal writing must never mention the law

questions.explanation: Legal writing should analyse issues in the light of social realities; a purely legal solution to cultism that ignores its psychological, social, economic and political causes would be like putting 'something on nothing'. Option D goes too far, since the legal analysis remains central.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: The acronym IDBC, used for answering law essay questions, stands for:

options.a: Introduction, Discussion, Bibliography, Citation
options.b: Issue, Definition, Basis, Case
options.c: Introduction, Definition, Body, Conclusion
options.d: Issue, Decision, Body, Conclusion

questions.explanation: IDBC is a conventional structure for law essay questions: Introduction, Definition, Body and Conclusion. Option D mixes in elements of the problem-question method. Options A and B are invented expansions.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: Law problem questions are commonly tackled using IRAC (or IPAC), which stands for:

options.a: Introduction, Reasoning, Analysis, Comment
options.b: Issue, Ratio, Authority, Case
options.c: Issue(s), Rule (or Principle), Application (or Analysis), Conclusion
options.d: Introduction, Rule, Argument, Citation

questions.explanation: In IRAC or IPAC, the answer identifies the Issue(s), states the Rule or Principle, Applies it to the facts, and reaches a Conclusion. Option D begins with Introduction, which belongs to the essay structure IDBC. Options B and A are invented expansions.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: An examination question sets out facts about a trader in Onitsha whose customary claim is challenged, and ends with 'Advise him.' Which method is most suitable for answering it?

options.a: A descriptive essay on how the trader feels
options.b: IRAC: identify the issues, state the rules, apply them to the facts, and conclude
options.c: IDBC: introduction, definition, body, conclusion
options.d: A narrative essay retelling the facts in date order

questions.explanation: A question that gives facts and asks you to advise is a problem question, best answered with IRAC (or IPAC). Option C suits essay questions; using the essay format for a problem question is like putting old wine into a new wineskin. Options D and A do not apply the law to the facts at all.

questions.topic: Legal Research and Legal Writing
questions.question: What is the common mistake many students make in the introduction to a law essay answer?

options.a: Starting the body of the essay in the introduction, instead of giving background and a thesis statement
options.b: Writing a thesis statement that tells the examiner what will be discussed
options.c: Giving a brief background analysis of the question
options.d: Beginning with an apt quotation from a scholar or a court

questions.explanation: Many students start answering the question in the introduction, so the examiner treats it as the body and no marks go to the introduction. The introduction should instead give the background and end with a thesis statement. Options B, C and D are all recommended practices, not mistakes.
